en: Preface to the Treatise on the Nature of Goodness and Evil:
The doctrine that human nature is evil is something shunned by non-Buddhist (external) scriptures.

Yet the Tiantai school proclaims that it is the inherent possession of true nature, and that the exclusive function of its spiritual efficacy constitutes the family treasure [of this tradition]. Unless one has studied these teachings, even veteran śramaṇas, upon hearing of them, will...
I covered my ears and fled.
Having read Great Master Youmen’s *Treatise on the Nature of Good and Evil*, I sighed in admiration for the profound and deep compassion of the Fourth Reliance Bodhisattva.
Why is this? We beings of this world possess the three poisons like a cluster of *akṣa* fruits; throughout vast kalpas of successive births, we have dwelt and cultivated within evil.
When we turn toward the good, errors and difficulties abound. If we forcefully suppress [the poisons], we become intoxicated by the wine of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*);

if our revulsion reaches its limit, we fall into the pit of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). This is what is meant by "error. To contemplate purity while suspended [in such states] is utterly beyond the reach of the beginner's mind. Thus it continues...

To cultivate and realize [the Way] separately requires many kalpas to achieve; this is what is meant by "arduous. When one examines the reason for this, it is truly because evil is different from good.

Were there not the Dharma-gate of the inherent nature (*xingju*), which fuses good and evil together, how could one know that the ten realms are identical in their suchness, or awaken to the fact that sentient beings are themselves Buddhas?
Everything is already perfected and manifest—how could anything be more perfectly round and sudden than this? Therefore...
Regarding those who discuss Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), they do not find it difficult to speak of its goodness, but find it difficult to speak of its inherent possession (*yujū*).

Therefore, it is said that the two masters of the Tiantai and Jingxiu schools possessed profound and deep compassion. Wujin, whose nature was defiled, reversed the intent of the *Awakening of Faith* to emphasize purity alone;

Zhiyi, whose principle was poison, expounded the discourse on the "two kinds of identity" from the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*. Although they established their school based on the doctrine of "inherent possession," their primary intention lay in the contemplation (*guan*) of the harmonious integration of evil.

Spontaneously encompassing the good, it establishes the "Wondrous Commentary" (*Miaozong*). It exposes the conditions and causes of evil, thereby surpassing other schools; thus, this secret is now revealed for the first time.
Like the wish-fulfilling gem among ocean treasures or the vessel of virtue that grants all wishes, no masters outside the [Tiantai] Mountain school can attain such excellence.

Therefore, those who discourse on the Tiantai school do not find it difficult to speak of its "completeness," but find it difficult to speak of its "pervasiveness. Thus it is said: "Since the time of the masters from Siming onwards..."
How profound and deep is his compassion! This one school that came from the West points to excrement and urine as the *dharmakāya* and demonstrates the grasping of reality within sound and form;

this accords with the teachings of the Mountain School (Tiantai). How could it exhaust the chirping of birds? Yet, regarding what lies beyond words and outside of phrases, it waits exclusively for those of superior capacity.
As for the textual treasury of the Tiantai school, its universal moisture is like rain; with such a compassionate heart and tongue, he seems only to fear that [people might not understand].
To explain this without detail is to leave its understanding unclear. In this treatise, the Great Master extensively cites collateral evidence and provides indirect proofs;
he traces the origin and examines the end, establishing arguments for clarification, adding expositions for elaboration, illustrating through concrete events, and binding them with diagrams.
Although I, whose intellect is as dull as the hub of a wheel, have long looked toward the gentlemanly way, I am still as bewildered as a dung beetle regarding the ultimate purport of these teachings.

Gazing at the vast ocean, he felt as though he had finally entered its depths upon completing his studies. Thus, those who discourse on the inherent evil of human nature do not find it difficult to speak of evil;

rather, they find it difficult to speak of it so that their words must penetrate to the very marrow of one's bones, like opening a door to behold the treasures stored within one’s home before finally ceasing.
Therefore, it is said that the Master’s compassion was profound and grave. When the treatise was completed, it stood preeminent among the Confucian scholars.

"Is it not somewhat inappropriate to use such arguments to cross-examine one another? I replied, "Indeed, indeed; no, no. The sages of the Three Teachings are identical in their discourse on nature (*xing*). Yet, Mencius alone speaks of 'endowment' (*bei*).
To speak of endowing only the good while omitting the evil—how can this be said to be universal? Throughout the *Sūtras*, it is stated everywhere that all beings are originally Buddhas.
Why, then, would the disciples of the Buddha not also speak of the goodness of nature? It is merely a matter of considering the world..."

The teachings of the secular world are strict in their prevention of evil; the teachings that transcend the world are subtle in their integration of goodness. Adapting to the times and accommodating the capacities of beings, each has its appropriate application.
Regarding the Confucian discourse on human nature: how could it be that all are inherently good? Yet, they do not deviate from nor conceal this truth. Does one possess this single nature?
Confucius spoke of "possessing" it, while Mencius spoke of it as "good. However, although Mencius spoke of it as good, Yangming of Yaojiang further stated that it is "non-existent."
Goodness is without evil, yet the study of the sages becomes ever more luminous. The Tathāgata spoke of goodness; Tiantai and Zhiyi spoke of its "endowment" (*ju*).

However, when Tiantai and Zhiyi spoke of this "endowment," the various patriarchs of Siming and the Great Master (Zhanran) further clarified that it encompasses both good and evil, whereby the Buddha-mind was fully expressed.

This single stream from the Yao River has been studied and savored by the Confucian tradition without ceasing until the present day. Now that the Master’s treatise has appeared, during this final five-hundred-year period...

As for those who are called the bridge and ferry for realizing the nature, who else could it be but this? The sages and worthies of the Three Teachings all value having virtuous descendants—indeed, they value having virtuous descendants!
They value having virtuous descendants!
Preface to the *Treatise on the Nature of Good and Evil*, written with palms joined by the Tiantai disciple, the layman Xiangguang Wang Liguo, in his Yuan-i Studio.
Those who adhere to partial emptiness deviate from the Way of governing the world; those who cling to [the mere] dependent origination are separated from the path to Nirvana. For this reason...
The objects of knowledge are like a mound of sand, and the river of views and craving is deep. To fall into views and craving is to swirl within the waves of birth and death;
to obstruct the objects of knowledge is to sink into the pit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

How could one know that from the low-lying, damp mud there constantly grows the *pundarīka* lotus that adorns the world, while one must sigh at how the high plateaus of dry land have yet to produce the *utpala* that appears in response to the times? Such is this Dharma of wondrous existence.
This is why Śākyamuni Tathāgata grasped his whisk and spoke three times over; it is why the great Bodhisattvas beat their hands in rhythmic approval and chanted in response.
Why is this? It is because when one word expresses its existence, the myriad practices thereby gain the opportunity to flourish and spread.

As for the transformative guidance exercised by the Perfected Man (zhiren), a single word of its wondrousness causes True Suchness (zhenru) to become vast and expansive, thereby severing the birth and death of ordinary beings (fanfu).
When existence is wondrous, the wonder does not exist of itself; when wonder exists, existence does not exist of itself.
Since existence does not exist of itself, throughout the years and through the passage of time, one follows the single path of purity, forgetting all conditions.
The wondrous is not wondrous of itself; thus, throughout the day, one dispels all emotional attachments, and the myriad dharmas are established in their majestic array.
Being thus, the "wondrous existence" (miao-you) is eternally identical yet not identical, eternally detached yet not detached. Why should I alone marvel at its wonder, or alone possess its existence?
This is the concise method of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Great Beings; it is truly beyond the reach of thought or deliberation.
Furthermore, if one does not acknowledge that which is non-conditioned within conditioned existence, there is no basis for establishing the fundamental tenet of the inherent nature (*xing*).

If one does not acknowledge that this inherent nature is all-pervasive rather than partial, there is no way to fully exhaust its meaning through the ten realms (*daśadhātu*). It is from this that the distinction between cultivation and nature (*xiu-xing*) arises, and it is by means of this that good and evil are differentiated.

Therefore, [the text] employs the device of interlocutors and respondent to establish its arguments based on the inherent nature of good and evil. Nevertheless, while the Way encompasses both Confucianism and Buddhism, their principles remain distinct.
The partial and the perfect each have their respective destinations; how could they possibly be treated as one and the same?

The principles of the mundane and the supramundane must be distinguished as being as far apart as heaven and earth. The tenets of the Great and Small Vehicles, and the Sudden and Gradual teachings, must stand as distinct as clouds and mud.

Furthermore, cultivation and nature are presented side by side, and the Dharma and its metaphors are reiterated. Citing events and citing persons, and corroborating through the sūtras and the śāstras, these words amount to sixty thousand.
I have recorded this with brush and ink; how could I possibly possess words of exquisite beauty?
The eight categories are arranged at the gate, set forth according to my own inclination, merely to accord with the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous nature.
I took up the pen at the beginning of the middle month of summer in the first year of the Huangming Tianqi era; the writing was completed during the final ten days of the second month of autumn.
The Lamp of the Unending Dharma,
composed by the Śramaṇa Wuxi of Mount Tiantai, respectfully wrote this preface at the Eastern Hall of the Unblinking Eye within the *Śūraṃgama* Altar.
Recorded by the lay disciple Wenlong Zhengyuan, who aspires for rebirth [in the Pure Land].
Lanling Mengze Layman Zhang Shiyi;
Chu Qi Cangru Layman Disciple Yuan Shizhen; Xiangguang Layman Disciple Wang Liguo.
Revised and collated by the lay disciple Liu Xixuan of Xincheng;
the lay disciple Guan Longzhengjian; and the lay disciple Ma Tengzhengyan.
The Discourse on the Nature of Good and Evil, Volume One Compiled by Yu Rixin,
disciple of Layman Yuan Guan; and Xu Bo Shouquan,
disciple of Layman Yuantan.
Written by the Śramaṇa Chuandeng of Youxi at Mount Tiantai.
Now, as for "nature" (xing), it is principle (li). This nature, as principle, is fundamentally neither good nor evil.

That those of past and present have established their arguments by speaking in terms of good and evil—does this not mean they are discussing nature by relying on cultivation, and naming principle by borrowing from phenomena? It is like seeking the source of an echo by following its resonance.
Sound. One seeks form by relying on its shadow. As for the principle of *xing* (nature), how could it be adequately described in terms of good or evil?
There was a guest who wore the scholar’s cap yet harbored a Buddhist mind; he passed by me at Youxi and asked:
"I have heard that in your Tiantai teachings, you always take the doctrine of the inherent evil of nature (*xing-è*) as the primary tenet. Is this so? I replied: "It is. The guest said:

Now, to love what is good and hate what is evil is the common sentiment of humanity. The sages of the Three Teachings established their teachings and arguments by honoring the worthy and loathing the unworthy;
they did so not merely as one who loves beautiful colors, fearing lest they fall short, nor like one who hates foul odors, fearing lest they have too much.
Thus, the scholars of the Tiantai school have based their doctrines upon this principle: to encompass all things within the category of the good and to instruct people accordingly.
"Is Dao'an still here? I replied: "The ultimate principle startles the mind; the ultimate words fear to be heard.

If one uses the trivial teachings of the mundane world to doubt the profound and mysterious principles that transcend the world, it will surely confuse the ears and alarm the heart—how could this be considered strange?"
Moreover, regarding the establishment of this school’s doctrine, it simply states that the single term "inherent" (*ju*) alone most clearly reveals the present school’s position.

While other masters also acknowledge the inherent nature of good, they all fail to fathom the inherent nature of evil as it is understood through conditions. How could [this school] ever have definitively spoken only of evil while omitting good?

Generally speaking, when the Tiantai school speaks of "nature" (*xing*), it maintains that both good and evil are fully present therein. When it speaks of "cultivation" (*xiu*), only then do good and evil become distinguished.
Thus, the Buddha-realm inherently present [within nature] is taken as "inherent goodness," while the nine realms inherently present are taken as "inherent evil.

The cultivation that results in the realization of the Buddha-realm is "cultivated goodness," and the cultivation that results in the realization of the nine realms is "cultivated evil. Other schools, however, know only that nature is endowed with goodness, but do not understand this.
If evil were inherent in nature (*prakṛti*), then within the Buddha-realm there would be something to be grasped and within the nine realms something to be abandoned;
thus, one could not accord with the intent of the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* regarding the non-duality of equality—namely, that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa and afflictions are themselves bodhi.

Therefore, the Perfect Principle (*yuanli*) is established to refute partial doctrines, desiring to assist those who possess the cultivated evil of the nine realms so that they need not undergo transformation or shifting, but may directly attain realization.
The nature is evil; yet this evil nature is interfused and harmonized, such that there is no dharma that does not incline toward it.

It spontaneously encompasses the Buddha-realm’s nature of goodness, serving as the wondrous gateway for directly pointing to the human mind and seeing one's nature to achieve Buddhahood. This is precisely what it means to transform things into goodness; it is the Great Way for instructing humanity.
Those who practice this teaching establish their words so as to be fearless. A guest asked again:

"Now, the doctrine that human nature is good originally derives from Mencius; the doctrine that human nature is evil originally derives from Xunzi; and the doctrine that human nature is a mixture of good and evil originally derives from Yangzi.
Yet, the teachings of your school (the Tiantai school) speak of the 'inherent inclusion' [of all phenomena] within nature, and say regarding this nature:"

The [Laozi] contains both good and evil. When it speaks of "cultivation," it distinguishes between good and evil. Is this not because it incorporates the three schools while claiming to be a superior doctrine?
I replied: "The doctrines of these three masters each speak of only one partial aspect of human nature; they are certainly not what the Gate of Sages accepts.
Nevertheless, they all speak of nature based on talent and emotion (*cai-qing*); they do not speak of nature by taking nature itself as the basis for speaking of nature."
This is so; how much more so when speaking from within the realm of human emotion and talent!
It is not that my teaching fundamentally possesses the ten dharma-realms as inherent good or inherent evil. I fear that Your Reverence’s understanding of my Way is still not yet profound.
Let me first speak briefly by way of worldly teachings, and then speak in detail and at length according to our fundamental doctrine. Broadly...

I cite scriptural evidence to elucidate this, so that you may understand how the teaching on the inherent nature of phenomena (xingju famen) is profoundly efficacious for the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) and immensely beneficial for perfect cultivation (yuanxiu).
It is like consuming milk-gruel, after which nothing else is required; it is like obtaining a mani-jewel, after which there is no need to seek anything else.

The guest asked, "How is the worldly teaching? I replied, "Observe the books composed by the Sage Confucius; he rarely spoke of human nature (*xing*). Thus, when his disciples praised their Master, they said:
'The Master's literary works (*wen-zhang*) can be heard, but his discourse on human nature and the Way of Heaven (*xing yu tian-dao*) cannot be heard.
Nevertheless, he did speak of it sparingly, saying: 'Natures are close to one another; it is through habituation that they differ.'"

This was a distant matter, yet it had never been definitively judged in terms of good and evil. It was not until his grandson Zi Si established his own theory that the subtle meaning was finally articulated, saying:
"What Heaven mandates is called nature; following one's nature is called the Way; cultivating the Way is called instruction."
It is further said: "The non-emergence of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure is called the Mean (zhong); their emergence in accordance with the proper measure is called Harmony (he).
The Master’s contemplation of this is the Mean; is this not what is called 'nature' as mandated by Heaven? And Harmony is not what is called 'the Way' through the following of nature?
When it comes to discussing the Way of following nature, it is simply said: "Even the ignorance of husband and wife can participate in its knowledge," and so forth.
Regarding its ultimate reach: even the sages have things they do not know. Yet, as for its basic application, even those who are inferior, such as husband and wife, can practice it.
Regarding its ultimate reach: even the sages have things they cannot accomplish.
Thus, the Way of the sages begins with what husband and wife can understand, while it culminates in what even the sages cannot know.
It begins with what can be practiced by ordinary husbands and wives, yet reaches the heights that even the sages cannot fathom;
thus, there is nothing in the world that cannot be learned. It reaches the limits of what even the sages cannot know;
thus, the student never knows where their learning will end. When it is thus, then compassion (*cèyǐn*) is sufficient for benevolence (*rén*), yet benevolence does not stop there.
Compassion and shame are sufficient to constitute righteousness (*yi*), yet righteousness does not stop at shame alone.

Such is the manner in which the principle of the inherent goodness of human nature (*xing shan*) was hidden and then brought forth; it has never been determined by means of a dichotomy between good and evil.
The various and confused debates concerning good and evil in later generations actually began with Mencius, yet Mencius’s statements that human nature is good were all—
These emerged from the writings of his teacher, Zisi. The writings of Zisi consist entirely of the subtle words and earnest discourses of the Sage Confucius.
Mencius obtained them but did not make good use of them; he was able to speak of the Way, yet he did not understand the names and principles by which those words were formulated.
Taking the vastness of the world as his basis, he insisted upon the doctrine of the inherent goodness of human nature, regarding it with such clarity that he considered it self-evident.
Throughout the world, every passerby would wish to draw his bow and shoot him.
Thus, after Mencius had already declared that human nature is good, Xunzi, wishing to advance a divergent theory, could not help but declare that human nature is evil;
he claimed that the nature of Jie and Zhou was such, while Yao and Shun were merely hypocrites. He further stated that it was Zi Si and Meng Ke who brought disorder to the world.
I suspect that as a person he must have been stubborn, headstrong, and insolent, overestimating his own worth;

thus, he delighted in propounding eccentric views without yielding and dared to offer lofty discourses without regard for consequences. While Xun Qing had already declared that human nature is evil, Yang Xiong possessed both these traits and more, asserting:
"Human nature is a mixture of good and evil; cultivate the good and one becomes a good person."
To cultivate evil is to become an evil person. Now, when discussing human nature as being a mixture of good and evil, one has already come close to the truth.
If it is said that all people can become Yao or Shun, does this not mean that by cultivating goodness, one becomes a good person?
Yet why may one not also say that all people can become Jie or Zhou, for is this not the case when they cultivate evil and become evil persons? Thus speaks the critic.
This means that Yangzi did not understand it. Now, good and evil are what the nature is capable of doing, but they are not what the nature is inherently possessed of.
Furthermore, when speaking of the nature, how can one define it as being good or evil?
Since Yangzi already held that good and evil are mixed, Han Yu further took the doctrines of these three masters and refuted them by appealing to Confucius.

In your discourse, you distinguish natures into three categories, stating: "The person of middle capacity can move toward either the superior or the inferior, whereas those of superior wisdom and the lowest folly do not change.
You maintain that these three types all emerge from the middle while excluding the superior and the inferior.

If the person of middle capacity can move toward the superior, is this not Mencius’s doctrine of the goodness of human nature? If they can move toward the inferior, is this not Xunzi’s doctrine of the evil of human nature?

Is it not so? [Yangzi] held that "the nature is a mixture of good and evil," yet he omitted the point that those of superior intelligence are fixed in goodness and those of inferior stupidity do not migrate to evil.
By separating nature into three categories, he established a doctrine of transcendence and superiority.
He did not realize that when the Master said the "average person can rise or fall," this did not apply to those of superior intelligence or inferior stupidity.
"To shift" refers to discussing the *cai* (talent or manifestation), not the *xing* (nature). Furthermore, this is not merely my own opinion;
if one were to take all people throughout ancient and modern times and examine their discourse on nature, they would all speak of it by way of its manifestations (*fang*).
Consequently, there has been much clamor and no single consensus. Mǎn Yù’s argument does not stop at this alone; it even goes so far as to separate nature from its manifestations.

If one combines the capacities (*cai*) to constitute *xing* (nature) and separates *xing* to constitute *qing* (emotion), then the afflictions of hunger and cold and the desires of male and female are all *qing*, not *xing*.
If *qing* is distinct from *xing*, then that which is tranquil and non-active must be taken as *xing*.
Yet, whenever Han Yu took the refutation of Buddhism and Daoism as his own mission, even when speaking of *xing*, he did not... [The text continues].
They fail to realize this and fall into the discourse of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) within our own teaching; therefore, their treatises ultimately remain unable to achieve thorough penetration.
This is because the Confucian account of human nature differs from that of our Buddhist teaching. Since they have already spoken of good and evil, what they call "sentiment" (qíng) is as follows:
This is what the Confucians call "nature. If the sage lacked this, there would be no basis for him to be a sage;
if the petty person lacked this, there would be no basis for them to be evil.

The sage employs these seven—joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, hate, and desire—to guide himself toward goodness; the petty person employs these same seven to guide themselves toward evil. Is this not goodness?

Is it that evil is something the nature can do, rather than something the nature can possess? Having once examined the discourse established in the world, there are those who delight in private theories;

they invent heterodox arguments, striving solely to surpass others while completely disregarding their own points of defeat—this is precisely what Xunzi first proposed regarding the "evil nature. There are also those who take pleasure in public discourse...

As for this, the arguments of later proponents must necessarily surpass those of their predecessors. For instance, once Mencius had already asserted that human nature is good, Xunzi then declared it to be evil;
consequently, Yangzi could not help but synthesize the views of these two masters, stating that "human nature is a mixture of good and evil.
As for Hanzi (Han Yu), he did nothing more than take the surplus left over from Yangzi and strike a compromise between them.

The perfected words of the Sages distinguish nature (*xing*) into three categories. Although they sought to surpass one another, they did not realize that their error lay in treating "separation" as an emotional state and "conjunction" as the essence of nature.
One must understand that among the four philosophers, only Yangzi’s assertion that human nature is a mixture of good and evil accords with reason.
This is because the discourse on good and evil involves both nature and cultivation; it pertains to the state before nature has yet taken form.

It is certainly not appropriate to judge [the nature] solely by means of good and evil. If one observes the nature through its cultivation, who could claim that there is a "functioning without substance" distinct from the cultivation of the nature?
Therefore, when discussing the nature based on cultivation—since cultivation already possesses both good and evil—how could the nature possibly be devoid of them?
However, regarding cultivation, one must discuss three principles: namely, capacity (*cai*), wisdom (*zhi*), and emotion (*qing*). If...
The Master’s words regarding those of middle capacity being capable of ascending or descending refer to the discussion of human talent:
that one may become a Yao or a Shun, or one may become a Jie or a Zhou. If it were said that all people can become Yao or Shun, and that they actually do so, then they would be the virtuous and wise;
this would simply mean they have cultivated goodness. If goodness were not inherently possessed by their nature, how could they be able to do so?

Why is this so? It is because it is clear that the nature is endowed with goodness. If one were to say that all people can become Jie or Zhou and indeed do so, this is merely the sentiment of the ignorant;
it refers to cultivated evil. If the nature did not inherently possess evil, how could one be capable of it, and for what reason would one do so?
Thus, it is also clear that the nature is endowed with evil. Even the sages have never... [The text ends here.]
One must speak clearly of both good and evil. As for Zisi, he had indeed once initiated the fundamental principles of this meaning in the *Zhongyong*.
He said: "When joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have not yet been aroused, it is called the Central (zhong). Does this not refer to one's nature?
When they are aroused and all hit the mark of moderation, it is called Harmony (he). Does this not refer to goodness? Although he did not explicitly mention evil, could one not say [the following]?"
"To express emotions that do not accord with the proper measure is called disharmony; does this not signify their wickedness? Furthermore, it is said:

'The superior man's practice of the Mean is that he is a superior man who acts according to the timeliness of the Mean. The petty man's practice of the Mean is that he is a petty man who lacks all restraint.
Acting according to the timeliness of the Mean is good; lacking restraint is evil. Now, whether the harmony or disharmony of joy and anger—none [is fixed]..."
If they do not arise from an inherent nature, could it not be that good and evil are fundamentally possessed by nature?
It is only because the sages lament that human nature does not fully possess goodness that one can become a Yao or a Shun, a sage, a worthy, or a gentleman.
For this reason, the sages repeatedly established teachings to encourage and exhort them.

Fearing that human nature, though inherently complete, could lead one to become a Jie or a Zhou, an ordinary person, a base fool, or a petty man, they repeatedly established teachings to punish and warn them.
Thus, regarding the *Shi* and the *Chunqiu*, the Master’s intent from beginning to end was fundamentally [to achieve this].
In conclusion, each of these has its own systematic order. Why is it that the very foundation of the King’s transformation of the people begins with what is easiest to practice throughout the world?
It is because the world naturally knows there are fathers and sons; when father and son do not harm one another, this is sufficient for filial piety (*xiao*).

The world naturally knows there are elder and younger brothers; when brothers do not encroach upon one another, this is sufficient for fraternal respect (*ti*). When filial piety and fraternal respect are sufficient—
Thus, the Way of the King is complete. This is certainly not something profound and difficult to perceive, nor is it something arduous and difficult to practice.

Therefore, the teaching of the *Shi* (Odes) causes people to sing and dance in pleasure and joy, reaching every possible extent; its essential requirement is simply that one does not lose what is correct.
Nevertheless, the Master (Confucius) had indeed that which he feared most: a single lapse in deportment is the source from which ritual propriety (*li*) declines.

[This section is omitted. (If one loses a single word, the underlying principle is thereby lost. When rulers and ministers encroach upon one another, and those above and below destroy each other, the great chaos of the world has never failed to begin with this way. For this reason, the *Spring and Autumn Annals* strives for precision within the space of a hair’s breadth.)

Yet he profoundly understood the fine line between what appears similar but is actually distinct, and was resolute in his determination regarding that which absolutely must not be done. This is the general outline of the Master’s teaching on encouraging the good and punishing the evil. Thus, it follows that Mencius was one who had a deep mastery of the *Shi* and the *Chunqiu*.

It may be appropriate to clarify the transmission of the ancestral lineage of the Way and to diligently teach people to do good; however, it is not permissible, when discussing human nature, to insist upon the doctrine of the inherent goodness of nature for such a vast multitude of people across the world.

Furthermore, the Song Confucian Zhang Hengchu stated that there is "the nature of Heaven and Earth" (*tiāndì zhī xìng*) and "the nature of physical constitution" (*qìzhì zhī xìng*). He claimed that the nature of Heaven and Earth is inherently good and devoid of evil, whereas the nature of physical constitution possesses both good and evil.

His intention was to suggest that when Mencius spoke of the inherent goodness of nature, he was referring exclusively to the nature of Heaven and Earth, while when other philosophers spoke of the mixture of good and evil, they were referring to the nature of physical constitution. I maintain, however, that the meaning of "nature" (*xìng*) lies in its unchanging essence; how could there be a separate "nature of Heaven and Earth" [distinct from the nature of physical constitution]?

"The nature of qi and temperament is indeed different. Furthermore, humans receive the five elements of heaven and earth to form their bodies, and the nature of heaven and earth is likewise bestowed upon them. Thus, heaven and earth constitute the substance (*ti*), while qi and temperament constitute the function (*yong*).

There must be substance before there can be function; how could there be substance alone without its corresponding function? Based on this, the words of Zhang Zai (Hengqu) are also not correct. The guest said:
"I have already heard your brief discourse on the worldly teaching regarding human nature. As for the supramundane teaching, what distinctions does it make regarding nature?"

"What is the meaning of this? I replied: "In our teaching, those who discuss its distinctions maintain that Śākyamuni Tathāgata preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, which are categorized into five periods and eight teachings:
first, the period of the Avataṃsaka; second, the period of the Āgamas; third, the period of the Vaipulya."

The four [periods] are: first, the time of the *Prajñāpāramitā*; second, the time of the *Avataṃsaka*; third, the time of the *Nirvāṇa*; fourth, the time of the *Saṃdhinirmocana*; fifth, the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; and sixth, the time of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*. Regarding the eight teachings: first, the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*);

second, the Gradual Teaching (*jian-jiao*); third, the Secret Teaching (*mimi-jiao*); and fourth, the Indeterminate Teaching (*buding-jiao*). These four teachings are called the "Modes of Transformation" (*huayi*), which are like worldly medical prescriptions.

First, the Tripitaka Teaching (*zangjiao*); second, the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*); third, the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*); and fourth, the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). These four teachings are called the "Dharma of Transformation" (*huafa*), which are like... [the ingredients of the medicine].

Discerning the flavors of the teachings: the four teachings of the manifested images have no distinct substantial nature or characteristics; rather, they take the four teachings of the manifested dharma as their characteristics.
At present, I have not had the leisure to discern these four teachings of the manifested images in detail;

instead, I shall clarify whether the nature is endowed with or devoid of good and evil by means of the four teachings of the manifested dharma as taught during the five periods. First, regarding the period of the *Avataṃsaka*: at this time...

In elucidating the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) by incorporating the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), although the latter fully clarifies the ten realms (daśadhātu), when speaking of the inherent nature (xingju), it speaks only of possessing the goodness of the Buddha-realm and not possessing the evil of the nine realms.

This is because the True Suchness-Buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha-buddhadhātu) as clarified therein is like the moon beyond the clouds, transcending the two extremes; one must first sever the evil of the nine realms before the Buddha-nature can be manifested.

Regarding the goodness of the realms (*dhātu*): if one correctly explains the complete teaching of the *Sūtras*, it clearly elucidates that all ten realms are inherently possessed (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*).
The nine realms inherently possessed are termed "inherent evil" (*prakṛti-pāpa*); the Buddha-realm inherently possessed is termed "inherent goodness" (*prakṛti-kuśala*).

The nine realms accomplished through cultivation are termed "cultivated evil" (*bhāvanā-pāpa*); the Buddha-realm accomplished through cultivation is termed "cultivated goodness" (*bhāvanā-kuśala*). Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* translated during the Jin dynasty states:
It can follow conditions of defilement and purity, thereby dividing into the ten dharma-realms. It is further said: "The mind is like a skilled painter, creating the various five aggregates;
within all worlds, there is nothing that is not created by the mind. As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha; as it is with the Buddha, so it is with sentient beings.
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. It is further said: "If a person wishes to thoroughly understand the three..."
All Buddhas of the world should contemplate the nature of the *dharmadhātu*; all things are created solely by the mind.

During the second period of the *Āgamas*, specifically the three weeks [following his enlightenment], after the sudden teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*, the Tathāgata cast off his precious and majestic *sāmbhogakāya* robes and donned the tattered, soiled garments of the six-foot [form].
For twelve years thereafter, he preached the four *Āgama* sūtras, which is known as the beginning of the gradual teaching; he taught only this.

Regarding the teachings of the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna: although these teachings include Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, if one examines what they realize, they merely destroy the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*) and realize the principle of partial emptiness, which is identical to that of the Two Vehicles.
This, then, involves the elimination of the dharma-realm of the three realms and the six classes of ordinary beings.
One departs from outside the three realms and enters only the quiescent extinction of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. The realms consist of only eight; these merely discuss constructed [realms].

How could they discuss the ten realms as being intrinsically complete? During the period of the Third [Vehicle], the Perfect and Equal, within the eight years following the twelve years [of the second period], he preached various Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Vimalakīrti*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, *Śūraṃgama*, and *Awakening of Faith*. At that time, he criticized the partial and rejected...
Small indeed, yet greatly praising the Perfect [Teaching]. It universally moistens the three faculties and discusses the four teachings in tandem.

At this time, the Buddha most thoroughly and fully expounded the dharma-gates of the inherent nature (xingju) and the inherent evil of nature (xing'e). As the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "Birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa;
afflictions are themselves bodhi. It further states: "The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and all the sense-faculties are all the Pure Land. Furthermore...
It is said: "Those who possess overweening pride (*adhimāna*) claim that freedom from lust, anger, and delusion is called liberation;
those without overweening pride hold that lust, anger, and delusion are themselves liberation. It is further said: "The sixty-two views constitute the lineage of the Tathāgata.
The *Caryā-apagata-sūtra* states: "Lust itself is the Way; so too are anger and delusion. Within these three dharmas, all Buddhas are fully present."

Regarding the Dharma, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome. This principle is scattered throughout the Vaipulya scriptures, not merely in these instances.

As for the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* (*Léngyán jīng*), they further elucidate the doctrine that good and evil are intrinsically possessed within the nature.
All such sutras that specifically discuss this intrinsic possession of nature belong to the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuántùn zhèjiào*). If...

Those who do not reach this level are merely those for whom the Vaipulya Perfect Teaching (the *yuanjiao*) serves as the counterpart to the *zang* and *tong* [teachings], as well as the counterpart to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).
During the fourth period, that of Prajñā, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* were preached for twenty-two years.

It is argued that during this time, the water of the wisdom of emptiness was used to wash away the attachments of the three vehicles; thus, it seems that the inherent nature (*xingju*) was not discussed. If one says that the *Prajñā* [teachings] discuss...
The eighty dharma-gates are fully manifested within emptiness. This is precisely using true emptiness to shatter deluded attachments while not destroying the dharmas;

thus, at that time, it incorporates both the Shared and Distinct teachings while correctly expounding the Perfect Teaching. It takes the inherent presence of all phenomena (*xingju*) as its primary principle.

Fifth is the period of the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. During this time, the preaching of the *Lotus Sūtra* lasted for eight years, while the preaching of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* lasted for only a single day.
At midnight, these two sutras were combined to form the Dharma of the fifth period.

As for the *Lotus Sūtra*, it is the time when the Tathāgata spoke of the inherent completeness of nature (*xingju*), the ultimate culmination where all is perfected and gathered together. Indeed, during the first four periods, the Tathāgata established provisional teachings based on the real;
he did so by employing the three provisional means for those who lack [the realization of] this single reality-path of the inherent completeness of nature. Upon reaching the *Lotus*...

"Opening the provisional to reveal the real" means opening up the provisional teachings that were incomplete across the four previous periods and three vehicles, in order to reveal the real, perfect, and complete teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
"Abolishing the provisional to establish the real" means abolishing the provisional teachings that were incomplete across the four previous periods and three vehicles.
This is because it establishes the reality of the perfected fruit within the Lotus Sūtra. This is true for all three dharmas of the Essential Gate (Honmon).
Therefore, at the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter, after the Tathāgata has emerged from samādhi, he praises the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real, saying:
"The wisdom of the Buddhas is exceedingly profound and immeasurable; its gateway is difficult to understand and difficult to enter. Yet, in the subsequent text, it says: "Only the Buddha and..."
The Buddha is indeed able to exhaustively investigate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
That is to say, all phenomena possess such characteristics, such natures, such essences, such powers, such functions, such causes, such conditions, such fruits, and such retributions;
they are equal from beginning to end in these ten aspects. It is precisely because the phenomena of the ten dharma-realms and their ten "suchnesses" are all...

Regarding the true aspect (*dharmatā*): only Buddhas, in communion with other Buddhas, possess the ultimate perfection of both provisional and real wisdom, and are thus able to exhaustively fathom the reality of the true aspect and the provisionality of all phenomena.

Therefore, the sutras reveal the provisional [path] for humans and devas, stating that even "a single bow of the head, a single joining of palms, a single snap of the fingers, or a single scattering of flowers" leads to the attainment of the Buddha-way. They also reveal the provisional [path] for *śrāvakas*, stating that... [the sound] of the *śrāvaka*...
Having heard this Dharma, the net of doubt has been entirely removed. The twelve hundred arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas.
The śrāvakas, having attained understanding, said: "We are now truly śrāvakas; by means of the sound of the Buddha-way, we cause all to hear."
"We are now true Arhats; among all these beings, we should receive offerings.
As for the prophecy given to Devadatta and the Dragon Girl’s attainment of Buddhahood, was this not to reveal the provisional nature of the nine realms to manifest the reality of the Buddha-realm?
Or was it to reveal the cultivation of goodness to ultimately reach the nature of goodness, or to reveal the cultivation of evil to ultimately reach the nature of evil? Only the Buddha [knows]."
Only with the Buddha can one exhaustively fathom this; does it not lie herein? As for *nirvāṇa*, he speaks exclusively of the inherent evil of nature (*xing-è*).
Thus he says: "Both the icchantika and the virtuous person both possess Buddha-nature; these are termed the 'causes and conditions of good and evil.

This is fully contained in that section [of the sutra], though I cannot cite it in its entirety here. Therefore, if one wishes to clarify the single great cause and condition for the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world, if—
If one does not understand the principle that nature is inherently endowed with both good and evil, it is like wandering at night without eyes;
how then could one point directly to the human mind, and how could one see one's nature and attain Buddhahood?

If it were not for the Tiantai school’s teachings and contemplation which elucidated this principle, the doctrine of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching would have nearly perished. Master Huizhe of Huxi said: "The single character 'endowed' (ju) alone..."

This clarifies our own school’s tenet: that while other masters also recognize the inherent presence of good, they do not comprehend the inherent presence of evil, which others cannot fathom—this is precisely what is meant.

Therefore, those who wish to engage in the Tathāgata’s Perfect and Sudden Dharma-gate must know and must study the Way of inherent presence. Likewise, those who propagate this Way must likewise [do so].
I shall lecture, yet it must be explained extensively. Therefore, I now address Your Majesty by establishing eight major sections to elucidate this:
first, the gate of True Suchness remaining unchanging while the ten realms lie latent; second, the gate of True Suchness following conditions while the ten realms manifest their distinctions.

1. The gate of the three unchanging [natures] following conditions, being without difference yet appearing as different; 2. The gate of following conditions while remaining unchanging, being different yet without difference;
3. The gate of the causal mind being inherently complete, lacking nothing whatsoever; 4. The gate of the fruition stage being interpenetrating and harmonious, with not a single thing altered.
7. The Gate of Cultivating the Full Perfection According to Purity Abiding in the Nature; 8. The Gate of Raising One to Encompass All According to the Full Realization of Purity.
A guest asked: "What is meant by the Gate of True Suchness Remaining Unchanging While the Ten Realms Latently Reside? I replied: "This treatise concerns all Buddhas and sentient beings.
Since the beginningless kalpas prior to the arising of the conscious mind, the wondrous mind of True Suchness has never shifted."
It is unchanging, pure, vast, eternally abiding, and firm. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* calls it the "one true dharma-realm" (*eka-dharmadhātu*) or the "pure dharma-body" (*viśuddha-dharmakāya*).

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* calls it the "true reality of all phenomena" (*sarvadharma-bhūtatathatā*). The *Mahāśrī-mahāyāna-paripūrṇabodhicitta-uttaratantra-sūtra* (or *Awakening of Faith*) calls it the "great *dhāraṇī* gate."
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* refers to it as the "primordially pure essence of bodhi and nirvāṇa.

It is also called the "empty tathāgatagarbha," the "amala-vijñāna," "true suchness" (*tathatā*), "buddha-nature," and the "great perfect mirror wisdom. The *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda Śāstra* calls it "original enlightenment" (*mūla-bodhi*). The treatise states:
What is called the meaning of "awakening" (bodhi) refers to the essence of mind being free from thought. This state of being free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space;

it pervades everywhere without exception and eternally abides in a single mark. This is precisely the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding Dharma-body. Based on this Dharma-body, it is termed "original awakening" (mūla-bodhi).
Furthermore, this nature of original awakening fully possesses the ten realms, the five aggregates as substantial dharmas, the lands of dependent retribution, and the ten realms.

It is a provisional name (*prajñapti*), entirely without deficiency. Furthermore, it is fully endowed with the three causes of Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*): first, the direct cause (*samyak-hetu*), which is the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);

second, the revealing cause (*parijñā-hetu*), which is the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*); and third, the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), which is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*). Nirvāṇa is thus called the three causes of Buddha-nature.
Regarding the direct cause, the Dharma-body, one takes its meaning of vertically exhausting the past and horizontally pervading all things. Regarding the revealing cause, wisdom, one takes its...
The meaning of "illumination of the substance" refers to liberation through conditions.

Taking the sense of being pure and untainted, this fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), although it possesses the ten realms of both the environment and its inhabitants, remains hidden within the single nature because it has not yet followed conditions; thus, it has never been manifest.
Speaking in terms of the ten realms of the environment and retribution that are inherently complete, this is what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* refers to as "the true emptiness of the nature of form."
The true form of the emptiness of nature—water, fire, wind, and space—is all like this. It is primordially pure and pervades the entire dharma-realm;

this is what is meant. Speaking in terms of the primary retributions of the ten realms inherently possessed, it is what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* refers to as "the nature of seeing and the luminosity of awareness."
It is the awakening to the luminous clarity of seeing; it is the nature of consciousness being luminously aware; it is the awakening to the luminosity of true consciousness.
There is nothing that is not originally pure and pervading the entire dharma-realm. The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "Good son, these bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age..."
Having realized all illusions and extinguished their reflected images, one then attains directionless purity.
Because the awakened mind is fully manifest and its luminosity is perfected, it reveals the purity of the mind; because the mind is pure, the objects of the senses are seen to be pure.
Because vision is pure, the eye faculty is pure. Because the faculty is pure, eye-consciousness is pure.
Because consciousness is pure, the intervening dust is pure. Because the intervening dust is pure, the ear faculty is pure. Because the faculty is pure, ear-consciousness is pure.
Because consciousness is pure, the objects of cognition are pure. It is the same for the nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Good son, because the sense organs are pure, the objects of form are pure; because form is pure, the object of sound is pure.
It is the same for odor, flavor, touch, and mental phenomena. Good son, because the six objects are pure, the great earth is pure. The earth...
Because the water element is pure, it is greatly purified; the fire element and the wind element are likewise so.
Son of good family, because the four great elements are pure, the twelve bases, the eighteen realms, and the twenty-five states of existence are pure.
Because those are pure, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are pure.
The dharmas are pure. In this manner, up to and including the eighty-four thousand dharani-doors, all are pure.
Good son, because the nature of all true marks is pure, the single body is pure; because the single body is pure, many bodies are pure;
because many bodies are pure, in this manner, up to and including all sentient beings in the ten directions, they are pure in perfect enlightenment.
Good son, because one world is pure, many worlds are pure;
because many worlds are pure, this extends even to the end of space, encompassing the three periods of time—all are equally pure and immovable.
"Good son, just as space is thus equal and immovable, you should know that the nature of awakening is equal and immovable.
Because the four great elements are immovable, you should know that the nature of awakening is equal and immovable.
In this way, up to and including the eighty-four thousand dharani-doors being equal and immovable, you should know that the nature of awakening is equal and immovable. Good son, awakening..."
Because their nature is all-pervasive, pure, immovable, perfect, and boundless, you should know that the six sense organs pervade the Dharma-realm.

Because the sense organs are all-pervasive, you should know that the six sense objects pervade the Dharma-realm. Because the sense objects are all-pervasive, you should know that the four great elements pervade the Dharma-realm.
In this manner, it extends even to the gateways of dhāraṇī pervading the Dharma-realm. Good son, because of that—
Because the wondrous enlightened nature is all-pervasive, the nature of the faculties and the nature of the objects are neither destroyed nor mixed.

Since the faculties and objects are neither destroyed nor mixed, this extends even to the gates of *dhāraṇī*, which are likewise neither destroyed nor mixed. It is like the light of hundreds of thousands of lamps illuminating a single room;
that light is all-pervasive, neither destroyed nor mixed. This also clarifies that sentient beings inherently possess the wondrous nature of perfect enlightenment, endowed with the ten [perfections].
Because one plants the seeds within the dharma-realm, one reaches the fruit and realizes all illusions, extinguishing the images within the phenomena of the ten realms.

This causes the ten realms to be possessed of their inherent nature, such that there is nothing that is not pure, immovable, and all-pervading; this is because True Suchness possesses the three virtues of unchanging nature.
Thus, the ten realms are the three causes, and the three causes are the ten realms. Although they are thus mutually identical, [they remain distinct].
Yet there is a distinction between the nature of goodness and the nature of evil. Originally possessing the three causes of the nine realms is called "nature-evil" (*xing-è*);
originally possessing the three causes of the Buddha-realm is called "nature-good" (*xing-shàn*).

Since these three causes of good and evil within the ten realms reside within a single nature, they are utterly distinct when approached directly, yet eternally united when analyzed. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* refers to this as "containing [all things] within a single atom."

The *Daban niepan jing* (Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra) states that the *Śūraṅgama* [Samādhi] is like pounding ten thousand kinds of incense into pellets; if one burns even a single particle, it fully possesses the fragrance of all.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that those who enter this room perceive only the fragrance of the merits of all Buddhas.
The *Mahāsannipāta* Sūtra likens this to a person entering the ocean to bathe after having already used the waters of all the rivers; this is precisely its meaning.
Fearing that this meaning may not yet be fully understood, I have further provided a diagram to enable those who read this book to contemplate the image and thereby grasp the underlying principle.

A guest asked: "What is meant by the gate of the differentiation of the ten realms through true suchness following conditions? I replied:

"In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* cited previously, it was stated that [the mind] 'is able to follow defiled and pure conditions to fully create the ten dharma-realms. This is precisely because the essence of the dharma-realm is perfectly interfused."
The nature of the unchanging True Suchness (tathatā) is like that of a gentleman who is not limited to a single vessel; it is capable of both good and evil.
This is the essential point of the sudden teaching’s path of non-effort (anabhoga-mārga), established entirely upon this single character "capable.

If one follows the Buddha-nature of the "Middle" (buton) as the primary tenet of the Separate Teaching (biejiao), it possesses only good and does not possess evil; thus, in the scriptural texts, it is treated as being exclusively good.
Regarding such matters, some may indeed be capable; yet, when it comes to military strategy and the affairs of warfare, they are not so capable.

How then can one be considered a man of accomplished virtue who possesses every talent without exception and masters every art? As for what is clarified by the principles of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching:
since the unchanging essence of True Suchness already possesses the natures of the ten realms—both good and evil—it has not yet followed conditions.
At that time, it remains fundamentally unchanged; yet, when following conditions, it manifests the functions of the ten realms—both defiled and pure.
That is to say, it can follow defiled conditions to create the nine dharma-realms, and follow pure conditions to create the Buddha-dharma-realm.

Since these ten dharma-realms are both inherently possessed and active functions, they merely manifest one's own inherent capacity; what fault could there be? This is not comparable to the case of a person who is purely good by nature.
All evil deeds are fundamentally beyond one's capacity; it is only when coerced by wicked people that one is forced to commit evil.

Fearing that both one's reputation and virtue will be lost, one feels such shame and remorse that there is no place to hide—this constitutes a transgression. Nevertheless, this single category should be divided into cause and effect.

One must first discuss the cause before practicing, and the effect before experiencing retribution. Regarding the cause for practice, there are further two types: first, the mere arising of a thought is termed "creating" [the act].
The second is "construction," which refers to "creation. Regarding the creation of arising thoughts: it is like the daily lives of worldly people, where the sense organs and their objects correspond;

whenever a single thought arises, it necessarily belongs to one realm. The arising of one realm is called "phenomenal creation" (*shijiao*), while the nine realms remaining latent are "inherently possessed" (*lizhi*).

Because they remain latent, they do not exist [as manifest phenomena]; because they arise in the present, they are not non-existent. Since they are fully created yet inherently possessed, they do not exist [as separate entities].

Yet it is eternally present; it is created as something fully complete. Therefore, it is not non-existent, yet it is eternally non-existent. It is neither existent nor non-existent, and thus the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is revealed.

Consequently, for one who skillfully contemplates a single thought-moment, the three types of wisdom are attained within a single mind. Second, "construction" (*nirmāṇa*) refers to that which is called "creation" (*kṛti*).
Based on this single thought arising from suchness, it gradually increases and constructs the two causes of defilement and purity;
because it constitutes the nature of karma, it manifests or remains latent, as explained above. Therefore, one who is able to skillfully contemplate the single mind as the realm [of reality]—
The three types of wisdom are also attained within a single moment of mind. Regarding the discussion of the fruition as karmic retribution, this is analyzed according to the three periods of time:
if the cause currently being cultivated is in the past, then the fruit of retribution is in the present;

if the cause currently being cultivated is in the present, then the fruit of retribution is in the future. Furthermore, regarding the cause currently being cultivated, there are cases where it is transformed and cases where it is not. As for the retribution...

The fruits [of karma] are either determinate or indeterminate. If they are transformed, they are indeterminate; if they are not transformed, they are determinate. For example, if a single thought of greed arises, it becomes a cause for rebirth in hell.

However, if one can rectify prior errors through shame and remorseful repentance, that karma may be transformed into a human or celestial rebirth, or even into one of the four noble stages of holiness.
This depends on the differences in one's application of mind and diligent practice. Below, a diagram shall be provided to clarify this in detail.

Regarding the first [point], the "Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*), the *Fajie tu shuo* (Explanation of the Diagram of the Dharma-realm) by Master Ciyun states:

"If a person, through reading the *Pūrṇa-sūtra* and hearing the teachings of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), gives rise to pure faith and believes that the nature of the three paths within their own single thought-moment is itself the nature of the three virtues:
the path of suffering is the *dharmakāya*, afflictions are *prajñā*, and karmic fetters are liberation."
Liberation. The Dharma-body is ultimate; Prajñā is pure; liberation is sovereign. The ultimate of one is the ultimate of all;
the ultimate of Prajñā and liberation is likewise ultimate. The purity of one is the purity of all;

the purity of the Dharma-body and liberation is likewise pure. The sovereignty of one is the sovereignty of all; the sovereignty of the Dharma-body and Prajñā is likewise sovereign. Thus, they are three while being one. Thus...
Three yet one; neither vertical nor horizontal, nor identical nor different. The Dharma-body is eternally abiding, and all else is likewise eternally abiding.
Bliss, self, and purity are also thus. This is the secret treasury of the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, which pervades all places.
All dharmas are entirely the Buddha-dharma. Having already believed this, bind the mind to the object, and bind the object to the mind. Mind...
If the objects of perception continue in an uninterrupted succession from moment to moment, one will inevitably perceive the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

Even if one has not yet attained realization, one should rely upon the four truths of non-action based on the single reality and give rise to the four great vows. Within that which is sought for nothing, I therefore seek it. Relying on the aforementioned path of suffering is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*);

there, one should give rise to the first vow: "May those who have not crossed over be caused to cross over. Afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma are the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); there, one should give rise to the [second vow].
The Vow: To cause those who have not attained understanding to attain understanding—suffering is identical to the Dharma-body; this is the Truth of Cessation. To make one vow:

To cause those who have not attained *nirvāṇa* to attain *nirvāṇa*—afflictions are identical to Bodhi; this is the Truth of the Path. To make one vow: To cause those who have not attained peace to attain peace.
If the Four Great Vows do not enter [the mind], one should skillfully settle the mind through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Such is the sequence.

By fully cultivating ten dharmas, one will certainly enter the five stages (*pañca-vasthā*), the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), and the stage of partial realization; this is called the Buddha-dharmadhātu.

The commentary states: If we consider the Buddha-dharmadhātu in terms of the causes being cultivated—whether they are evolving or not—and the fruits of retribution—whether they are determinate or indeterminate—the fruit of Buddhahood is the ultimate three bodies (*trikāya*).
Therefore, it is exclusively determinate and possesses no quality of indeterminacy. If [it were] merely...
Regarding the causes for its cultivation: within these two types [of causes], it is precisely through the manifestation of the Buddha-realm that the nine realms remain in latent dormancy.
Within this single nature, depending on the varying strength of external conditioning factors (*pariṣkāra*), there is a distinction as follows:

when one first gives rise to the mind of the Buddha-realm, this is termed "creating [the cause] while abiding as an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana*) or being among those of "indeterminate destiny" (*aniyata-rāśi*). Among these human categories, there are two grades. The first is: if a person gives rise to the mind of the Buddha-realm...
Thus it is. Their resolve is firm and steadfast; every thought-moment dwells upon the Way. Once entered, they enter forever; herein there is no further regression.
Second, although such a person has initially resolved their mind to seek Buddhahood, their aspiration is not firm and their great vows are not steadfast.

Should they encounter adverse conditions, they may regress to the partial vehicles; or should they encounter favorable conditions, they may immediately give rise to mundane thoughts regarding the realms of humans and devas.
The Way involves drifting along with external conditions; one falls into the three miserable realms and the evil paths when encountering circumstances.

Since it is thus with the creation of a single thought, so too is it with the cultivation of constructed practice. Those who do not regress are like Sudhana seeking in the south or Sadāprarudita requesting [the Dharma] from the east;

they would rather cut their own flesh to trade for a dove than retreat until death, or cast themselves to feed tigers, leaving their bones behind without wavering. By taking advancement as the standard, one measures regression.
It should also involve many people; it is insufficient as a model for instruction. Therefore, its records appear only sparingly.
Regarding the second [section], the "Diagram of the Nine Realms Manifesting from the Bodhisattva Realm and Remaining Latent," the *Exposition of the Diagram of the Dharma-realm* states:
"If one contemplates the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*), they constitute the basis of delusion and awakening. As for delusion..."
Thus, there are the ten realms of suffering and its accumulation. Through awakening, there are the four noble truths of cessation and the path.
Contemplating these immeasurable Four Truths, one gives rise to immeasurable vows: to cause those who have not crossed over to cross over; to cause those who have not been liberated to be liberated;

to cause those who have not attained peace to attain peace; and to cause those who have not attained nirvana to attain nirvana. With skillful means to deliver sentient beings and with eyes of compassion beholding all things, this is what has been accumulated.
"Sharing meritorious deeds with sentient beings"—one who gives rise to such a single thought is called a Bodhisattva’s *dharmadhātu*.

The commentary states: If, with respect to the Bodhisattva’s *dharmadhātu*, one were to discuss whether cultivation has progression or not, and whether the karmic fruit has regression or not, this section clarifies the two meanings of progression versus non-progression and regression versus non-regression. Regarding the term "non-... [the text here is truncated].
"Transformation" refers solely to the cultivation of this bodhisattva path. Furthermore, there are two types of transformation:

those who transform their minds toward the Buddha-way and advance without regressing, and those who, despite transforming, do not advance. Within the realm of karmic fruition, there are likewise two meanings: transformation and non-transformation.

As for "transformation," it refers to a Bodhisattva of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*) who, upon ascending to the First Ground (*prathamabhūmi*), destroys the delusions of ignorance (*avidyā-kleśa*) and transforms to enter the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-śikṣā*).
Regarding the "two stages": these refer to the paths of teaching and practice; although they are not yet perfected, as for the path of realization, realization and perfection are identical.
Regarding "non-retrogression": this means that from beginning to end, the three paths are distinct. However, once one has ascended to the first stage (bhūmi), [the paths are no longer separate].

Thus, there is only progress and no retreat; therefore, there is no principle of non-retreat. If one discusses retrogression with respect to individuals, it is as in the case of the Venerable Śāriputra.
In a previous kalpa, he was practicing the bodhisattva path when an outsider, a brāhmaṇa, begged for his eyes.
The Bodhisattva asked, "What use would you have for my eyes? You may ask for something else. The outsider replied, "I require nothing else."
He insisted on having the eyes. Since the Bodhisattva had not yet perfected his power of patience, he forced himself to gouge them out and give them away.

When the heretic obtained the eyes, he looked at them with anger and threw them to the ground, saying: "I thought the eyes of a Bodhisattva would surely be fragrant, pure, and beautiful; that is why I came to beg for them.
If they are still foul and filthy, how are they any different from those of an ordinary man? I have no need of such things! He then trampled them underfoot and departed. The Bodhisattva said:
The sentient beings of this defiled age are so stubborn and headstrong that they insistently seek after useless things; yet once they obtain them, they treat them with contempt and humiliation.
Truly, they are difficult to deliver. It would be better for them to abandon the Bodhisattva path and cultivate the way of the Śrāvaka to emerge from birth and death on their own.
Consequently, they gradually regress and fall back into the state of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). As the *Śāstra* states: "Śāriputra cultivated the Bodhisattva path for sixty kalpas."

They fall back from within the six mental states. Furthermore, as at the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, there were among the śrāvaka multitude those who, prior to the kalpa of "Dust-Point" (*rajas-lekhā*), had together with the sixteen princes of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū heard the Lotus Sūtra, resolved upon the unsurpassed mind, and practiced the bodhisattva path.
Among them, some did not fall back and have long since attained Buddhahood; others who did regress abandoned the Great for the Small and fell back into [the state of]...

Ordinary beings and those of the Small Vehicle whose faculties have ripened are now [taught] for the sake of the Two Vehicles. From this very life until now, the Tathāgata has further matured them by preaching the Dharma in five periods;
only then do they receive the prediction that they shall become Buddhas in the future. Thus, one should know that this is the practice of the Buddha-way.
Regarding the Bodhisattva path, there is a distinction between those who regress and those who do not.

As for the "Diagram of the Manifestation of the Dharmadhātu of the Pratyekabuddha and the Latent Submergence of the Nine Dhātus," the *Dharmadhātu Diagram Treatise* states: "If the sense faculties, objects, and thoughts arise, one realizes they proceed from ignorance."

Birth. Because of birth, there are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Volitional formations give rise to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), continuing thus through to old age and death. These three periods of time are linked together like a whirling firebrand.

Their causes and conditions are fundamentally empty; they are illusory transformations without reality. One seeks spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), delights in solitary tranquility, and contemplates the mind of emptiness.
[This is] weighty. [Such a person] dwells deeply in tranquil concentration; although they have attained the fruits of the Path, they do not seek to transform others.

Furthermore, there are those who observe the flourishing and falling of all things, awakening to the impermanence of the world, and attaining the Path upon hearing of emptiness; these are called Pratyekabuddhas (Solitary Realizers). Such practitioners are termed the Dharma-realm of the Pratyekabuddha.
Regarding the cultivation of its causes—whether they turn back or not—and the retribution of its fruits—whether they regress or not—[this is discussed] within the lower Dharma-realm of the Śrāvaka.
A Joint Discussion.
Regarding the diagram of the nine realms that lie latent while the Śrāvaka dharma-realm manifests:
the *Dharma-dhātu-śāstra* states, "If, through the causal conditions of sense faculties and objects, there arises even a single momentary thought..."

Because of form and mind, there is suffering (*duḥkha*); because of afflictions (*kleśa*), there is origination (*samudaya*). One loathes suffering and abandons origination. How could this not be the application of the antidote?
Thus, based on the Four Noble Truths, one cultivates the sixteen aspects and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as if putting out a fire on one's head.

Through the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), one attains entry into the four untainted fruits of the śramaṇa and realizes the two types of nirvāṇa. Having realized the partial truth, they do not obtain the Buddha-dharma and have no aspiration for it.
The "transformed person" (nirmāṇapuruṣa) is like a takin leaping alone without looking back at the herd. Such a single thought-moment is called the *dharmadhātu* of the *śrāvaka*.

The commentary states: If one discusses the two *dharmadhātus* of the *pratyekabuddha* and the *śrāvaka*, there is a distinction between those who practice with transformation and those who do not, and those whose karmic retribution may regress and those whose does not.
This is because when one realm arises, the other nine realms remain in a state of latent dormancy; thus, within the single nature (*ekaprakṛti*), [all are present].

Depending on the strength or weakness of external conditioning factors, their nature cannot be fixed. The remaining meanings are the same as those discussed regarding the turning or non-turning of bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, there are two further pairs of meanings: advancing versus not advancing, and retreating versus not retreating. As for "non-turning," it refers merely to practicing the dharmas of the two vehicles.
"Turning" is of two kinds: first, turning the resolve to become a bodhisattva; second, turning the resolve to reach the realm of Buddhahood.
Regarding the transformation of these two realms, there are further two types of mind: one that, after undergoing transformation, progresses and does not regress;
and one that, despite transforming, does not progress. Furthermore, regarding the fruition of retribution, there are two meanings: transformation and non-transformation.

Those who do not transform are the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas of fixed nature. Those who do transform are the followers of the Two Vehicles of the Tripitaka Teaching who are transformed by the Mahāyāna of the Shared Teaching.

"Receiving" refers to either being received by the Distinct or Complete Teachings from the Shared Teaching, or entering from emptiness into the provisional to study the bodhisattva-dharma, or entering from emptiness into the provisional and then into the middle to cultivate the Buddha-way. This is what it means.
The Diagram of the Nine Realms Manifesting in the Heavenly Realm and Remaining Latent in Darkness.

Regarding the Dharma-realm, the *Dharmadhātu-ṭīkā* states: "If a thought arises in the mind that takes great delight in celestial pleasures, one firmly cultivates a virtuous heart and yearns for future retribution;
thus, one maintains pure observance of the precepts, provides meals for śramaṇas, and constructs stūpas, temples, and images of the Buddha."

To create images, transcribe Mahāyāna scriptures, provide relief and charity to the poor and the sick, and fully cultivate both the prohibitions and the practices of the ten wholesome dharmas until they become one's natural disposition;

or to restrain the six sense faculties so that the six emotions do not wander and the six sensory objects do not enter, thereby attaining the dhyānas of the desire realm as well as the concentrations of the form and formless realms,
such that body and mind are tranquil and the three karmas are harmonious and excellent— this single thought-moment is called the celestial dharma-realm.
The commentary states: With respect to the celestial *dharmadhātu*, one discusses whether cultivation proceeds or does not proceed. Furthermore, while one realm manifests, nine realms remain latent.

Within this single nature, depending on the varying strength of external conditioning factors (*paribhāvana-pratyaya*), one may cultivate the merit of a lower heaven and thereby ascend to a higher heaven, or transform it into supramundane dhyāna, or even diminish the merit of a higher heaven.
They may instead be reborn as gods of the lower heavens, or as humans, or as asuras; their destination among these three realms is initially indeterminate.
Regarding the retribution of their fruits, there are those who regress and those who do not.

Those who do not regress will long experience the retribution of the heavens, or they may ascend further to higher heavens, or through the cultivation of the dhyāna of desire, the *anāgamya* stage, or attain the first, second, third, or fourth dhyānas.
Through meditative concentrations such as dhyāna, one advances upward to higher realms; this is not merely a matter of non-retrogression, but is further characterized by progress.
If, however, celestial merit is exhausted, one may enter the human realm or become an asura—this is what is meant by the decline of virtue and falling into degradation.
Or, when celestial merit is exhausted and the latent seeds of evil from previous lives begin to sprout, one ultimately falls into the three miserable paths, as was the case with Udraka Rāmaputra.
No. Possessing sharp faculties and intelligence, he was able to subdue his afflictions and attain the state of non-conceptual absorption (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).

When his celestial retribution of eighty thousand kalpas had ended, after his life came to a close, he fell into the body of a flying wildcat. Alternatively, as his life was about to collapse, he ascended and transformed his karmic fruit;
thus he avoided the evil realms and was reborn in a good path. It was like when the five signs of decay appear in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and the intermediate state (antarābhava) manifests.

He was destined to take the body of a pig. Śakra taught him the method of taking refuge in the Triple Gem, whereby he was able to escape the retribution of an animal birth and was reborn into the family of an elder in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
