Having heard the Dharma, he entered the Path; therefore, [his body] followed the arising of his mind and transformed in accordance with the mind.
In the beginning, there was no fixed essence.
Regarding the diagram of the human realm manifesting while the nine realms remain latent, the *Fajie tu shuo* (Exposition of the Diagram of the Dharma Realm) states:
"If, in every thought-moment, one establishes virtue through impermanence, [one upholds] the five precepts."

Cultivate the self. Be loyal toward the state and filial toward the family. Practice humility and self-effacement when among the multitude; maintain uprightness and sincerity within. Attribute virtue to others and take blame upon oneself.
Honor superiors and show compassion to subordinates; provide for the solitary and relieve the poor. Let shame and remorse be the destroyer of transgression; let kindness and harmony be one's nature.
Have deep faith in the Triple Gem and revere the Three Refuges. Diligently practice the precepts and fasts, and establish stupas and monasteries—this alone is what is hoped for.
Regarding worldly pleasures, lacking the resolve to transcend them, being covetous of one’s own person, and being attached to one's kin—such a single moment of thought is called the "human realm.
The commentary states:

it is in reference to the human realm that one discusses whether practice proceeds or does not proceed, and whether there is regression or non-regression from the karmic fruit; this is also based on a single [moment].
The nine realms manifest, while the other nine realms remain latent. Within this single nature, according to external conditioning factors, their strength and weakness differ.

Furthermore, it cannot be fixed that among the human paths of the four continents, only this Southern Continent possesses sharp and wise minds that are easily transformed and whose minds are most readily turned.
As the treatise explains, one should practice by giving rise to mindfulness; thus, in the midst of daily life, when the sense faculties encounter their objects—
When consciousness arises, it must necessarily fall into one of the ten realms.

For those who have not yet heard the Great Way, their goodness does not exceed that of humans or devas, while their evil leads to falling into the three miserable paths. It is as the saying goes: "All people can become Yao or Shun.
If one actually achieves this, before death they do not fail to be a great sage among men, and after death they do not fail to be reborn in the higher realms.
To the Office of Heaven. Every person can become a Jie or a Zhou, and yet they ultimately do so. In life, they lose their station and perish;
after death, they will surely receive retribution in the three paths of suffering. Is this not the turning of the human way into becoming a sage among men and a sage among gods?
Therefore, whether one revolves through the six realms of existence—humans and devas—or does not revolve, one has never departed from this [fundamental nature].

This is precisely the single thought that functions in daily life. Whether one has heard of the Great Way, or has attained a shallow realization of the partial vehicle (*pratyekabuddhayāna*), or possesses deep faith in True Suchness (*tathatā*), one is currently cultivating the path of humanity.
Yet, this may either turn toward the partial vehicle for transcending the world, or turn toward the Great Way of Nirvana.
Therefore, those who attained liberation and realized the Way during the Buddha’s lifetime were mostly kings, ministers, and officials.
Elder householder, those in this region who have attained Buddhahood or become patriarchs are all the most eminent among men and heroes of the Confucian and Daoist traditions.

Regarding whether karmic retribution is fixed or unfixed: if one examines the cause to verify the effect, or uses the effect to certify the cause, then poverty, wealth, nobility, and meanness are determined by prior karma.
However, if these states arise spontaneously from the mind, then retribution shifts according to that karma and cannot be fixed. It is as follows:
One may be poor and lowly by way of retribution for past deeds; yet if one possesses even a single virtue that moves Heaven, there are those who are transformed into the wealthy and noble.
Conversely, when one holds a position of wealth and nobility, if they commit a single lapse of conduct or lose their virtue, there are those who are transformed into the poor and lowly.
The cases of Pei Du returning his sash and Song Qi measuring the ants are both examples of this.
The Diagram of the Nine Realms Manifesting from the Asura Realm and Remaining Latent:
Regarding the Dharma-realm of the Asuras, the *Dharmadhātu-cakra-śāstra* states:

"If, in every thought-moment, although they cultivate goodness, practice generosity, and observe the precepts, they are full of suspicion and envy, and their hesitation and indecision cause the meritorious deeds they perform to be mostly for the sake of surpassing others."
When people practice goodness, their hearts are often full of jealousy and envy; they are arrogant and conceited, cherishing themselves while disparaging others.

They desire that others submit to them and cannot endure humility or self-effacement. Like an owl soaring high and looking down, they outwardly proclaim benevolence and righteousness while inwardly possessing no real virtue.

In discourse before the multitude, they draw out their own importance; they do not follow correct principles and feel no shame before the worthy and capable. Such conduct and state of mind belong to the asuras.
"Regarding the *dharmadhātu*.

The commentary explains: With respect to the realm of cultivation (*bhāvanā-dhātu*), one discusses the transformation or non-transformation of application (*prayoga*) and construction (*abhisamskāra*).

As for the certainty or uncertainty of the retribution (*vipāka*), it likewise arises from one realm while nine realms remain latent; within this single nature, [the result] follows external conditioning causes (*paribhāvaka-pratyaya*).
Strength and weakness differ. If one establishes practice in this manner at every thought-moment, it will certainly become the cause for rebirth as an asura;

its momentum cannot be turned back. However, if one gives rise to a sense of shame and remorse, reforming evil and turning toward good, then it may be transformed into the wholesome paths of humans and devas.
If one hears of the Great Way and turns it toward a supramundane mind, that [state] cannot be fixed;

yet if it turns downward toward this inferior state—becoming an animal, a ghost, or a denizen of hell—once mindfulness is lost, there is no evil one will not commit and no realm of rebirth into which one will not fall.
Regarding whether karmic retribution is fixed or unfixed, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* speaks of four kinds of asuras: namely, those born from the womb, the egg, moisture, and...
They are transformed beings belonging to the realms of devas, humans, pretas, and animals; all others are fixed and not indeterminate.
Relying solely on the power of the Dharma-protecting spells, they ride the Way to enter emptiness. These kinds of asuras constantly dwell beneath the assembly of the Tathāgata’s Dharma;

having heard the Great Way, they give rise to a mind of dedication and repentance. They are individuals for whom spiritual urgency is swift while their observance of precepts is lax, and they subsequently turn toward the path of the Bodhisattvas.
The Buddha-way is difficult to measure.
Regarding the "Diagram of the Manifestation of the Nine Realms and the Latent Submergence of the Dharma-realm of Hungry Ghosts," the *Dharma-realm Diagram* states:
"If, in every thought-moment, one is without shame or remorse, greedily seeking..."

He was insatiable, stingy, and mean-spirited, not giving away even a single hair’s breadth. He exploited others to amass wealth for himself. When he saw others practicing charity, he would create obstacles;
when he saw others gain profit, his heart burned with resentment. By nature he was full of flattery and crookedness, constantly harboring false views.
He maintained a proper countenance in public but acted wantonly in private; he violated the monastic rules and broke the precepts, indulging greedily in food and drink, and lacked faith.

Regarding transgressions and merits, disbelief in cause and effect, disbelief in the Triple Gem, and lack of filial piety toward one's kin—these are termed the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-dharmadhātu*).

The commentary states: concerning the realm of hungry ghosts, when discussing the cultivation, construction, transformation, or non-transformation of results—whether determinate or indeterminate—it is precisely because one realm manifests while the other nine realms remain latent; thus, within this single nature, [the result] follows according to its cultivation.

The strength of their power fluctuates, sometimes arising and sometimes subsiding; their nature cannot be fixed. If their every thought remains thus, they are certainly within the realm of hungry ghosts (preta-dhātu), and its momentum cannot be reversed.
However, if they give rise to a sense of shame and remorse, reforming their evils and turning toward the good, they will shift into the wholesome paths of humans or devas.
Or, upon hearing the Great Way, they may transform into a supramundane mind; thus, it is not fixed. If they should turn back...
For those at the lowest level, there are the realms of animals and hells. Once mindfulness is lost, there is no evil one will not commit, and no destiny into which one will not fall.
Regarding whether karmic retribution is fixed or unfixed: this path is divided into the categories of spirits and ghosts.

As for the way of spirits, it is what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* refers to as "fewer emotions and more thoughts," where they are light and agile, not far from [the human realm], and thus become powerful ghost-kings who can fly.
Rākṣasas and terrestrial rākṣasas roam throughout the four continents, moving without obstruction.

Among them, those who possess virtuous vows and virtuous minds, who protect those who uphold the precepts, or who protect divine mantras according to the mantra-holder, or who protect meditative concentration and maintain the patience of the Dharma—these dwell personally beneath the seat of the Tathāgata.
These, too, belong to the class of those for whom the vehicle is swift but the precepts are lax; such is their karmic retribution.
Although [the retribution] is fixed, if one is able to hear the Dharma and protect the Dharma, or transform heavy retribution into light retribution, then it is not fixed.

If the seven emotions and three thoughts sink into the water-wheel and one is born at the boundary of fire, receiving the fierce heat of fire and becoming a hungry ghost whose body is constantly being burned—
if even water can harm such a being, who has neither food nor drink for hundreds of thousands of kalpas— then this is fixed.

It is not that this is indeterminate. When the Ghost King Mianran received the Tathāgata’s teaching on the bestowal of food, although it was an manifestation by Avalokiteśvara, there could be no realization without the provisional, and no guidance toward realization without the provisional.

Moreover, those who receive the Tathāgata’s yoga-food can escape suffering for many kalpas and transcend rebirth into the wholesome realms; how could such a karmic fruit and retribution be anything other than real?
It is certain.
Regarding the diagram of the animal realm (*tiryag-yoni-dhātu*) manifesting while nine realms remain latent, the *Dharmadhātu-tu-shuo* states:
"If one is moment by moment immersed in the five desires and craves them excessively..."

Their retinue increased day by day and grew more numerous month by month, yet they remained insatiable. They perverted principles and treated others with injustice, never deciding matters with impartiality.

They seized wealth through illegal means and acted contrary to righteousness at every turn, plotting only for their own profit. They felt no compassion for the solitary or the greedy; they openly defrauded others of their property.
They were arrogant and aggressive, defaulting on market debts and openly practicing robbery. They were neither loyal nor filial, showing no regard for the wise or the foolish, and possessed no faith.
Regarding cause and effect, they do not believe in the Three Jewels; being foolish, ignorant, and shameless, they manifest as identical to animals.

This is called the animal dharma-realm (*tiryagyoni-dharmadhātu*). The commentary states: With respect to the animal dharma-realm, one discusses the transformation and non-transformation of cultivation and construction.

Furthermore, while one realm manifests, nine realms remain latent. Within this single nature, according to the strength or weakness of external conditioning factors (*bāhyapratyaya*), the nature does not... [text truncated].
It may be determined. If their every thought remains thus, they are certainly within the realm of animals; their momentum is such that it cannot be turned back.
However, if they give rise to a sense of shame and remorse, reforming their evil ways and turning toward the good, they will shift into the realms of humans or devas.

Or, if they hear the Great Way and transform their minds toward the supramundane, then it cannot be so determined. If they instead turn downward, they will fall into the destiny of the hells. Once [this occurs], it is settled.
When mindfulness is lost, one commits the ten grave evils, slanders the Triple Gem, violates the bodhisattva precepts, and there is no evil that one will not do.

Regarding the discussion of whether karmic retribution is fixed or unfixed: if the mental conditions are fulfilled, the fruit follows the cause and turns accordingly, as in the case of the karmic retribution for raising livestock, which is fixed upon being slaughtered to provide food for the kitchen. Yet, there are also cases where misfortune is transformed into fortune, as in the following example:
"O virtuous deer king! You have substituted yourself for your mother deer to go to the royal kitchen. When the king asked why this was so, the deer answered with the truth.
Thereupon, the king repented and spoke a verse to the deer: "You are a man with the head of a deer; I am a deer with the head of a man. From now on I release you to go;
follow your own will to seek water and grass. Consequently, together with the herd of deer under the authority of the wicked deer king, they all attained liberation from the hunt.

Is it not possible that even the retribution for the difficulty of hunting may be transformed? Furthermore, consider the ten thousand wandering fish who were protected from slaughter and provided with food by the Elder Flowing Water;
he preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to them. After their lives ended, they were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Upon reaching the assembly of the Radiant Light, they attained the prediction of future Buddhahood due to the causes and conditions of having heard the Dharma. Therefore, within the six realms of existence, there are [those who attain liberation].

Through the power of the Buddha, the power of the Dharma, and the power of compassion, heavy [karmic burdens] are transformed into light, and evil is transmuted into good, leading ultimately to liberation;
none of these can be predetermined.
The Diagram of the Nine Realms in Which the Dharma-realm of Hell Manifests and the Other Realms Remain Latent.
Regarding the "Dharma-realm of Hell," the *Dharma-realm Diagram* (*Fajie tu shuo*) states:

If a person associates with evil friends, or by their own nature commits evil, giving rise to an intensified mind that continues uninterruptedly from moment to moment, they commit the ten grave unwholesome acts (*daśākuśala*), namely: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and so forth.
This refers to frivolous speech, double-tongued talk, and harsh abuse; greed, anger, and false views;

as well as the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*), the violation of the four grave prohibitions, defiling those who practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*), selling intoxicants to cause drunkenness and disorder, failing to reflect upon the kindness and virtue of sovereigns, parents, and teachers, giving rise to groundless affliction, suppressing the worthy and capable, siding with the unworthy, destroying stupas and monasteries, burning or damaging scriptures and images, slandering and毁 (ruining) the Mahāyāna, and severing [the roots of goodness].

They study the *prajñāpāramitā* while slandering the non-existence of all Buddhas; they break the precepts yet accept offerings; they misappropriate property belonging to the Triple Gem or the property of the Saṃgha;
they give rise to the various views of external paths regarding annihilationism and eternalism; they destroy the correct laws of cause and effect throughout the three periods of time;

and they practice twelve kinds of evil, unrighteous disciplines: (1) butcher, (2) executioner, (3) pig-breeder, (4) poultry-keeper, (5) fisherman, (6) hunter, (7) bird-catcher, (8) python-trapper, (9) dragon-charmer, (10) jailer, (11) thief.
Those such as these—those who serve as kings to capture criminals, those engaged in the work of raising silkworms, and so forth—enter the great hells of intense heat and intense cold, such as Avīci;
this is called the dharma-realm of hell.

The commentary states: Regarding the dharma-realm of the hells, in terms of the two causes of spatial cultivation and constructed activity, as for whether it evolves or does not evolve, it is also because the vision of one realm gives rise to nine realms, which lie latent within a single nature according to the strength or weakness of their formative power.

One's nature cannot be fixed. If, in every thought-moment, one creates the causes for this hell, continuing them without interruption until they become habitual and form one's very nature, then it cannot be changed.
However, if one is able to feel shame and reform, turning the mind back even for a single thought-moment, that is itself the path of goodness.

If one illuminates and shatters the evil thoughts of this hell—whether by means of the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the Six Perfections, or the Three Truths and Three Contemplations of Emptiness, Provisionality, and the Middle Way—then these are transformed into supramundane states.

Whether the mental activities of sentient beings transform or do not transform, based on their inverted causes and how they arise, cannot be fixed with certainty. For example, King Ajātaśatru killed his father and harmed his mother, yet his physical sores...
He suffered from swelling and fever. After seven days, he was destined to fall into hell. Following the exhortation of the minister Jīva, he came to the presence of the Buddha.
Having been illuminated by the light of the Tathāgata’s Moon-Love Samādhi, he immediately attained refreshing coolness; the sores on his body were healed.
Hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, his mind became deeply repentant. The signs of hell vanished, and he attained rootless faith. This is a cause already established. It will—

Regarding the fruits of falling [into the lower realms]: by relying on the power of the Buddha-dharma, the power of repentance, and the power of great faith, one can even transform the realm of hell into the realm of the Buddha-dharma;
how much more so for one who does not let their offenses remain, thereby giving birth to a realm of goodness? Furthermore, as stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"The words of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are never false. If there is a person whose body has committed the four grave offenses and the ten transgressions..."
Pārājika offenses cause one to pass through this world and other worlds, even to the Avīci Hell, and throughout the ten directions, reaching the limits of the Uninterrupted Suffering,
experiencing them all without exception. Yet, if one can, with a single thought, take up this Dharma-door and reveal it to those who have not yet studied during the final kalpa,
that person’s karmic obstacles will be extinguished at that very moment, and the causes for the suffering of the hells they were to undergo will be transformed into peace.

Is the desire for a blissful land not itself a cause for hell? Yet, through the power of the Dharma, can this cause be transformed? Regarding the discussion of retribution in terms of what is fixed or unfixed:
if one follows the conventional discourse on cause and effect, once one has entered hell, the experience of retribution is certain, and there is no principle of uncertainty.
However, if one does not contemplate the power of humility and the power of repentance, even a fixed retribution can be turned back, allowing one to be born in a good realm.
As for the case of King Śreṇika: after he had finished executing five hundred Brahmins and non-Buddhists, he fell into the Avīci Hell.
There, he gave rise to three thoughts: first, he knew this was hell; second, he knew he had been killed by Śreṇika;
and third, he knew it was because of the sin of his wrong views that he had fallen into hell. From this, he felt great shame and remorse, and repented his past deeds.
Karma immediately extinguishes hell and enables rebirth in heaven;

thus we know that the Avīci Hell resides entirely within the self-mind of the Ultimate Sage, and the body and land of Vairocana do not exceed the single thought-moment of an ordinary person at the lowest level. To transform and change them depends solely upon the individual.
If one possesses profound repentance and profound awakening, it takes but a moment to transform hell into paradise.
*Discourse on the Innate Goodness and Evil of Human Nature*, Volume One;
*Discourse on the Innate Goodness and Evil of Human Nature*, Volume Two.
Written by the Śramaṇa Chuandeng of Youxi at Mount Tiantai.
The guest said: "I have already heard the teaching regarding the matter of the ten realms differentiating according to conditions.

What is meant by the gate of 'unchanging while following conditions'—being without difference yet appearing as difference? I replied: "This refers to the gate of the ten realms differentiating according to conditions, as explained in the preceding passage."
According to the conditions of defilement and purity, the ten dharma-realms are thereby distinguished.

Within this context, it is appropriate to definitively discuss the nature of inherent goodness and inherent evil, as well as the principle of cultivated goodness and cultivated evil. Inherent goodness and inherent evil refer to the essence of the unchanging *tathatā* (suchness).

Cultivated goodness and cultivated evil refer to the differentiated functions that follow conditions. This is precisely because within the unchanging essence of *tathatā*, [all capacities] are fully present.

Because the two natures of good and evil exist, when they encounter conditions, they manifest the functions of good and evil. Thus, the nature that is capable of following conditions is called "good and evil," while the conditions being followed are called "defiled and pure.
The natures of good and evil within the ten realms fully possess the real dharmas of the five aggregates, which are termed the "primary retribution" (zhengbao).
They also fully possess the real dharmas of the environment, which are termed the "secondary retribution" (yibao). —From the Tiantai [Great Calming and Contemplation].
The Master: Herein, one clearly understands the ten realms and the ten suchnesses. Since each single realm possesses ten suchnesses, the ten realms possess one hundred suchnesses.

As each of the ten realms mutually encompasses the others, they constitute one hundred dharma-realms. As these one hundred dharma-realms mutually encompass one another, they are further endowed with one thousand suchnesses.
There are one thousand real dharmas, one thousand lands, and one thousand provisional names; thus there are three thousand.

Within the nature of *tathatā*, none of these are not fully present. Because this nature is fundamentally complete, when conditions of defilement or purity arise, the three thousand phenomena of primary retribution and environmental retribution manifest.
These are the unchanging essence of *tathatā* itself functioning as the随缘 (*suíyuán*—following conditions).

It is used by taking that which is without differentiation as the basis for differentiation. Such meanings are fully contained within the various Mahāyāna sūtras of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuantun*).
If one were to manifest their characteristics, none surpasses the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*.

Within its section on the "Seven Elements" (*saptadhātu*), it clearly elucidates such principles as the true emptiness of the nature of form (*xingse zhenkong*) and the meaning of responding to conditions according to the minds of sentient beings and the capacity of what is known.
The five great elements—earth, water, fire, wind, and space—are the dependent retribution (*i-bō*) of the ten realms.
The two great elements—seeing and consciousness—are the primary retribution (*shō-bō*) of the ten realms.

I shall now cite them in full to elucidate this point, so that those who have deep faith in this school may have something upon which to rely, and may also come to know how the tenets established by the Tiantai school are profoundly in accord with the Buddha’s intent.

In the section clarifying the meaning of the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) being immutable yet conforming to conditions, the Tathāgata first provides an instruction based on a matter easily understood through direct perception, saying:
"Observe the nature of earth: grossly it is the great earth; subtly it is minute dust, down to the *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal particle).
If one were to divide that ultimate limit of form (*rūpa-paryanta-lakṣaṇa*) into seven parts, and further divide each *paramāṇu*..."
The reality of emptiness. Next, to clarify that the substance is void according to conditions, it is said:

"Ānanda, if these atoms were analyzed until they became empty space, you should know that empty space gives rise to the appearance of form. You have now asked by what means of conjunction the various transformative appearances of the world arise.
For your part, observe this single atom: by how much empty space must it be conjoined to exist?"

It is not possible for atoms (*paramāṇu*) to combine with one another to form an aggregate atom. Furthermore, when an aggregate atom is analyzed into emptiness, by means of how many material characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) is emptiness formed?

If it were formed by combining material characteristics, then that which combines would be matter, not emptiness; if it were formed by combining emptiness, then that which combines would be emptiness, not matter.
Form may still be analyzed, but how can emptiness be joined? The Three Illuminations explain the principle that the nature of *tathatā* (true thusness) is inherently complete:

"From the beginning, you have not known that within the *tathāgatagarbha*, the nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form; it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
The *tathāgatagarbha* is the very substance of the unchanging *tathatā*. The nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form."

This refers to a portion of the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) and its corresponding portion of the space element (*ākāśa-dhātu*) contained within the unchanging essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

The term "nature" (*xing*) used in the text is spoken in contrast to "characteristic" (*xiang*). Thus, there is nature-form (*xing-se*) and characteristic-form (*xiang-se*), as well as nature-space (*xing-kong*) and characteristic-space (*xiang-kong*).
Characteristic-form and characteristic-space are the forms produced by the ten dharma realms according to defiled or pure conditions.
"To be with emptiness" refers to the cultivation of both good and evil. Here, it points to the color-form and emptiness of inherent goodness and inherent evil;
yet these color-form and emptiness exist within a single nature, their essence eternally non-dual and without distinction, identical to the nature of the three virtues they possess.
The essence is likewise non-dual and without differentiation; therefore, it is said to be "pure and fundamental, pervading the Dharma-realm.

Purity is the prajñā-virtue within the earth element, also termed the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya). Being fundamental and natural is the liberation-virtue (vimukti-guṇa) within the earth element.

It is also called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which pervades the entire dharma-realm; it is the merit of the *dharmakāya* within the element of earth. It is also called the ultimate truth of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad-paramārtha-satya*).

Regarding the meaning of "following conditions" (*sui-yuan*), Siming stated: "It follows the minds of sentient beings according to the capacity of what they know, manifesting in accordance with their karma.

This is identical in meaning to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s principle that [the Buddha-nature] can follow defiled or pure conditions to fully create the ten dharma-realms. As for that which is followed...

Regarding conditions: there is mind and there is karma. Mind refers to the two types of mind—defiled and pure—within the ten dharma-realms. Karma refers to the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—within the ten dharma-realms.
Within the Buddha-realm, the mind of the three wisdoms is called the pure mind; the mind of the three delusions within the nine realms is called the defiled mind.
Within the Buddha-realm, conduct that accords with nature is called wholesome karma; conduct that opposes nature within the nine realms is called unwholesome karma. That is to say:

Suchness (tathatā) is the unchanging essence of the Buddha-realm’s nature of goodness; it can, in accordance with the pure mind of the Buddha-realm, manifest the form of cultivated goodness within that realm.
In terms of the person, this refers to the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha.

In terms of the primary retribution (vipākaphala), it refers to the ocean-like marks of the minute dust-particles of the Dharma-body, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya—the eighty-four thousand marks and signs and the eighty secondary characteristics.
Regarding the *yibao* (retributive environment), it refers to the colors of the *changjiguang* (eternal quiescent light) and the *shibao wuzhang'ai tu* (fruition-recompense land of non-obstruction).

Furthermore, the unchanging aspect of *tathatā*—the essence of the "evil nature" within the nine realms—is able to follow the defiled minds of the nine realms to produce the colors of the "cultivated evil" of the nine realms.

Regarding the *zhengbao* (retributive body), this refers to the colors of the *bianyi shengsi* (transformation-death) of the three sages, as well as the *fenduan shengsi* (segmented-death) of the six paths of existence.

This refers to the nature of form (*rūpa*). In terms of the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment), it refers to the Formless Realm of Unobstructed Reward, the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder, and the Land of Common Dwelling for both Mundane and Holy Beings—all of which are the nature of form.
As for the most extreme evil, even the *niśraya-vipāka* and *sabhāga-vipāka* (retributive body) of the Avīci Hell are none other than its manifestations.
Thus, within the human realm today, the six-foot physical body that constitutes one’s *sabhāga-vipāka*—
It receives the characteristics of the earth element; it is the retributive environment of mountains, rivers, and lands, comprising all material forms characterized by obstruction.
These are not the "evil" colors inherent in the unchanging aspect of True Suchness (tathatā).

Rather, they are the retributions summoned by the creation of evil karma in the human and celestial realms, resulting from the mind being defiled since beginningless time by the three delusions—the dust-like and sand-like views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] responds according to the minds of sentient beings.
The objects of knowledge manifest according to karma. "Mind" refers to what is called the "defiled mind" (*kliṣṭa-citta*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*;

"karma" refers to the karma of the five precepts and ten wholesome actions created by humans and devas. Compared to the three miserable realms and evil paths, this mind and its karma are termed a "pure mind" and "wholesome karma.
However, when viewed in light of the supramundane Four Noble Truths and Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, both are defiled minds and unwholesome karma.
How much more so for the Buddha’s Dharma-realm, the pure mind of the three wisdoms, and the wholesome karma of the six perfections!

Next, regarding the meaning of the fire-element being unchanging while following conditions, the Tathāgata first provides instruction by means of matters currently visible and easy to understand, saying:
"The nature of fire has no self; it relies upon various conditions. Observe within the city those who have not yet eaten..."

In a household, when one wishes to cook, one holds a *sūryakānta* (sun-crystal) in the hand and seeks fire from the sun. Next, [the Buddha] clarified that according to conditions its substance is fundamentally empty, saying:
"Ānanda, that which is called 'conjunction'—for example, myself and you, along with these one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, now form a single assembly.
Although the assembly is one, if one examines its fundamental basis, each possesses a distinct body, and each has their own [identity]."
Regarding birth, clan, and name: for example, Śāriputra was of the Brahmin caste, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa was of the Kāśyapa caste, and so on up to Ānanda, who was of the Gautama clan.

Ānanda, if this nature of fire exists because of a combination of conditions, when one holds a mirror in the hand and seeks fire from the sun, does this fire emerge from within the mirror, or does it emerge from the tinder? Or...
"It comes from the sun, Ānanda. If it comes from the sun, it should naturally burn the moxa in your hand; the forests through which it has passed on its way should all have been consumed by fire.
If it emerges from the mirror, it should naturally emerge from the mirror and ignite the moxa; why then does the mirror not melt?
Even when held in your hand, it shows no sign of heat, so how could it ever liquefy? If it were produced within the moxa itself, what need would there be for the sun?"
When the light of the mirrors meets, fire is then produced. You should observe this closely: the mirror is held by the hand, the sun comes from the sky, and the moxa grows from the earth;
from what direction does the fire travel to reach here? The sun and the mirror are far apart; they are neither blended nor joined.

It cannot be that the fire-light exists of itself without a source. Thus, the three clarifications explain the principle that the nature of True Suchness (Tathatā) is inherently complete. You still...
One does not realize that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of fire is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true fire;
it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. The Tathāgatagarbha is the essence of the unchanging True Suchness (*tathatā*). "The nature of fire is true emptiness;
the nature of emptiness is true fire" refers to a portion of the fire-element and its corresponding portion of emptiness contained within the unchanging essence of True Suchness.
The "Great" refers to what is spoken of as "nature. To speak of nature is likewise to do so in contrast to "phenomena" (lakṣaṇa). For there is the fire of nature and the fire of phenomena;

there is the emptiness of nature and the emptiness of phenomena. The phenomena of the Great and the emptiness of the Great are the void and the fire produced by the ten dharma-realms according to defiled or pure conditions—that is, the cultivation of good and the cultivation of evil.
Now, it is these fires and emptinesses of innate goodness and innate evil that are being pointed out.
This fire is precisely true emptiness; this emptiness is precisely true fire. Thus, the nature of fire is precisely true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is precisely true fire.
Therefore, they are described reciprocally as "the nature of fire is true emptiness" and "the nature of emptiness is true fire. This emptiness and fire exist within a single nature (*ekasvabhāva*);
their essence is eternally non-dual and without distinction. This is identical to the essence of the three virtues (*triguṇa*) that they possess.
It is neither dual nor differentiated; therefore it is said: "Pure and fundamentally such, pervading the entire dharma-realm.

"Purity" refers to the virtue of *prajñā* within the fire-element, also called the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). "Fundamentally such" refers to the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*) within the fire-element, also called the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
"Pervading the entire dharma-realm" refers to the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) within the fire-element, also called the Middle Way Supreme.
Regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): since it is said to be pure, this fire-element within the single nature is fundamentally free from defilement.
Since it is said to be primordial (*mūla*), this fire-element within the single nature is fundamentally not something produced by artifice.
Since it is said to be all-pervading throughout the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), this fire-element within the single nature is fundamentally beyond all dependence. — Sīmānta (Sima Ming)
Regarding the meaning of "the unchanging following conditions": it accords with the minds of sentient beings, responds to the scope of their cognition, and manifests according to their karma.

This is identical in meaning to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s principle of being able to follow defiled or pure conditions to fully create the ten dharma-realms. That which is followed consists of both mind and karma.
The mind is the single mind of the ten dharma-realms, both defiled and pure. Karma is the two types of conduct—good and evil—within the ten dharma-realms.
The mind of the three wisdoms within the Buddha-realm is called the pure mind; the mind of the three delusions within the nine realms is called the defiled mind.

Conduct that accords with the nature within the Buddha-realm is called good karma; conduct that opposes the nature within the nine realms is called evil karma. This refers to the unchanging aspect of True Suchness as the Buddha.
The nature of the realm is wholesome. It is able to follow the conditions of wholesome karma from a pure mind to create the fire of cultivating goodness within the Buddha-realm.
In terms of the individual, this is Ucchuṣma; in terms of the primary retribution, it is the Buddha’s sun of wisdom, whose radiance shines perfectly and universally.
In the Dharma-realm, the sun, moon, and various devas withdraw their heavy radiance.

Regarding the *paratantra* (dependent) retribution, immeasurable clouds of fragrance serve as pedestals for light, and the seven-jeweled towers and pavilions are constantly luminous; all these are manifestations of this principle.

Furthermore, the unchanging *tathatā* (suchness) possesses the nature of evil within the nine realms, which, following the conditions of defiled mind and evil karma, creates the fire of the cultivated evil of the nine realms. This is discussed in terms of the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) nature.
As for retribution, the various sensations of warmth and cold within the body arise as the fire of afflictions; the breath becomes smoke, acting as an obstruction, heat, and parching thirst.
Regarding the environment of dependence (*niśraya-vipāka*), there are the light of the sun and moon, the smoke and flames of forests and trees.
At the extreme limit of cultivated evil, there are fire-dragons, fire-snakes, fire-unicorns, fire-rats, and various hungry ghosts, who constantly receive the fierce fires of their elemental energy.

They are scorched and burned, reaching as far as the eight hot hells. The fires above penetrate below, and the fires below penetrate above; they interpenetrate from east to west, burning for kalpas on end.
As for their environmental retribution, it extends as far as that which is consumed by the kalpa-ending conflagration, reaching upward to the First Dhyāna Heaven.

All that exists within the world is reduced to ashes and embers. Is there anything that is not the Tathāgatagarbha, the unchanging nature of True Suchness, which possesses both the nature of goodness and the nature of evil?
It is the fire produced according to the conditions of defilement or purity; therefore it is said that "it accords with the minds of sentient beings and responds to the measure of what they know.

A solitary mind does not stand alone, and karma accomplished in isolation is difficult to achieve. Since there is a mind of defilement or purity, there must necessarily be karma of good or evil; therefore it is said that "it manifests in accordance with karma."

In the section concerning the meaning of the water-element remaining unchanged while following conditions, as set forth by the Threefold Knowledge (*traividya*), [the Buddha] first provides an instruction based on matters easily understood through direct perception, saying:
"Ānanda, the nature of water is not fixed; its flowing and ceasing are not constant.
For instance, there are the great illusionists of Śrāvastī, such as the sages Kapila, Kālakā, and Padma-Hrasvaja, who seek..."
The essence of the moon is used to compound illusory medicines. These masters, during the bright fortnight, hold a *fangzhu* (a concave mirror) in their hands to catch the water from the moon.
The two luminosities follow conditions while their substance is empty. [The Buddha said: "Ānanda, does this water come out from within the pearl?"

"It exists naturally within the air; does it come from the moon? Ānanda, if it came from the moon, since it is capable of causing water to emerge from the pearl even from a great distance, then all the trees and forests it passes by should likewise discharge flowing water.
If they were to flow, what need would there be for the water produced by the *fangzhu* (the concave mirror)?

If they do not flow, it is clear that the water does not descend from the moon. If, on the other hand, it emerges from the pearl itself, then this pearl should constantly produce flowing water; why then wait [for the moon]?"
At midnight, the white moon was received during the day as if it had arisen from space. Since the nature of space is boundless, the water should likewise be limitless;
from humans to devas, all would equally be submerged. How, then, could there still be those who travel by water, land, or air?

You should observe this more closely: the moon ascends from the heavens, while the pearl is held in the hand. The basin for receiving the pearl-water was originally set out by a person; from what direction, then, did the water flow in?
In this regard, the moon and the water-crystal are neither joined nor conjoined; yet it is not that the water-crystal arises spontaneously from nowhere.

Thus, the principle of the true nature of *tathatā* (suchness) being inherently complete is explained: you still do not know that within the *tathāgatagarbha*, the nature of water is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true water;
it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*. The *tathāgatagarbha* is precisely the unchanging aspect of *tathatā*.
This is the essence (*tattva*). The nature of water is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true water.

This refers to a portion of the element of water (*āpas*) and a corresponding portion of the element of space (*ākāśa*) inherent within the unchanging essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*). The term "nature" (*xing*) is also spoken in contrast to "phenomenal appearance" (*lakṣaṇa*);

for there is the nature-water and phenomenal water, as well as the nature-emptiness and phenomenal emptiness. Phenomenal water and phenomenal emptiness constitute the ten realms of existence (*daśadhātu*).
According to conditions of defilement or purity, they give rise to what are termed "emptiness" and "water"—that is, the cultivation of good and the cultivation of evil.

Here, "emptiness" and "water" refer to innate goodness and innate evil. This water is true water; this emptiness is true emptiness. Thus, innate water is true emptiness, and innate emptiness is true water.
Therefore, to express this through reciprocal phrasing, it is said that "innate water is true emptiness" and "innate emptiness is true water."
Water. This water and space exist within a single nature; their essence is eternally non-dual and without distinction.
Furthermore, it is non-dual and without distinction from the three virtues (*guṇa*) that it possesses. Therefore, it is said to be "pure and fundamentally so," pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*.

"Pure" refers to the virtue of *prajñā* within the element of water, also called the "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*). "Fundamentally so" refers to [the virtue of goodness] within the element of water...

The virtue of liberation is also called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Pervading the entire dharma-realm, it is the virtue of the Dharma-body within the water element, and is also called the ultimate truth of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-prathamārtha-satya*).
Since it is said to be pure, this water element is fundamentally free from defilement.

Since it is said to be "original," this water, in its fundamental nature, has no creator. Since it is said to be "pervading the Dharma-realm," this water, from the very beginning, is beyond all dependence.
Regarding the meaning of "the unchanging following conditions" (*bùbiàn suíyuán*), it is said:

"It accords with the minds of sentient beings, responds to the measure of what they know, and manifests according to their karma. This is identical to the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra’s teaching that [the Tathāgata-garbha] can follow defiled or pure conditions and is fully endowed with...

The meaning of "creating" the ten dharma-realms is the same [for all]. That which they follow consists of mind and karma. Mind refers to the two types of mind—defiled and pure—within the ten dharma-realms.
Karma refers to the two types of conduct—wholesome and unwholesome—within the ten dharma-realms. Within the Buddha-realm, the mind of the three wisdoms is called the pure mind;

within the nine realms, the mind of the three delusions is called the defiled mind. Within the Buddha-realm, conduct that accords with nature is called wholesome karma; within the nine realms, [conduct that] opposes...

The conduct of one's nature is called "evil karma. This means that while True Suchness (tathatā) is unchanging and the nature of the Buddha-realm is inherently good, it can, by following the conditions of a pure mind and wholesome karma, create the water of cultivated goodness within the Buddha-realm.
In terms of the person, this refers to the Tathāgata Water-Heaven (Jaladeva) and the youth Moonlight (Candraprabha).
In terms of the primary retribution, it refers to entering the earth as if it were water and treading upon water as if it were earth, such that the moisture of the throat flows freely.
One attains the supreme flavor among all flavors. In terms of the retributive environment (*niśraya-vipāka*), the waters flow into the seven-jeweled colors of the land;
they are all soft and supple, bathing one in purity. The depth of the flowing water accords with one's wishes, and its currents emit radiance while constantly expounding the wondrous Dharma.

Ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks warble together in harmonious and elegant tones. Surrounding the beams of the four courtyards, the Mahāyāna is proclaimed. Furthermore, True Suchness (*tathatā*) does not change throughout the nine realms.
Intrinsic evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*) can, following the conditions of defiled mental states and evil karma, produce the water of the nine realms of conditioned evil.
In terms of the primary retribution (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), this refers to excrement, urine, pus, blood, saliva, and lymph;

in terms of the secondary environment (*pariṇāma-nimitta*), it refers to rain, dew, frost, snow, rivers, streams, oceans, seas, brooks, ravines, and gullies—all such waters. Reaching the extreme of evil, it becomes the river of ashes and blood within the hells.
The ponds freeze and crack during the eight cold hells. Furthermore, when things reach their ultimate evil, the world is about to perish;
a catastrophe of water arises, surging and overflowing until it reaches the Second Dhyāna Heaven. Mencius said: "The goodness of human nature is like water’s flowing downward.
There is no person who does not possess goodness, just as there is no water that does not flow downward. This statement by Mencius merely understands the nature of water.
This is merely a characteristic. One does not yet know the nature of water; one only knows the water’s cultivated evil, while remaining ignorant of its cultivated goodness.
What is the nature of water? It is as stated in the Sūtra: "The nature of water is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true water.
It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. When water abides in its nature in this way, how can there be any distinction between superior and inferior?
Regarding the directions—below, east, west, and so forth—it is as if the eye were the essence of the Great Yin (the moon).

When the light of the moon travels through the vast emptiness of space, whether from the west or the east, from the south or the north, from above or below, there is no place where those seeking water do not turn.
Holding a *fangzhu* (a concave crystal) in their hands, they receive the water from within the moon; wherever one holds the bead, there water emerges.
Pervading the entire Dharma-realm and arising throughout the entire Dharma-realm, it fills the world; how could it have a fixed location?

Now, as for the nature of water, must it necessarily flow downward? Why then does the water of the virtuous cultivation of water rise from below to above, like the waters within the pools of the seven treasures in the World of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī), which gush forth from the King of Wish-fulfilling Jewels and flow upward like tears?

Amidst the flowers, one seeks [the source] as it moves up and down through the trees, dividing into four branches. Is this not like what Mencius described—how that which can be made to flow in the mountains is stirred into action?

Furthermore, in Maitreya’s Inner Court, the water of eight virtues likewise flows from below upward, circling between the beams while proclaiming the profound and wondrous Dharma; this too is not something that has been forced upward. One must understand this.
The downward flow of water in the world is the manifestation of water within the cultivation of evil.
Since the cultivated appearance of water can be either superior or inferior, it is clear that the nature of water is fundamentally pure and pervades the entire dharma-realm;
thus, the inherent presence of both good and evil within its nature is evident. Furthermore, Mencius said, "I am able to nourish my vast and mighty qi. This...
Vital energy (qi) fills the space between heaven and earth. Is it earth? Water? Fire? Wind? Space? Is it singular? Or is it a composite?
It is designated as "vital energy," and it is fitting that it be considered the residual radiance of the five great elements.
Nevertheless, the present scripture selects the seven bases that are easily perceived and reveals them first; these still pertain to the matters of cultivating good and cultivating evil.

This does not refer to the so-called inherent goodness or evil of nature. As for the fact that the nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form—being pure and fundamental by nature and pervading the entire Dharma-realm—it must certainly not be limited merely to the space between heaven and earth or the six directions of the physical world. Such is the element of water.
The same applies to all other great elements. Thus, the nature of the earth, water, fire, wind, and space upon which one relies is entirely pure and fundamental;
it is nothing other than pervading the entire dharma-realm. It possesses both inherent goodness and inherent evil. How much more so, then, is this true for the six sense faculties of the human body?
Does this not mean that the six consciousnesses and the nature of mind are likewise not possessed of both inherent goodness and inherent evil?

However, the goodness and evil of the *nature* (xing) differ from those of *cultivation* (xiu). While the goodness and evil of cultivation certainly entail the distinctions of ascent and descent, or suffering and joy, as for the goodness and evil of the *nature*, its substance embodies the three virtues (*triguṇa*), all of which are non-dual yet dual, and dual yet non-dual; how, then, could there be ascent or descent, or suffering?
How extraordinary is this joy!
Within the meaning of the wind-element of the Four Ming Mountains—remaining unchanged while following conditions—it is first revealed by means of matters readily apparent before one, stating:
"The nature of wind has no substance; its movement and stillness are not constant. When you regularly adjust your robes to enter the great assembly, O monk..."

When the corner of the *kāṣāya* moves and another person is nearby, a subtle breeze arises that brushes against that person's face. Next, to clarify that the substance is empty according to conditions, it is asked:
"Does this wind emerge from the corner of the *kāṣāya*, arise from empty space, or is it produced upon that person's face? Ānanda!
If this wind were to emerge from the corner of your *kāṣāya*, you would be wearing the wind; your robe would flutter and fly away, and you would be separated from your body.
Now, as I preach the Dharma, my robe hangs down within the assembly. Look at my robe: where is the wind? It cannot be within the robe.

There is a ground that stores wind. If it were produced from empty space, why does your robe not move when you are born therein? For what reason is there no stirring? Since the nature of emptiness is eternally abiding, the wind should be constantly produced.
If there were times when there was no wind, then empty space would have to perish. If the perishing of wind could be seen, what would the state of the perishing of empty space look like?
If there were arising and ceasing, it would not be called empty space. Since it is called empty space, how could wind emerge from it?
If the wind arose spontaneously from the face being brushed by it, then that wind should brush you; you yourself should adjust your robes—why then do you brush them away?

Examine this with careful scrutiny: your adjusted robe belongs to you, while your face belongs to that person. Space is tranquil and does not participate in movement. From which direction does the wind stir and come here?
The natures of wind and space are distinct; they are neither blended nor conjoined. It cannot be that the nature of wind exists spontaneously without a source.
Thus, the third [point] clarifies the principle that the nature of True Suchness (Tathatā) is inherently complete: "You do not yet know the Tathāgatagarbha."
Within this, the nature of wind is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true wind. It is pure and originally so, pervading the entire dharma-realm.
This is the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha, the unchanging True Suchness (*tathatā*).

The phrases "the nature of wind is true emptiness" and "the nature of emptiness is true wind" refer to one portion of the element of wind (*vāyu-mahābhūta*) inherent within the unchanging essence of True Suchness, as contrasted with one portion of the element of space (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*). Thus says the text.
"Nature" (xing) is also spoken of in contrast to "characteristics" (xiang). There is the wind of nature and the wind of characteristics; the emptiness of nature and the emptiness of characteristics.

These winds of characteristics and emptiness of characteristics are the True Suchness (tathatā) of the ten realms, which, following conditions of defilement or purity, produces both emptiness and wind—namely, the cultivation of good and the cultivation of evil.
Here, we refer to the winds of inherent goodness and inherent evil. These winds are true emptiness, and this emptiness is true wind.
Thus, the nature-wind (*prakṛti-vāyu*) is itself true emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*), and the nature-emptiness is itself true wind.

Therefore, they are expressed reciprocally as "the nature-wind is true emptiness" and "nature-emptiness is true wind. This wind and this emptiness, existing within a single nature, are eternally non-dual in essence and without distinction.
They are likewise non-dual in essence and without distinction from the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) they possess. Hence, it is called "Pure."
Pure by nature and pervading the Dharma-realm: "purity" refers to the virtue of *prajñā* within the great element of wind, also termed the Truth of Ultimate Reality (*paramārtha-satya*).
"By nature" refers to the virtue of *vimukti* within the great element of wind, also termed the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

"Pervading the Dharma-realm" refers to the virtue of the *dharmakāya* within the great element of wind, also termed the Middle Way, the Truth of the Supreme Meaning (*paramārtha-madhyamā-pratipad*). Since it is said to be "pure," then this great element of wind—
It is fundamentally free from defilement. Since it is said to be "fundamentally so" (*tathatā*), this wind-essence is fundamentally without a creator.

Since it is said to be "pervasive throughout the dharma-realm," this wind-essence is from the beginning beyond all dependence. Regarding the meaning of "the unchanging following conditions" (*bùbiàn suíyuán*), the Four Ming [Master] says:
"It accords with the minds of sentient beings, responds to the measure of what they know, and manifests according to their karma. This is identical to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The capacity to follow along with conditions of defilement or purity is identical in its meaning to the principle of fully creating the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*).

That which is followed consists of mind and karma: "mind" refers to the two types of mind—defiled and pure—within the ten dharma-realms; "karma" refers to the two types of action—conformable and contrary—within the ten dharma-realms.

The mind of the three wisdoms within the Buddha-realm is called the pure mind; the mind of the three delusions within the nine realms is called the defiled mind. The action that conforms to the nature within the Buddha-realm is [the conformable action].

It is called virtuous karma (*kuśala-karman*). The conduct of the nine realms that runs contrary to the nature [of reality] is called non-virtuous karma (*akuśala-karman*). That is to say, the unchanging *tathatā* is the inherently virtuous nature of the Buddha-realm (*buddha-dhātu*).
When it encounters conditions that accord with a pure mind, it creates the wind of cultivating goodness within the Buddha-realm.

In terms of the person, this refers to the Dharma Prince Yuan from the lineage of Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata. In terms of the primary retribution (*pratyaya-phala*), it refers to the Wind of the Path and the Wind of Virtue.
They circulate throughout the Dharma-realm; whether going, coming, sitting, or standing, they never experience weariness or fatigue.

With respect to their environmental retribution (*pariṇāmanavipāka*), eight kinds of pure breezes blow pleasantly, harmoniously, and refreshingly, blowing upon the various jeweled nets and jeweled trees to produce subtle and wondrous sounds.

It is as if hundreds of thousands of kinds of music were performed simultaneously; those who hear these sounds spontaneously give rise to mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Saṃgha.
The mind of the nine realms possesses inherent evil. Capable of following the conditions of the defiled mind’s evil karma, it creates the winds of the cultivated evil of the nine realms.

In terms of the primary retribution (*nirmāṇakāya*), the tendons turn and the vessels vibrate; blood circulates and the vital breath moves; walking, standing, sitting, and reclining exist in mutual dependence.

In terms of the secondary environment (*bhājanaloka*), there is the mildness of spring, the heat of summer, the severity of autumn, and the cold of winter; there are mountains collapsing and whirlwinds swirling, as days pass and months go by.
Furthermore, as for those of extreme evil: when the evil winds of hell blow and destroy the land, the deceased spirits fly through the air and fall;
their bodies, frozen and cracked by the cold wind, become blue and white lotuses. Furthermore, as for those of the utmost great evil:
when the kalpa comes to an end, the Vairambha winds arise, blowing the great earth until it is pulverized, and Mount Sumeru is transformed.
Even down to a single atom and up to the third dhyāna heaven, nothing is exempt from destruction by the calamity of wind. One must know that among all powers, the power of wind is the greatest.
In the formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness of the world-systems, there is nothing that can be maintained or sustained without the power of wind.
The great earth, the floating banners, and the royal lands cannot be upheld without the wind-wheel. The coming of the sun and the going of the moon cannot occur without the power of wind.
Nothing can be set in motion; the spring, summer, autumn, and winter could not bring about birth or death without the power of wind.

Walking, standing, sitting, and reclining could not be performed with bending and turning without the power of wind. Speaking, talking, laughing, and smiling could not be expressed or silenced without the power of wind.
When one reflects and deliberates upon this, it cannot be made to burn by the power of the wind alone; these are all the functions of inherent evil and the outbursts of cultivated evil.
As for the winds of inherent goodness and cultivated goodness, they are eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, unmoving, and all-pervading.
Since there is no arising, how could there be cessation? Since there is no place of dwelling, how could there be transition? This is precisely what [is meant].
This refers to practicing in accordance with the true nature and realizing that which is beyond all dependence.

Within the meaning of the Great Emptiness—being unchanging yet conforming to conditions according to the five sciences—the following first employs phenomena currently visible and easy to understand as a point of reference.
He then revealed this, saying: "The nature of emptiness has no form; it is manifested through form.
For example, in the city of Śrāvastī, far from the river, various kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, as well as pāraśavas and caṇḍālas, have recently established a residence.
They dug a well in search of water; when they had removed one foot of earth, within that space there was one foot of void."
It is empty. In this manner, even up to when one has excavated the earth for ten feet, one likewise obtains ten feet of empty space in between.

The depth of this empty space corresponds to the amount of earth that has been removed. Next, to clarify that the substance is empty in accordance with conditions, it is asked: "Does this emptiness arise because of the earth?"
"It arises spontaneously without cause. Ānanda, if this space were to arise spontaneously without cause, why was there no unobstructed passage before the earth was excavated?
One would have seen only the great earth, with nothing penetrating through it.
If it arose because of the earth, then at the moment the earth emerged, one should have seen space entering. If the earth emerged first without space entering, how could space be caused by the earth?

And yet it emerges. If there were no entering or emerging, then empty space and the earth would fundamentally have no distinct causes; being non-distinct, they would be identical. If they are identical, then when the earth emerges, why does space not emerge as well?
If it emerges because of digging, then it is space that is emerged by the digging, and it should not be the earth that is emerged.

If it does not emerge because of digging, then the digging itself emerges from the earth—how then can one perceive space? You should examine this more carefully, examining it with the utmost precision. As for the digging...
Human hands take hold of it and transport it according to their direction; the earth shifts as the ground moves. If this is so, from what does empty space arise?
If one digs into emptiness, the void and the solid do not serve each other’s function; they are neither blended nor joined. It cannot be that empty space emerges of its own accord without a source.

Thus, the three elements combine to form the great element of space, balancing it with the four great elements mentioned previously. If this nature of empty space is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally [unborn]...
They are in motion. You should know that the present earth, water, fire, and wind are all equally called the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*). Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious;

they are all the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally without arising or ceasing. Ānanda, your mind is deluded and confused; you do not realize that the four great elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.

One should contemplate space as being neither exiting nor entering, nor non-exiting and non-entering. The Four Clarities explain the principle of the true nature (*tathatā*) as inherently complete, saying:

"You do not know at all that within the Tathāgatagarbha, there is the true emptiness of the nature of awakening (*prakṛti-bodhi-śūnyatā*) and the true awakening of the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bodhi*).
It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. This is the unchanging essence of the Tathāgatagarbha-tathatā. [The phrase] 'the true emptiness of the nature of awakening'..."

"Emptiness and True Awakening. This refers to the integration of one portion of the element of emptiness (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*) and one portion of the element of awakening (*bodhi-mahābhūta*), both of which are inherent within the unchanging essence of *tathatā*.

To speak of "awakening" in broad terms, it refers to the sense organs (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Furthermore, when the text uses the term "nature" (*svabhāva*), it is spoken in contrast to "phenomenon" (*lakṣaṇa*);
for there is the emptiness of nature and the emptiness of phenomena, as well as the awakening of nature and the awakening of phenomena. [The latter] is the emptiness of phenomena.

Regarding "the realization of characteristics": this refers to how the True Suchness (*tathatā*) of the ten realms, following conditions of defilement and purity, gives rise to both emptiness and awareness.

Here, we specifically point to the emptiness and awareness of inherent goodness and inherent evil. This emptiness is ultimate emptiness; this awareness is ultimate awareness. This, then, is the inherent awareness.
This is precisely true emptiness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*). Essential emptiness is itself true awakening (*tathatā-bodhi*). Therefore, it is stated reciprocally: "Essential awakening is true emptiness;
essential emptiness is true awakening. This emptiness and awakening reside within a single essence (*ekasvabhāva*); their substance is eternally non-dual and without differentiation.
Furthermore, this is non-dual and without differentiation from the three virtues (*triguṇa*) that they embody. Hence it is said: "Pure and fundamental, it is all-pervasive."

The purity of the *dharmadhātu* is the virtue of *prajñā* within the great emptiness; it is also called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Its primordial nature as the great emptiness is the virtue of *vimukti*;
it is also called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Its pervasiveness throughout the *dharmadhātu* as the great emptiness is the virtue of the *dharmakāya*;
it is also called the Middle Way, the supreme truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Since it is said to be "pure," this space is fundamentally free from defilement.

[It is so. Fundamentally, this Great Source of emptiness has no creator. Universally pervasive, this Great Source of emptiness has from the beginning been beyond all dependence. [The text] establishes the meaning of "changing according to conditions" as follows: it accords with the minds of sentient beings and responds to the measure of their cognitive capacity.
Ānanda, it is like a single well being empty; emptiness gives rise to one well. The empty space of the ten directions is also like this:

it fills the ten directions—how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma. This is just as the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra states that [the mind] can follow defiled or pure conditions to fully construct the ten dharma-realms.
That which it follows consists of the mind and karma: the "mind" refers to the two types of mind within the ten dharma-realms, both defiled and pure; "karma" refers to the ten...

Regarding the two modes of progression and regression within the *dharmadhātu*: the mind of the Buddha-realm characterized by the three types of wisdom is called the "pure mind," while the mind of the nine realms characterized by the three delusions is called the "defiled mind.
The practice of the Buddha-realm that accords with its nature is termed "wholesome karma," whereas the practice of the nine realms that opposes its nature is termed "unwholesome karma.

This refers to the unchanging wholesome nature of the *tathatā* (suchness) of the Buddha-realm, which, by virtue of the conditions for practicing in accordance with the pure mind, is able to manifest.
The emptiness of cultivating goodness within the Buddha-realm: in terms of the person, it is the Tathāgata King of Emptiness and the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha;

in terms of the primary retribution (*pratyaya-vipāka*), it is the pure *dharmakāya*, the precious awakening of true emptiness; in terms of the environmental retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*), it is the void as seat, the land of eternal quiescent light.
This body is itself the land, and this land is itself the body. Although it is said to be accomplished through cultivation, in reality, it is entirely [the original nature].
The nature of cultivation and realization is darkly merged with the true emptiness of the nature-awakening and the true awakening of the nature-emptiness.

Furthermore, the unchanging nature of evil within the True Suchness (tathatā) of the nine realms can, following the conditions of defiled minds that act in opposition, create the emptiness of the cultivated evil of the nine realms.
In relation to Bodhisattvas, it is the emptiness of the "only-middle" (but-madhyama-śūnyatā). In relation to those of the Two Vehicles, it is the partial, true emptiness (pradeśika-bhūta-śūnyatā).

In relation to worldly dhyāna, it is the emptiness of the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). In relation to non-Buddhists, it is the emptiness of the thoughtless state of the Fourth Dhyāna.

In terms of the teaching on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is the empty space of obscurity and darkness. In terms of the icchantika, it is the lack of faith in the causality of the three periods of time;
they claim that when a person dies, it is like the extinguishing of a lamp, and they negate the existence of sin and merit through an emptiness of denial.

This extends even to the emptiness of the sixty-two views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Although such people take their own deluded attachments to be "emptiness," how could the retribution of their death possibly be empty?
The three miserable realms and evil paths are like pleasure gardens and scenic excursions; camels, donkeys, pigs, and dogs are the places where one travels.
Sixth, in the section clarifying the meaning of the Great Unchanging Manifesting According to Conditions, [the text] first relies on matters currently visible that are easy to understand.
Yet Kaiyun said: "Ānanda, seeing and awareness have no inherent knowledge; they exist because of form and emptiness. It is as when you are now in the Jeta Grove:
in the morning it is bright, in the evening it is dark. Even if it were mid-night, there would be light during the white fortnight and darkness during the black fortnight.

Thus, brightness and darkness are distinguished by means of seeing. Next, he clarified that the essence is empty according to conditions, saying: 'Does this seeing, moreover, [coincide] with brightness...'"
Is it identical in essence with darkness, as well as with great empty space? Is it not identical? Is it both identical and not identical?
Or is it different and not different? Ānanda, if this seeing were fundamentally one essence with light, with darkness, and with empty space, then...

Thus, the two entities of light and darkness are mutually exclusive: when it is dark, there is no light; when it is light, there is no darkness. If light were identical with darkness, then light would lack the capacity for vision.
Conversely, if it were necessarily identical with light, it would have to cease to exist during darkness. If it has ceased, how can it perceive light or perceive darkness?
If light and darkness are distinct, yet your vision neither arises nor ceases, how can it be one?

If this essence of vision is not of the same substance as darkness or light, then, setting aside light, darkness, and empty space, what form or appearance would you find when analyzing the source of vision?
Detached from light and detached from darkness, and likewise detached from empty space, this faculty of seeing is fundamentally identical to the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.

Light, darkness, and empty space—these three things are all distinct; from what, then, could seeing be established? Light and darkness are mutually opposed; how could they ever be the same? Apart from these three, seeing simply does not exist.

In what sense are they different? The space and the vision are divided, yet originally they have no boundaries. In what sense are they not the same? They see darkness and they see light, yet their nature does not undergo change.
In what sense are they not different? You should examine this more minutely, scrutinize it with great care, and observe it with profound and subtle discernment.
Brightness comes from the sun; darkness comes from the dark moon. Penetration belongs to empty space; obstruction returns to the great earth.

Such being the case, from what source does this essence of vision arise? Vision is conscious while emptiness is inert; they are neither blended nor joined. It cannot be that the essence of vision arises spontaneously without a cause.

The third formation constitutes the Great Perception. It is said that this is equal to the aforementioned four great elements. Whether seen, heard, or known, its nature is perfectly pervasive and fundamentally unshakable.
One should know that this includes the boundless, immovable space as well as the shifting earth, water, fire, and wind.
All are equally named the six great elements; their nature is truly perfect and interfused, all being the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally without birth or extinction.

Ānanda, your nature is mired in samsara because you do not realize that your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. You should observe this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing:
are they born or do they perish? Are they identical or different? Are they neither born nor perishing? Are they neither identical nor different? (The Fourth Clarification)
Regarding the principle that true suchness (*tathatā*) is intrinsically complete:

you have never known that within the *tathāgatagarbha*, the nature-vision and the awakening-clarity, and the awakening-clarity and the spirit-vision, are primordially pure and pervade the entire dharma-realm.

This refers to the single [aspect] inherent within the unchanging substance of the *tathāgatagarbha*’s true suchness: "the nature-vision and the awakening-clarity, and the awakening-clarity and the spirit-vision."
The "Great" (Mahat) is seen as divided; it possesses one portion of the Great Consciousness (Vijñānamahat). By harmonizing these, the text speaks of "nature" (*xing*).

This is said in contrast to "phenomena" (*xiang*); for there is the seeing of nature and the seeing of phenomena, the awakening to nature and the awakening to phenomena, and the seeing of phenomena and the awakening to phenomena.

These constitute the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) within the ten realms, which, according to defiled or pure conditions, produces seeing and awakening. Now, this refers to the inherent goodness and inherent evil of that nature.
This seeing is true seeing; this awakening is true awakening. Thus, the nature of seeing is itself the clarity of awakening, and the essence of awakening is itself the clarity of seeing.
Therefore, speaking of it in reciprocal terms, one says: "The nature of seeing is the clarity of awakening; the essence of awakening is the clarity of seeing.
Furthermore, this seeing and awakening are in their substance eternally non-dual and without distinction; they are likewise non-dual in substance with the three virtues (triguṇa) that they possess.
Furthermore, there is no differentiation; therefore, it is said to be "pure and fundamental, pervading the dharma-realm.

This purity is the perception of the Great Wisdom (prajñā) within the [Three] Dharmas, also called the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya). This fundamental nature is the perception of the Great Liberation (vimukti) within the [Three] Dharmas, also called the Conventional Truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Pervading the entire dharma-realm, one immediately perceives the virtue of the Dharma-body within the "Middle. It is also called the Middle Way, the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Since it is said to be "pure," these six roots are fundamentally free from defilement. Since it is said to be "primordial" (*prakṛti*), these six roots are fundamentally not something created by an agent.
Since it is said to "pervade the dharma-realm," these six roots have been, from the beginning, utterly beyond [limitation].

This refers to the principle of the five consciousnesses remaining unchanging while following conditions. It is said: "In accordance with the minds of sentient beings, they respond to the extent of what is known.

Take, for example, the faculty of sight: its vision pervades the entire Dharma-realm. So too do hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the sensory awareness of touch; their wondrous qualities are brilliantly pure."
Pervading the entire Dharma-realm and filling the ten voids, how could there be any fixed location?
