It manifests according to karma, which is identical in meaning to the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra’s principle that [the mind] can follow defiled or pure conditions to fully create the ten Dharma-realms. That which it follows consists of the mind and karma:

the "mind" refers to the two types of mind—defiled and pure—within the ten Dharma-realms; "karma" refers to the two types of action—contrary and compliant—within the ten Dharma-realms. As for the three wisdoms of the Buddha-realm...

The mind is called the pure mind (*viśuddha-citta*). The minds of the nine realms characterized by the three delusions are called defiled minds (*kliṣṭa-citta*). The practices that accord with the nature within the Buddha-realm are called wholesome practices (*kuśala-karman*);

the practices that oppose the nature within the nine realms are called unwholesome practices (*akuśala-karman*). This refers to the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the Buddha-realm, which is the unchanging, wholesome nature.
Regarding the conditions that accord with the pure mind and follow its course, one forms the perception of cultivating goodness within the Buddha-realm.

From the perspective of those who have attained the fruit, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions gaze upon every single pure land, as numerous as atoms, without exception. Furthermore, the True Suchness (*tathatā*) of the nine realms remains unchanging;
yet, through conditions that oppose the defiled mind and follow its course, it forms the perception of cultivating evil within the nine realms. This applies to all Bodhisattvas and others.
He sees hundreds of thousands of worlds. Yet Āniruddha sees Jambudvīpa as clearly as one gazes at an *āmra* fruit in the palm of one's hand.
Venerable Ānanda, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, sees the first dhyāna without obstruction; he perceives sentient beings with penetrating vision.

It is simply that one has not yet reached the full measure. If we speak from the perspective of those who have reached the ultimate extremes of good and evil, then one gazes upon sentient beings with eyes of compassion, and the mass of their merit is an immeasurable ocean.

Just as a frightened pigeon entering the Buddha’s eye finds peace and is no longer afraid—like one who has entered the third dhyāna—even when first entering the shadow of Śāriputra, one is still startled and terrified, trembling and unsettled. This is not because the śrāvaka lacks ignorance.

Is it because the murderous intent has not yet been exhausted? Furthermore, when the dragon prince received the sutras from an Arhat, he did not allow him to look directly at his teacher because he still possessed the poison of sight;
were he to look at a person even once, the poisonous vapor would assault that person's skin and cause it to be consumed and scorched.
Seventh, regarding the meaning of the Great Consciousness being unchanging yet following conditions: first, it is revealed by means of phenomena currently visible that are easy to understand, saying:
"Ānanda, the nature of consciousness has no source; it arises falsely due to the six kinds of faculties and objects.
As you now observe the assembly of holy ones here, using your eyes to scan them, as those eyes look around, it is just like [the reflection] within a mirror. There is nothing...
Analyze them separately. Within this, your consciousness sequentially points them out:
"This is Mañjuśrī; this is Pūrṇa; this is Maudgalyāyana; this is Subhūti; this is Śāriputra. Next, clarify that the essence [of these] is empty according to conditions, saying:
"Does this consciousness that cognizes arise from seeing? Does it arise from forms? Does it arise from empty space? Or does it arise without cause, appearing suddenly?"
And so it emerges. Ānanda, if the nature of your consciousness were born within seeing, then the four—namely, darkness, light, and empty space—would necessarily not exist;
since your seeing would fundamentally be non-existent, and the nature of seeing itself would not even exist, from what could consciousness arise?

If the nature of your consciousness were born within the objects of perception and did not arise from seeing, then you would neither see light nor see darkness; light and darkness would not be beheld by you.

In the formless realm there is emptiness; since even its characteristics do not exist, from what could consciousness arise? If it were to arise within emptiness, it would be neither characteristic nor seeing.

Without seeing, there is no discernment, and thus one cannot know for oneself the clarity, darkness, form, or emptiness. When characteristics cease and conditions are extinguished, there is no seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.

There is no place for it to be established, as it lies outside these two categories. If it were empty, it would be the same as nothingness; if it were existent, it would not be the same as material objects.
Even if you were to give rise to consciousness, what would there be to differentiate? If it emerged suddenly without any cause, why do you not perceive a distinct moon during the day?
Examine this further with meticulous and subtle scrutiny. You see that consciousness relies upon your pupils to project toward external objects;

it takes form as existence and does not take form as non-existence. Given such conditions for consciousness, from what source does it arise? Consciousness moves while vision remains still; they are neither blended nor joined.
Hearing, listening, perceiving, and knowing are likewise thus. It should not be that consciousness arises from nowhere without a source.
These three aggregates form the "Great Consciousness," which is equalized with the aforementioned six elements.

If this conscious mind fundamentally has no origin, one should know that the discernment of seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing is perfect, tranquil, and its nature does not arise from any external source; this includes the empty space, earth, water, fire, and wind.
All are equally named the Seven Great Elements. Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious; they are all the Tathāgatagarbha. Ānanda, your mind is coarse and flighty;

you do not realize that seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. You should contemplate these six faculties of consciousness: are they the same or different? Are they empty or existent?
Are they neither the same nor different? Are they neither empty nor existent? [This clarifies] that the nature of True Suchness is inherently complete.
The principle of this is as follows: You originally do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature-consciousness is luminous knowing, and the awakened luminosity is the true consciousness.
This wondrous awakening is profound and still, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; it encompasses and emits the ten voids, so how could it have a specific location?

The "Tathāgatagarbha" refers to the essence of True Suchness (tathatā) which is immutable. "Nature-consciousness is luminous knowing, and the awakened luminosity is the true consciousness"—this points to the immutable essence of True Suchness.

Within this, the portion of the *vijñāna-mahābhūta* (consciousness element) that is possessed is contrasted with "clear knowing" (*jñāna*) and "enlightened awareness" (*bodhi*), and these are brought into harmony.

As for the term "nature" (*svabhāva*) used in the text, it is also spoken of in contrast to "phenomena" (*lakṣaṇa*). That is to say, there is the nature of consciousness and the nature of awareness, as well as the phenomena of consciousness and the phenomena of awareness.

These phenomena of consciousness and phenomena of awareness constitute the nature of the *tathatā* (suchness) of the ten realms; depending on defiled or pure conditions, they give rise to what are termed "consciousness" and "awareness. Here, the text points specifically to the goodness of the nature.
The consciousness of the nature of evil is awakening; this consciousness is clear knowing, and this awakening is true awakening. Therefore, it is said in reciprocal terms:

"The consciousness of nature is clear knowing; clear knowing is true consciousness. Yet this consciousness and awakening are, in essence, eternally non-dual and without differentiation from the nature itself.
They are likewise eternally non-dual and without differentiation from the nature of the three virtues that they possess. Hence, it is called "wondrous" (miao).
Awakened awareness is profoundly still and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, encompassing and manifesting the ten directions; how could it have a fixed location?

This profound stillness of wondrous awakening exists above the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-mahābhūta*), and it possesses the two virtues of *prajñā* (wisdom) and liberation (*vimukti*). It is also termed the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional.

Being pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, it is the merit of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) existing above the element of consciousness; it is also termed the Middle Way, the Truth of the Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-satya*). Since it is called "wondrous awakening,"...

In its profound stillness, these six consciousnesses are fundamentally free from defilement and agency. Since it is said that they pervade the entire dharma-realm, these six consciousnesses are, from the beginning, beyond all dependence.
Regarding the principle of "following conditions without changing," the Five Sciences explain:

they respond to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what is known, manifesting in accordance with karma; this is precisely the capacity of the *Avataṃsaka* to conform to both defiled and pure conditions.
They create the ten dharma-realms. That which accompanies them consists of mind and karma. Mind refers to the two types of mind—defiled and pure—within the ten dharma-realms.
Karma refers to the two modes of action, favorable and adverse, within the ten dharma-realms. Within the Buddha-realm, the mind of the three wisdoms is called the pure mind;

the minds of the three delusions within the nine realms are called the defiled mind. Within the Buddha-realm, action that accords with nature is called wholesome karma; [action] within the nine realms that opposes nature is...

"Action" refers to unwholesome karma. This means that the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the Buddha-realm, which is intrinsically good and immutable, can follow the conditions of wholesome karma arising from a pure mind to produce the consciousnesses that cultivate goodness within the Buddha-realm;

these are the *amala-vijñāna*, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), the Wondrous Observing Wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*), and the Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
Furthermore, the true suchness of the nine realms [of sentient beings], which is intrinsically evil and immutable, [functions in a corresponding manner].
Able to follow the conditions of defiled mental states and evil karma, it creates the consciousnesses of sentient beings in the nine realms.

Regarding Bodhisattvas who have not yet severed ignorance, they still abide within the eight consciousnesses. Regarding those of the Two Vehicles, with ignorance fully present, they are precisely within the eight consciousnesses.
Regarding ordinary beings of the six paths, the eight, seven, six, and five consciousnesses are all fully present.

The passages from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* concerning the seven elements cited above are all titled "True Suchness Unchanging Yet Adapting to Conditions," expressing the principle that there is no difference yet there is difference.
These are the sincere words from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata himself; they are not merely the arbitrary assertions of the Tiantai school.
To believe the Tathāgata is to believe Tiantai, and only by believing Tiantai does one truly believe the Tathāgata.
The guest said, “I have already heard the teaching regarding the principle that ‘the unchanging follows conditions, yet there is no difference within the differences.

How is it that this is called ‘following conditions while remaining unchanged’ and ‘differing while being without difference’? I replied, “If you can indeed believe in ‘no difference within the differences,’ how could you not believe in ‘difference while being without difference’?
However, superficial explanations are easy to understand, whereas the essential marrow of the meaning is difficult to clarify. If you wish to penetrate deeply into this principle, first...”

One must understand what has been cited above: within the single nature of True Suchness (tathatā), the principle that it is both undifferentiated yet differentiated, and differentiated yet undifferentiated, is already fully present.
For if one speaks in terms of the single nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, how could there be any distinction?

Nevertheless, since the nature of the Garbha already possesses the natures of the seven great elements, each of which is distinct and can serve as the cause for both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Thus, the principle that there is no difference yet there is difference is revealed. Although the seven great self-natures differ, they in reality abide together within a single nature;
herein the purport that there is difference yet no difference is revealed.

Since this single nature already possesses this principle, when it is able to follow conditions of defilement or purity to fully create the ten dharma-realms, then although defilement and purity—though [distinct]...

They are distinct, yet the distinction between good and evil arises; in reality, there is no differentiation within the unchanging essence of *tathatā* (suchness), yet distinctions emerge through the following of conditions (*pratyaya*).
For this reason, it is said that they are "undifferentiated yet differentiated. Since it is unchanging while following conditions, it must follow conditions while remaining unchanging.
Therefore, when following conditions to create the ten realms, it is said to be "differentiated yet undifferentiated. Now, I shall fully explain this according to the sutra.
Regarding the meaning of "responding to conditions within the midst," let us discuss it further with respect to the ruler. It is like the luminosity within the great element of fire:

when a household that has not yet eaten wishes to cook, one takes a sun-crystal (*ādityakānta*) in hand and seeks fire from the sun; in one place one holds the mirror, and in another place fire arises.

If one were to hold [the crystal] throughout the entire dharma-realm, fire would arise filling the world. Its arising pervades the world—how could it have a fixed location? Nevertheless, within the four quarters, zenith, and nadir...

Is it not the case that the same sunlight cannot be said to lack the nature of fire? When it pervades the world and fills the entire realm, can it not be said that what is without difference is yet different?
Thus, across thousands of places and ten thousands of locations, this is uniformly one fire;
can it not be said that what is different is yet without difference? Furthermore, fire has warmth as its nature; at the winter solstice, the yang...
The springing of wells and springs and the arising of warmth are fire. The arrival of spring and the emergence of the life-force within the myriad phenomena of the great earth are fire.
The circulation of warm breath from the crown of the head to the soles of the feet is fire. The radiance seen by the eyes and the smoke and flames rising from the nose are fire.
Yet, worldly people cling to the fire of form and are deluded regarding the fire of nature; they falsely give rise to distinctions between the self and its environment. Thus it begins.
The defiled mind discriminates between right and wrong; it may gain this while losing that, or cling to one thing while forgetting all others.
Yet the nature of that fire is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true fire—pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
The essence itself is luminous and illuminating; it is profoundly serene and pure. It has been so from the beginning, established by its own nature, without the slightest fabrication.
This is the body of Vairocana, which pervades the entire dharma-realm; how could it be subject to defilement or fabrication, or possess spatial location?

Such is the element of fire; the other elements may be understood accordingly. The principle that they are undifferentiated yet differentiated, and differentiated yet undifferentiated, is fully exhausted herein. — Guest.
He said, "I have already grasped the meaning of the *Saddharma*. May I hear it illustrated by a parable?

I replied, "The analogy of 'the unchanging following conditions while following conditions remains unchanging' was first demonstrated in general by the Tathāgata at the beginning of the section on the Seven Elements (*dhātu*).
Now that you wish to clarify it through a parable, I shall rely on the scripture’s metaphor of ice and water, proceeding by means of nine analogies."

These together constitute ten metaphors: first, the metaphor of ice and water; second, the metaphor of the space within a vessel; third, the metaphor of waves and water; fourth, the metaphor of bubbles and the ocean;
fifth, the metaphor of moonlight and water; sixth, the metaphor of sunlight and fire; seventh, the metaphor of wind and space; eighth, the metaphor of form and space;
ninth, the metaphor of gold and vessels; tenth, the metaphor of springtime.

First, the analogy of ice and water: Because Ānanda doubted the Buddha’s frequent teaching that all the various transformations in the world arise through the manifestation of the combination of the four great elements, [he asked] how it could be that the Tathāgata rejects both causes and conditions as well as spontaneity.
The Buddha then demonstrated the meaning of being neither combined nor non-combined. First, he demonstrated that it is not combined.

It cannot be said that they are combined. If the essence of those great elements were not itself a combination, it could not intermingle with the various elements, just as empty space does not combine with material forms.
An ancient said: "This refers to True Suchness following conditions; it is not like the nature of inert emptiness.
Next, he shows that it cannot be said that they are combined. If they were combined, they would be identical to transformations. At the beginning...
Ultimately, they form characteristics; arising and ceasing continue in succession. Birth and death, death and birth, birth and death, death and birth—like a whirling firebrand, there is no rest.
An ancient said: "This refers to the unchanging nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is not the same as the characteristics of transformation and so forth.
It is not that non-harmony is impossible, yet harmony is also impossible. This principle is profound and mysterious, ultimately difficult to demonstrate. Therefore...
He illustrates this with a metaphor, saying: "It is like water turning into ice, and ice returning to water.

This metaphor represents True Suchness (tathatā) remaining unchanging while following conditions, and following conditions while remaining unchanged. For when water turns into ice, it is the severity of the cold that causes it;

when ice turns into water, it is the warmth of spring that causes it. If there were no such harmonious convergence, for what reason would water become ice, and for what reason would ice [become water]?"
Thus, it becomes water. If they were merely a combination, how could water combine to become ice, and how could ice combine to become water?

It is simply this: "Unchanging yet following conditions; following conditions yet unchanging. In this analogy, one should take the nature of moisture to represent the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the seven great elements.
Water represents the appearance of the Buddha-dharmadhātu following conditions, while ice represents the nine dharma-realms following [conditions].

The characteristics of conditions: severe cold is a metaphor for defiled conditions, and the warm spring is a metaphor for pure conditions. Following the severe cold to form ice, the moisture remains unimpaired;

following the warm spring to form water, the moisture likewise does not change. This is a metaphor for how, following defiled conditions, the nine [realms] are formed, yet the nature of *tathatā* is not diminished;
and following pure conditions, Buddhahood is attained, yet the nature of *tathatā*— [Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
There is no increase. The subsequent text extensively elucidates the seven great elements (*mahābhūta*), none of which fail to reveal this principle.

By employing metaphors to illustrate the Dharma and the Dharma to illustrate the metaphors, the meaning of "unchanging yet conforming to conditions" (*avikṛta-anupravṛtti*)—the sense that there is no differentiation while there is differentiation, and differentiation while there is no differentiation—is established.
Regarding the second analogy of the empty vessel, the text also originates from the meaning of the original sūtra, though its interpretation differs slightly from the present one.
According to the sūtra’s meaning, because Ānanda doubted whether the nature of seeing expands or contracts, the Tathāgata refuted this by saying:

"All things in the world—whether large or small, internal or external—all various activities belong to the preceding sense-objects; one should not say that seeing expands or contracts. It is, for example," [as follows].
Within a square vessel, one sees a square void. I ask you again: Is this square void seen within the square vessel fixed as square, or is it not fixed as square?
If it were fixed as square, then when a round vessel is placed there instead, the void should not become round.
If it were not fixed, then while inside the square vessel, there should be no square void. You say that you do not know where this principle resides; such is the nature of the principle.
It is so. How can it be said to "exist"? Ānanda, if one wishes to cause [the space] to enter into that which has no squareness or roundness, one merely removes the squareness of the vessel;
the substance of space itself has no directionality. One should not say that there is a further removal of the spatial characteristics or their location within the void.

The meaning of the sutra uses space as a metaphor for the nature of vision (*darśana-svabhāva*), and the vessel as a metaphor for all the worlds and the various activities of great and small objects. Now, this [passage] borrows...
Space serves as a metaphor for the essence of True Suchness (tathatā), which is unchanging and undifferentiated.
The various square and round vessels are borrowed as metaphors for the differentiated functions of the ten realms that arise according to conditions.

Although space itself possesses no size, shape, or form, it does not hinder the manifestation of spaces of varying sizes and shapes according to the differences of the vessels; yet within space itself, there is certainly no differentiation. Within the various vessels, however—
Therefore, there are differences. Nevertheless, that which exists in empty space is the same as this emptiness; that which exists within the various vessels is likewise the same as this emptiness.

This may be used as a metaphor for "following conditions without changing" (不變隨緣), which is non-differentiated yet differentiated, and "not changing while following conditions" (隨緣不變), which is differentiated yet non-differentiated.
This is such that throughout the day there is no change and no deviation, yet it does not hinder the deviations that follow conditions;

throughout the day there are deviations following conditions, yet they do not hinder the state of being unchanging and non-deviating. Unchanging yet following deviation, essence and function are eternally identical;

non-deviating yet deviating, unity and difference are always the same. For one who skillfully contemplates these metaphors, there is neither innate goodness nor innate evil, neither cultivated goodness nor cultivated evil.
"Differentiation is differentiation; yet, through differentiation, the principle of non-differentiation is attained.
Regarding the metaphor of the waves on water: for example, in the world there is no water that is not wavy, nor are there waves that are not moist.
While the distinction between movement and stillness exists within the water itself, within the moisture there is certainly no difference between the waves and the water. Therefore...

Moisture is used as a metaphor for the nature of *tathatā* (suchness), which is unchanging and undifferentiated; water is used as a metaphor for its function, which manifests differentiations according to conditions.
Just as one knows that the moist nature is no different whether in water or in waves, one can thereby realize that the *tathatā* of practicing good and practicing evil is not distinct.
This demonstrates that not only are the natures of essence and function eternally identical, but it also reveals that the fundamental substance of the gates of seeing and cultivation is likewise one.
This is different. The principle that birth-and-death is itself nirvana and afflictions are themselves bodhi, as taught by Vimalakīrti, is thereby established.
Regarding the analogy of the hundred-thousand bubbles in the ocean, the Sūtra rebukes those who mistake the self for external objects, saying:

"It is like abandoning hundreds of thousands of clear, vast oceans and instead identifying with a single bubble, regarding its body as the entirety of the tide, exhausting the whole expanse of the sea. Yet, as for the bubble...
Is the bubble not the ocean? Is the bubble different from the ocean? The sutra merely refutes people who mistake objects for themselves and take the small to be the great.
If one realizes that the myriad things are one's own self, and transforms those things so as to be identical with the Tathāgata, then one knows that the entire ocean is but a bubble.
A bubble returns to encompass the ocean; one awakens to the fact that the entire bubble is identical to the ocean, for the ocean does not exist apart from the bubble.

This is spoken of in terms of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the bubble, which is merely a single floating froth. Compared to that great ocean, it is more vastly different than the distance between a hair-tip and a world-system (*lokadhātu*).

One who can contemplate the essence (*tattva*) of the bubble finds that although the characteristic of the bubble is small, the essence of the bubble is vast. Therefore, all Tathāgatas manifest [the Dharma] upon a single hair-tip.
The Jewel King’s land: sitting within a mote of dust, he turns the Great Dharma Wheel.

It is precisely because of this that the ocean serves as a metaphor for the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*), and the bubble serves as a metaphor for its function in accordance with conditions. Taking the entire ocean to constitute a single bubble can be used as a metaphor for the entirety of the unchanging essence of True Suchness functioning in accordance with conditions;
taking the entire bubble to exist within the ocean can be used as a metaphor for the entirety of the function of following conditions existing within [the essence].
The essence gives rise to a thousand bubbles; yet this does not hinder the undifferentiated state from appearing as differentiated. The single ocean remains tranquil;

yet this does not hinder it from following conditions without changing. If one can comprehend the metaphor of the bubbles and the ocean, then the principles of "unchanging while following conditions" and "following conditions while remaining unchanged," and of "non-differentiation within differentiation" and "differentiation within non-differentiation," will be understood by more than half.

Regarding the analogy of the water in the fifth month: the following four analogies originate from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. They originally pertain to the Dharma, but are now borrowed as metaphors to illuminate that Dharma.
This is because the explanations in the sūtra’s text employ matters that are relatively mundane and shallow to illustrate the practice of cultivation.
This clarifies the meaning of the nature of water following conditions (*pratyaya*). Now, speaking by way of analogy, there is no fault. As the sutra says: "The nature of water is not fixed;
its flowing and ceasing are not constant. For instance, in the city of Śrāvastī, there were the mahāsiddhas Kapila, Kālakarṇin, and Padma, who were great illusionists.
They sought the essence of the moon to mix with their illusion-inducing medicines. These...

O Masters: On a day during the waxing moon, one holds a *fangzhu* (the "square-jade" concave mirror) in the hand to receive water from the moon. If one holds the pearl in one place, water emerges in that one place;
if one holds it throughout the entire *dharmadhātu*, water arises filling the *dharmadhātu*. When it arises filling the world, how could there be any fixed location?
Now, the moon in the sky is used as a metaphor for the unchanging essence of *tathatā* (suchness), while the water received is used as a metaphor for [the essence] responding to conditions.
Regarding the function of differentiation: the moonlight in the sky does not hinder its remaining unchanged throughout the day while following conditions;
the water in one’s hand does not hinder its following conditions throughout the day without changing.

Therefore, those who can thoroughly understand the metaphors of the sky and the water will grasp the principle that the True Nature is unchanging yet follows conditions, and that it follows conditions without changing.

The *Six-Day Fire Simile Sūtra* states: "Observe the households within the city that have not yet eaten. When they wish to cook their food, they hold a sun-mirror (*ādityakānta*) in their hands and seek fire from the sun.
You should know that when worldly people hold a mirror in one place, fire arises in another.

Since this holds true throughout the entire dharma-realm, fire arises everywhere in the world; as it arises pervasively throughout the world, how could it have a fixed location? Now, consider the sun in the sky."

The fire filling the world symbolizes the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*) which does not change; the fire in the sky symbolizes its function that differentiates according to conditions (*pratyaya*).
The fire in the sky is no different from the fire in the hand, and the fire in the hand is no different from the fire in the sky.

This serves as a metaphor for the unchanging nature of True Suchness: it is undifferentiated yet differentiated, while its function of freely manifesting transformations is differentiated yet undifferentiated.
The meaning of this is very clear.
Regarding the analogy of the wind and space, the Sūtra says: "The nature of wind has no substance; its movement and stillness are not constant.

When you straighten your robes and enter the great assembly, the corner of your saṃghāṭī moves and reaches a bystander, whereby a subtle breeze arises that brushes against that person’s face. As it is said:
As you alone slightly move your robe, a subtle breeze arises; it sweeps throughout the Dharma-realm, fills the lands, and pervades the entire world.

How could it have a fixed location? Now, empty space is used as a metaphor for the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is immutable, while the wind is a metaphor for its function, which transforms and creates in accordance with conditions.
The wind in the sky is no different from the wind that brushes one’s face; the wind that brushes one’s face [is no different from the wind in the sky].
It is no different from the wind in the sky. The wind in the sky serves as a metaphor for the unchanging essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is undifferentiated yet differentiated.
The wind that brushes against one’s face serves as a metaphor for the function of transformation according to conditions (*pratyaya*), which is differentiated yet undifferentiated.
The meaning of this is exceedingly clear.
Regarding the eighth analogy of emptiness as color, the Sūtra says: "Ānanda, the nature of emptiness has no form; it is manifested through color.
For example, in the city of Śrāvastī, at a place far from the river, various Kṣatriyas and others have newly established a dwelling. They dig a well to seek water.

When they have removed one foot of earth, there is one foot of empty space within it. In this manner, even up to when they have removed ten feet of earth, there is likewise [ten feet of empty space] within."
One obtains one *zhang* of empty space. The depth of this empty space corresponds to the amount that has emerged, just as when there is the emptiness of a well, the emptiness arises within that well;
the empty space of the ten directions is likewise so. It fills the ten directions completely—how could it have a fixed location?

This passage extensively clarifies that empty space and earth fundamentally have no different causes, which is identical to the previous principle that "the nature of form is directly emptiness" and "the nature of emptiness is true form."

The meaning is this: thus, emerging from the earth one attains emptiness. Emptiness and form are fundamentally of one substance. The emptiness within emptiness is precisely the emptiness within the earth;
the emptiness within the earth is precisely the emptiness within emptiness. The emptiness within emptiness does not change, and the emptiness within the earth likewise does not change.
Since the emptiness within emptiness does not change yet follows conditions, it is able to become the emptiness within the earth. Thus...

That which is without differentiation appears differentiated; the space within a well, though it undergoes transformation according to conditions, is in reality differentiated yet without differentiation.

This serves as a metaphor for the essence of *tathatā* (suchness), which is unchanging. That it is "without differentiation yet differentiated" as it transforms according to conditions, and "differentiated yet without differentiation," is also exceedingly clear.
The metaphor of the nine gold vessels refers to gold that has been extracted from the ore, not gold still within the ore.

If one were to take the gold still within the ore, it would be indistinguishable from the "Middle Way Buddha-nature" taught in the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), wherein afflictions are distinct from bodhi and true suchness changes as it follows conditions.
Now, taking the gold extracted from the ore is like the gentleman who is "not a mere vessel"; he is beyond the constraints of good and evil.
All are capable; it is merely that one manifests one's own particular capability—what fault could there be in this?

Thus, among the various vessels made of gold, although there are distinctions such as Buddha images, statues of living beings, jars, basins, hairpins, and bracelets, when viewed from the perspective of their essential substance of gold, they are one and no different.

The essence of gold is non-dual; this may be used as a metaphor for the unchanging substance of *tathatā* (suchness). The differentiation of various vessels may be used as a metaphor for the functioning of transformation according to conditions (*pratyaya*).

Just as pure gold does not obstruct the various vessels, and the various vessels do not lose their golden nature, the principle is established that *tathatā* is undifferentiated in its unchanging state yet differentiated through its transformations, and differentiated in its transformations according to conditions yet undifferentiated in its essence.
The tenth analogy, that of the "Warm Spring," compares it to the way the warm spring brings all things into being. In reality, it is tranquil and motionless;

yet when it encounters a stimulus, it immediately manifests. Thus, when plants and forests are touched by it, they sprout at once; when peaches, plums, apricots, and willows are moved by it, they immediately blossom with fragrance.
The warm spring pervades the myriad species, yet it does not hinder its lack of differentiation from appearing as differentiation within each and every thing.
All possess the spirit of the "Warm Spring" (Yanchun); it does not hinder their differentiation while remaining undifferentiated.

This serves as an analogy for True Suchness (*tathatā*), which remains unchanging while conforming to conditions (*anuparivartin*), and conforms to conditions while remaining unchanged. Thus, the principle that "it is undifferentiated yet differentiated" becomes clear, and the meaning that "it is differentiated yet undifferentiated" is without error.

The guest said: "I have already understood through the preceding analogies the principle that True Suchness (Tathatā) remains unchanging while following conditions, being undifferentiated yet differentiated;
and that while following conditions it remains unchanged, being differentiated yet undifferentiated. What is meant by the 'Gate of the Innate Endowment of the Causal Mind, Lacking Nothing at All'?
I replied: "The 'causal mind' refers to the present state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), who aspires to the Buddha-fruit and cultivates the causes."
This is the mind [of the practitioner]. Although the arousal of the mind (cittotpāda) is indeed vast, in terms of its objective sphere, it still remains within the realm of the aggregates (skandha).

Thus, one takes as the object of observation the very thought that arises in daily life when the sense faculties (indriya) encounter their objects (viṣaya)—whether it be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate;
whether it be a mundane mind or a supramundane mind. Such a mind belongs to the sixth consciousness (manovijñāna).
It is called the "aggregate-mind" (*skandha-citta*) and is also called the "human mind.

Regarding the phrase "originally possessed," it refers precisely to this mind, which among the ten realms must necessarily belong to one realm. If the mind of the three bonds and five constants arises, this is the human realm.

When this one realm manifests, it is termed "phenomenal creation" (*shi-zao*); at that time, the other nine realms remain latent. Within the single nature, this is termed "principle-endowment" (*li-ju*).

Furthermore, this single realm possesses ten suchnesses (*tathatā*). That which is distinguishable by grasping at external objects is called the "suchness of appearance" (*lakṣaṇa-tathatā*) of the human realm.

That which, based on internal self-nature, remains unchanging, is called the "suchness of nature" (*svabhāva-tathatā*) of the human realm. The fundamental substance of the human realm is called its "suchness of essence" (*bhāva-tathatā*).
The functional capacity to cultivate the goodness of precepts is called the "suchness of power" (*bala-tathatā*) of the human realm. [The capacity for] constructing the framework...
Constancy is called the human realm acting in such a manner; practicing this habitually until it becomes a seed is called the human realm having such a cause;

being aided by the requisites for goodness and crossing over to liberation is called the human realm having such conditions; manifesting dignified deportment that makes one a venerable man is called the human realm having such a fruit;
and being reborn in a central land as a wealthy, noble king or lord is called the human realm having such a retribution.

The initial characteristic is the root; the final culmination is the branch. These ten suchnesses are compressed within a single thought-moment and are ultimately ungraspable—this is the truth of non-existence (*amṛṣā-satya*).
Although they are ungraspable, the ten dharmas remain distinct and manifest—this is the truth of existence (*satya*). All of these are Buddha-nature.
Each and every one is true and eternal; this is precisely the Middle Truth, which is called "the ultimate equality of beginning and end.

Furthermore, each possesses ten kinds of suchness regarding the five aggregates, ten kinds of suchness regarding the land, and ten kinds of suchness regarding provisional names, thus constituting thirty kinds of suchness.
Within this single realm, while existing within a single nature, its essential substance is interfused with the natures of the other nine dharma-realms, each...
Each is mutually complete. Thus, each single realm contains ten dharma-realms, forming one hundred dharma-realms. Within one realm there are ten "thusnesses" (yǒurúshì);
within one hundred realms, there are one thousand "thusnesses. When these are applied across the provisional names of the five aggregates and the lands, they form three thousand "thusnesses.
These three thousand are discussed merely in terms of a single round of mutual completion; if every successive round were mutually complete, they would amount to ten trillion.

These virtues cannot be enumerated by counting their heads. Since their nature is the three truths and the three virtues, this dharma of the "one thought-moment as the three thousand" has the Dharma-body as its essence;
it is omnipresent throughout the entire Dharma-realm. Therefore, its nature is prajñā.

Each and every thing is illuminated as clearly as a great light in the sky; there is no hidden place it does not penetrate. Being entirely free from afflictions (*kleśa*), one constantly dwells in liberation.

Transcending all worldly burdens, one is completely free from the bonds of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Thus, the mind of such a person is non-dual and indistinguishable from Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
To understand this in such a way is called "seeing nature" (*darśana-dharmatā*); to illuminate and perceive it in such a way is called "attainment."

The Buddha’s words and the teachings of Tiantai—specifically the statement that "directly pointing to the human mind, one sees one's nature and becomes a Buddha"—are precisely what is seen here and what is accomplished here.
To speak in this manner is called "discussing nature through cultivation" (*jiu-xiu lun-xing*); it is not "nature being accomplished through nature" (*ji-xing cheng-xing*).
As for discussing nature through nature, this has already been fully explained previously in the first section, "The Gate of the Ten Realms Lurking in the Unchanging True Suchness. Although...
This is the nature of cultivation itself. It is essentially no different from the first gate;

however, while the former is the nature of nature itself—like discussing the ocean as being the ocean—this present gate is the nature of cultivation—like pointing to a bubble and finding it to be the ocean.

This is truly because True Suchness (tathatā) remains immutable while following conditions to manifest this single thought-moment; thus, though there is no difference, there is a difference. Therefore...

In accordance with conditions, a single thought-moment is, in its very essence, unchanging. Though differentiated, it is without differentiation; within the thousand suchnesses of the realms and the three thousand natures and appearances, there is the Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Vimukti.
It is like carving sandalwood, where every fragment is fragrant; like breaking a white jade disk, where every piece is authentic;
like pounding ten thousand kinds of incense into pills, where even if one particle is burned, it fully possesses the fragrance of all.
It is like a person entering the great ocean to bathe; having already used the waters of all the rivers, it is further illustrated by the ten preceding metaphors:
just as water becomes ice, yet the ice is still water; just as space enters a vessel, yet the vessel does not differ from space;

just as water becomes waves, yet the waves are still water; just as bubbles arise from the sea, yet the substance of the bubble is entirely the sea; and even as with the moon reflected in water, and so forth.

It is like the sun and fire; like wind and space; like space and form; like golden vessels; like the warmth of spring. All these are unchanging yet follow conditions, and though they follow conditions, they do not change.
They are without difference yet differ; they differ yet are without difference.

The guest asked again: "In the previous 'Gate of True Suchness Not Changing While Following Conditions,' you have already fully discussed the two types of retribution—the environment and the body—across the ten realms.

Thus, the physical form and the environment of the body are nothing other than what is inherently possessed by nature (*xingju*). Consequently, when following conditions, there is nothing that is not universally created;

everything may be discussed in terms of the principle of 'following conditions while remaining unchanging. Now, however, you speak only of the mind being fundamentally possessed, addressing it solely from the perspective of the mind, and—"
"Why do you not speak of the body-color as being based on both the primary and secondary [realms]? I replied:

"This is because the Tiantai school’s Perfect Teaching of Innate Endowment (xingju yuanzong) specifically takes the nature-endowment of both matter and mind, as well as both the primary and secondary realms, as its basis. Thus, when following conditions, there is nothing that is not universally created.

Furthermore, the matter and mind, and the primary and secondary realms that are created, all, in their very essence, are the unchanging within the changing as they follow conditions. Therefore, the Patriarch Ziming said: 'Furthermore, one should understand...'"
Know that the wondrously inconceivable essence of the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm constitutes my single thought-moment;

furthermore, its entire substance manifests as sentient beings and Buddhas, as the support and the supported, as the sense organs and their objects. From the single mind to a single speck of dust, down to a single atom, there is nothing that does not manifest as the entire body [of the Dharma-realm].
Since each and every phenomenon manifests as the entirety of the Dharma-realm, to take up any single phenomenon is itself [the Dharma-realm].
The entire portion of the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm is the whole Dharma-realm itself. Since it is the whole Dharma-realm, what single dharma could there be that does not possess all dharmas?
Therefore, one knows that the three virtues of the Dharma-realm are not large; the three virtues of a single thought-moment are not small; the three virtues of an ocean of lands are not many;
and the three virtues of a single mote of dust are not few. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The mind is like a skilled painter, creating the various five aggregates. All...
In this world, there is nothing that is not created by the mind. As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha; as it is with the Buddha, so it is with sentient beings.

Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. The present school precisely relies on this principle to explain the "wondrous Dharma" (*saddharma*) in the title of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
That is to say, "Dharma" refers to the three dharmas of mind, Buddha, and sentient beings; "wondrous" refers to the non-differentiation of these three.
Indeed, although all three are without distinction, if we consider what is proximate and essential, nothing is more essential than the mind. Thus, the Great Master Tiantai said:
"The Buddha-dharma is too lofty and sentient beings are too vast; for a beginner, this is difficult. Yet, since the three are without distinction, contemplating the mind is easy.
Now, speaking from the perspective of what is proximate and essential for worldly people, I shall single out the dharma of the mind, rather than relying on the physical body or form.

It is correct, yet it is not discussed in full detail. Therefore, one should know that the sentient beings' form and mind, as well as their environment and its inhabitants—down to a single thought-moment and a single speck of dust—are in no way deficient compared to the unchanging essence of True Suchness (tathatā).
Treatise on the Innate Goodness and Evil of Human Nature, Volume Two;
Treatise on the Innate Goodness and Evil of Human Nature, Volume Three.
Written by the Śramaṇa Chuandeng of Youxi at Mount Tiantai.

The guest asked: "If the mind is fundamentally complete and lacks nothing from the very beginning, and one has already received this instruction, then how is it that upon the perfect realization of the fruit-ground there is not the slightest alteration?
What is the meaning of this? I replied: "In the previous section, we discussed the dharmas of the sentient being's mind as being fundamentally complete within the causal stage."
It is luminous and entirely without deficiency. Although it is discussed in contrast to the essence of *tathatā* (suchness), it is not deficient;

yet, when discussed in contrast to the state of the Tathāgata’s fruition, it is without discrepancy. Now, within this gate, although it is discussed in contrast to the unchanging nature of *tathatā*, it does not change;

yet, when discussed in contrast to the arising of the mind, it is without discrepancy. This is because, regarding the mental phenomena of sentient beings, once the faculties, objects, and thoughts arise...
Possessing the thousand suchnesses of the hundred realms and the three thousand natures and characteristics, these are precisely the true, the conventional, and the middle.

Therefore, that which is cultivated by the practitioner of the Perfect Teaching is the illumination of this inconceivable realm; as for the perfect realization at the stage of fruition, it is the verification of this inconceivable realm.
Thus, Master Jingxi said: "When the three thousand are not yet manifest, they are collectively termed ignorance. The three thousand...

Since this has been clarified, both are equally termed "Eternal and Blissful. The Venerable Master Siming said: "Furthermore, one should know that the meaning of the 'Six Identities' (liu ji) does not apply exclusively to the Buddha.

For all beings—whether provisional or real, belonging to the Three Vehicles, humans, or devas, and extending downward even to dung beetles (*kēqiāng*) and those in the hells, including their form and mind—one must distinguish their beginning and end through the six identities.
That is to say: there is the dung beetle of principle (*lǐ kēqiāng*), the dung beetle of name (*míngzì*), and so on, up to the ultimate dung beetle (*jiūjìng kēqiāng*)."

When discussing the ten realms (*daśadhātu*), since they are all the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), there is nothing that is not the *dharmadhātu*. Because this single essence is unalterable, the names [of the realms] do not merely manifest the Buddha;
rather, the other nine are likewise revealed. Upon the attainment of fruition, all ten reach ultimate perfection.

This is precisely because the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the ten realms, as an immutable substance, is able to follow conditions (*pratyaya*); thus, by following conditions, it brings about the formation of the ten realms. Its substance...
It is unchanging. Now, discussing the state of Buddhahood (*buddhatva*), it is formed through the pure conditions (*viśuddha-pratyaya*) that give rise to the Buddha-dharmadhātu;
yet the ten kinds of dharmadhātus inherent within the nature of *tathatā* (Suchness), as well as the three truths (*trisatya*), are all entirely unchanging.
It is simply that while the Buddha-realm manifests, the other nine realms remain latent; this is what is termed "Buddha. In reality, those nine realms that remain latent undergo no change whatsoever.

Now, to provide extensive citations from the scriptures, it is clearly demonstrated that this is not empty talk. There are five general points: first, to prove that the ground of fruition is the perfect realization of the nature of the ten realms;
second, to prove that the ground of fruition is the perfect realization of the substance of the three truths;

third, to prove that the ground of fruition is the perfect manifestation of the functions of both the one and the many; fourth, to prove that the ground of fruition is the perfect manifestation of the functions of the ten realms; fifth, to prove... [text ends]
Regarding the matter of the wondrous function of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*):

first, as for those who have realized the nature of the ten realms through the perfect realization of the stage of fruition—if one were to cite proofs from other Mahāyāna sūtras extensively, the passages explaining the perfect realization of the ten realms are exceedingly numerous.
For now, I shall briefly cite examples that are easily accessible before the eyes of the great assembly.
In the sutras—such as the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*—the Tathāgata, within the manifestation of his own realization, says:
"I, by means of the non-extinguishing and non-arising, unite with the Tathāgatagarbha. This Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally luminous and wondrously mental;

it is mind, it is emptiness, it is earth, water, fire, and wind, it is the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, it is forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and dharmas, and it is the sphere of visual consciousness."
In this way, it extends even to the consciousness-element (*vijñāna-dhātu*). This refers to the Tathāgata reaching the stage of fruition;

he is fundamentally endowed with the six realms of ordinary beings (*ṣaḍ-gati-dharmadhātu*) without losing his own nature. Furthermore, it says: "It is precisely enlightenment (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*); it is the exhaustion of enlightenment and ignorance.

In this way, it extends even to aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), and the exhaustion of aging and death; to suffering (*duḥkha*) and its accumulation (*samudaya*); to cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*); and to wisdom (*jñāna*) and...
It is so. This means that when the Tathāgata reaches the ultimate fruit, he is inherently endowed with the dharma-realm of the two vehicles and does not lose his original nature.
Furthermore, it is said: "It is itself *dāna*, it is itself *śīla*, it is itself *vīrya*, it is itself *kṣānti*, it is itself *dhyāna*, and it is itself *prajñā*;
it is itself the *pāramitā*. This means that when the Tathāgata reaches the stage of fruition, he is inherently endowed with the dharmas of the Bodhisattvas.
The realm (*dhātu*) does not lose its own nature. In this way, it extends even to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, Great Nirvāṇa, the Permanent, the Blissful, the Self, and the Pure.

This refers to the Tathāgata reaching the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), wherein the Buddha-realm originally possessed is finally realized as ultimate. Viewed in this light, is this not the ground of fruition?
Is it the perfect realization of the nature of the ten realms?
Second, regarding the perfect realization of the essence of the three truths upon attaining the fruit-ground: this is the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrously luminous primordial mind.

It is "neither" (non-existent) in relation to all ten realms; precisely because it is "neither," it eliminates conceptual clinging so that not even a speck of dust is established. Thus, the ten dharma-realms are all...
"Emptiness" is the virtue of *prajñā*. It is further said: "The Tathāgata-garbha is the original luminosity of the mind, wondrous;

the ten realms are all identical within it. This identity is precisely what establishes the dharmas; thus, the myriad phenomena appear in their full array, and these very ten dharma-realms all possess the virtue of liberation.
It is further said: "The Tathāgata-garbha is the wondrous luminosity of the mind's origin; the ten realms are all detached from it. This detachment is neither 'is' nor 'is not.'"

Precisely because both extremes—identity and difference—are simultaneously discarded so that neither remains, yet identity and difference are not absent, such that the true and the conventional are perfectly distinct;
this is the virtue of the Dharma-body. Furthermore, these three truths and three virtues are all expounded without departing from the ten dharma-realms.

Is it not the case that by possessing the ten realms and three truths as causes, one cultivates the three contemplations of the ten realms, thereby realizing the three virtues of the ten realms as the fruit?

Regarding the third point, the manifestation of the functions of unity and multiplicity upon the ground of fruition through realization, the Sūtra says: "I, by means of non-extinction and non-arising, unite with the Tathāgata-garbha;
and this Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, within it, one becomes the infinite, and the infinite becomes one. Within the small, the large appears; within the large, the small appears. Even upon the tip of a single hair..."

Manifesting the Jewel-King Land, one sits within a single mote of dust and turns the Great Dharma Wheel. This is precisely because the ten realms are inherently complete within the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

When the environmental retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*) is but a single mote of dust and the personal retribution (*pratibhoga-vipāka*) is but a single hair, every form and every mind is none other than the unchanging essence of *tathatā*.
When these manifest as the environment and the person, as form and mind, according to pure conditions, then every single hair and every single mote of dust is none other than [the true reality].
The Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Now, because it is perfectly realized in accordance with its nature, it is perfectly manifested in accordance with its nature.

One is precisely the Dharma-realm; it is the one within the immeasurable. The immeasurable is also the Dharma-realm; it is the immeasurable within the one. Thus, even the minute is the Dharma-realm, and the vast is also the Dharma-realm.

The primary retribution (vipākaphala) of a single hair is the Dharma-realm, and the secondary retribution (niśraya-phala) of a single speck of dust is also the Dharma-realm. A single hair, a single...
The dust of the dharma-realm is not small; the ocean of immeasurable lands and the dharma-realm are not large.

Being neither large nor small, they are thus able to contain one another within a single hair-pore, where the one and the many are sovereignly interpenetrating. This is precisely analogous to the bubble and the ocean, the vessel and the space, the wave and the moisture, and the ice and the water;

the remaining six metaphors are likewise so. Therefore, when the wondrous, enlightened nature of true suchness is manifested—the natural radiance of the original ground—it is realized that this is nothing extraordinary.
This is indeed special.

Regarding the fourth point—attaining the fruit of realization and fully manifesting the functions of the ten realms—the sutra describes Avalokiteśvara’s cultivation of the perfect penetration of the ear faculty:

"When birth-and-death has ceased and quiescent extinction is manifested before one, suddenly transcending both the mundane and supramundane worlds, [one perceives] the ten directions as a perfect whole."

Illumination. One attains two forms of excellence: first, above, one merges with the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind of all Buddhas of the ten directions, sharing the same compassionate power as the Buddha-Tathāgatas;
second, below, one merges with the sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, sharing the same sorrowful longing.
Now, to merge above with the Buddhas of the ten directions and below with the sentient beings of the six realms—could this not be the fruit-stage, the perfect realization of the ten realms?
Is this not their nature? As for the arising of function from essence, it is said:
"By virtue of my making offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, I have received from that Tathāgata the Vajra Samādhi of illusory-like hearing-perfuming and hearing-cultivation.
Because I share the same compassionate power as the Buddha-Tathāgatas, my body has become the thirty-two transformations, entering all lands. These thirty-two transformations...

Transcending the ten realms, the Sūtra says: "If there are bodhisattvas who enter samādhi and advance in the cultivation of the untainted (anāsrava), such that their resolute understanding (adhimukti) becomes fully manifest, I manifest in the form of a Buddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.

This is a manifestation from the fundamental, inherently possessed Buddha-dharmadhātu which has been realized. The Sūtra further says: "If there are those in training (śaikṣa) whose tranquil, wondrously luminous resolute understanding becomes manifest..."
"Oṃ! Before them, I manifest the body of a Pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.

If there are those in training who have severed the twelve links of dependent origination, and through the excellence of that severance, the supreme and wondrous nature manifests perfectly, I appear before them in the form of a Pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma, causing them to attain liberation.
This arises from the fundamentally inherent Pratyekabuddha-dharmadhātu which they have realized."

This refers to those who manifest [themselves]. The Sūtra says: "If there are those in training (śaikṣa) who have realized the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths and enter cessation through the cultivation of the path, such that their sublime and wondrous [attainments] are fully perfected, I appear before them in the form of a śrāvaka and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.
This is a manifestation from the inherently present śrāvaka-dharmadhātu as it is realized. The Sūtra says: "If there are sentient beings who desire..."
Their minds were clearly awakened; they did not transgress against the dust of desire, and their desire-minds were pure.

Before them, I manifested in the body of a Brahmā King and preached the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation. This was a manifestation from the inherently possessed Dharma-realm of the Brahmā Kings realized therein.
As the Sūtra says: "If there are sentient beings who wish for mastery over their bodies and to travel throughout the ten directions, I [manifest before them]..."
Before them, I manifest the body of Īśvara and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success.
If there are sentient beings who desire bodily mastery to fly through the void, I appear before them in the form of Maheśvara and preach the Dharma for them.

I cause them to achieve success. If there are sentient beings who love to govern spirits and deities and protect the land, I appear before them in the form of a Great Heavenly General and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.

If there are sentient beings who love to govern the world and protect all living beings, I appear before them in the form of one of the Four Heavenly Kings and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.

Regarding their accomplishment: if there are sentient beings who desire to be born in celestial palaces or to command spirits and deities, I manifest before them in the form of a crown prince of the Four Heavenly Kings and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve their goal.
All of these are manifestations from the originally inherent celestial dharma-realm that has been realized. As the Sūtra says: "If there are sentient beings who delight in being kings of men..."
Before them, I manifest in the body of a king of men and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment;
this is a manifestation from the supreme state within the person-dharma realm that has been realized. As the Sūtra says:

"If there are sentient beings who love their clan and lineage and are esteemed by the world, before them I manifest in the body of an elder and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment."

Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who delight in discussing names and terminology and dwell in purity, I manifest before them in the body of a layperson (*gṛhapati*) and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment.

If there are sentient beings who delight in governing territories and adjudicating matters within states and districts, I manifest before them in the body of a high official (*kṣatriya* or *amātya*) and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment. If there are sentient beings... [and so forth].
Born with a fondness for various arts and sciences, he dwells in self-restraint; before him, I manifest in the body of a brāhmaṇa and preach the Dharma to bring him to fulfillment.

If there is a man who delights in study and leaves the household life, upholding the various precepts and regulations, before him I manifest in the body of a bhikṣu and preach the Dharma to bring him to fulfillment. If there is a woman who delights in study...

If there are those who have left the household life and uphold the various prohibitive precepts, I appear before them in the form of a bhikṣuṇī and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.
If there are men who delight in upholding the five precepts, I appear before them in the form of an upāsaka.

I preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment. If there are women who abide by the five precepts, I appear before them in the form of an upāsikā and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.

If there are women who manage internal affairs to establish themselves and cultivate their households and nations, I appear before them in the form of a queen, a noble lady of the court, or a titled consort of high rank.

I appear before them and preach the Dharma to bring them to fulfillment. If there are sentient beings whose male organs are intact, I appear before them in the form of a young boy and preach the Dharma to bring them to fulfillment.
If there are virgins who cherish their state and do not seek violation, I appear before them in the form of a young girl and preach the Dharma to bring them to fulfillment.
These are all manifestations of the distinctions between persons and realms, arising from what has been realized as inherently possessed. As the Sūtra says:
"If there are devas who wish to leave their celestial status, I manifest a deva body and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success.
If there are nāgas who wish to leave their nāga status, I manifest a nāga body and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success. If there are..."
Yakṣas who delight in transcending their own kind: before them, I manifest in the body of a yakṣa and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success.

This extends even to gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others—whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception—who delight in liberation from their respective classes; before them, I likewise [manifest].
Previously, he manifested his body before all of them and preached the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve realization.

All of these manifestations—from the originally endowed *devas*, *nāgas*, and the eight classes of beings within the *dharmadhātu*, down to those in the three miserable realms—were without exception shown by him.

The following text further clarifies that because he shares the same compassion and longing as all sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time across the six realms, he causes all sentient beings...
Within my own body and mind, I have attained fourteen kinds of fearless merits, culminating in the four inconceivable states;

these are none other than the perfect realization of the ten realms as the manifestation of function arising from the essence. Indeed, there has never been a function without an essence, nor has there ever been an essence without a function.
Were it not for the fact that sentient beings inherently possess within their minds the perfect realization of the stage of fruition of all Buddhas, this would not be possible.

When the whole body gives rise to its functioning, all such instances are termed "conditioned supernatural powers" (*saṃskṛta-abhijñā*). How, then, can they be called "responding without deliberation"?
By examining the cause through the effect and verifying the cause by means of the effect, the principle of the inherent nature (*prakṛti-prakḷpta*) becomes vividly and clearly manifest.
Regarding the matter of the wondrous function of the stage of fruition as realized through the five proofs, it is as cited in the text above.

Upon realizing fruition, one gives rise to function, which is fully endowed with the ten realms (*daśadhātu*). Within this, there are two types of dharma-gates: the nature of goodness and the nature of evil. As for what is termed a "dharma-gate":
"dharma" (*dharma*) is designated as the "track" or "rule" (*vartman*), while "gate" (*mukha*) has the meaning of "entry and exit. Thus, these natures of goodness and evil are both...

The method for a person of fruition to deliver sentient beings: A person of fruition emerges from these two gates to benefit sentient beings, while sentient beings enter through these two gates to become Buddhas;
therefore, they are called the Dharma-gates of inherent goodness and inherent evil. Now, regarding these two gates:

If nature is good, it is constant; if nature is evil, it is subject to change. Thus, throughout his lifetime of transformative teaching, Śākyamuni Tathāgata performed nothing other than practicing goodness and following the Way of principle.
By means of the four kinds of Buddha-bodies, he expounded the teachings of the Half and Full [Vehicles]; all of these are the goodness of nature.
This is the eternal Way. If goodness is insufficient to transform beings, one cannot help but apply it through the means of evil;

this is simply what the Tathāgata did out of necessity, a mere singular transformation within the thousand constants. The Dharma-gate of the inherent goodness of nature is something understood by all people.

The matters involved span many categories; I cannot cite them all at length. Now, I shall briefly cite one or two instances where the principles transcend ordinary sentiment and strike the eyes and alarm the heart, in order to verify that the teaching on the "Inherently Evil Nature" (xing-è fǎmén) is not empty. This is divided roughly into four sections:
first, the gate of ultimate inherent evil; second, the gate of true nature inherent evil; third, the gate of semblance inherent evil; fourth, the gate of contemplation...
This is the Dharma-gate of the Nature of Practicing Evil.
The one who reached ultimate perfection is Śākyamuni Tathāgata. Regarding the traces of his transformative teachings throughout the five periods, there are those who have entered this gate;
these are fully contained within the Great Canon (Tripitaka), though I have not been able to examine them all in detail. Now, I shall briefly cite six conditions.
The *Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of Subduing Māra when First Attaining Enlightenment* states:
When Śākyamuni Tathāgata was about to achieve perfect enlightenment, the palace of the Māra King spontaneously shook.
The Mara King thought to himself, "Gautama is about to achieve perfect enlightenment; before he has attained the Way, I shall go to disrupt and confound him.

Thereupon, grasping bow and arrow in hand, he went with his retinue to the foot of the tree and said to the Bodhisattva, "You ought to cultivate the karma of a Wheel-Turning King and abandon the way of renunciation.
If you do not rise now, I shall test you by shooting at you. The Bodhisattva remained serene and unmoved.
He was not moved by this surprise. When the Māra drew his bow and released an arrow, it remained suspended in mid-air; its tip turned downward and transformed into a lotus flower.
The Māra again dispatched his three daughters, who said to the Bodhisattva, "O Benevolent One of supreme virtue, we pray that you will accept us as your attendants.
He replied, "You have planted small roots of merit and attained these celestial bodies; it is improper for you to act with such seductive allure amidst impermanence. You may now depart."
"Go! I do not need you. At that moment, the three celestial maidens transformed into old women with white hair and wrinkled faces.

The Māra then spoke to them with gentle words, attempting to entice them: "If you do not delight in the human realm, I shall relinquish my status as the Heavenly King and give all the pleasures of the five desires to you;
I will bestow them all upon you. The Bodhisattva replied: "In the past, you practiced giving to a small degree, and now you have attained the position of a sovereign heavenly king."
"Merit has its limit; it will inevitably lead back to drowning. This is not what I require.
Māra said, "My karmic retribution is known by you, but who knows your own retribution? The Bodhisattva replied, "Only this earth knows.
Thereupon, the great earth shook in six ways, and the Earth Deity emerged and spoke to Māra: "In the past, the Bodhisattva [gave] his head, eyes, and marrow..."
He has used his brains, his kingdom, city, wife, children, elephants, horses, and precious jewels as offerings in incalculable measure, seeking the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
Therefore, you should not now trouble or disturb him. When Māra heard this, he was terrified and thought to himself:
"I must now employ further skillful means; I shall assemble a vast army and use force to intimidate him. At that time, the various troops...
Suddenly they arrived, filling the void. Grasping spears and wielding swords, with many heads and many eyes, and possessing the forms of various evil species, they surrounded the Bodhisattva.
Smoke rose from the four directions, and the four oceans surged and boiled; all these hosts of Māras exerted their full power.
With eyes like horns and teeth gnashing, he flew crosswise and hurled [the tree] upward. The Bodhisattva observed this as if it were the play of a child.
A deity in the air, concealing its form, spoke: "The Bodhisattva has cultivated the fruits of goodness through kalpas in order to guide sentient beings;
why do you now disturb the Teacher? Today he will certainly attain the Unsurpassed Way beneath the tree. This very spot was [chosen by] the past..."
"The adamantine seat of all Buddhas is capable of sustaining sublime meditative concentration; it cannot be destroyed by you. You must now, in secret, cease your arrogant thoughts and serve it.
At that time, the Māra King, hearing the voice from the air, immediately returned to his own palace.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka Sūtra* says: "The evil Māra Pāpīyas, leading a host of eight billion, intended to come and destroy the Buddha, saying: 'You..."
"Do not hurry away; I shall hurl you into the ocean. The Buddha said to Pāpīyas, "If you can first move this water-pitcher, only then will you be able to hurl me into the ocean.
Pāpīyas was unable to move it, and his host was broken and dispersed.
The *Buddha-benxing-jing* (Sutra of the Buddha’s Past Deeds) states that Pāpīyas’s eldest son, Śreṣṭhidāraka, immediately prostrated himself before the Bodhisattva, seeking repentance, and said:
"My father was ignorant and has offended you, O Great Sage; I pray that you will grant him your forgiveness and understanding.
A guest asked, "The Mara King directed evil intentions toward the Buddha, yet the Buddha never once directed even a hair’s breadth of evil toward him.

How can this be considered 'evil nature'? I replied, "Even when the World-Honored One directed [what appeared to be] evil toward him, it was nothing other than the power of his roots of goodness and compassion."
This causes them to naturally disperse and dissolve. Although it is called "evil," it is in truth not evil. Moreover, the nature of good and evil is fundamentally interpenetrating.
When one gains benefit from that which is good, it is called "good nature"; when one gains benefit from what is evil, it is called "evil nature.
Now, "evil" takes non-conformity as its meaning; for example, as in the subduing of Māra, causing his arrowheads to become flowers and transforming—
Taking adverse conditions created by Māra as favorable conditions, and transforming celestial maidens into decrepit old women,
or altering Māra’s favorable conditions into adverse ones to disturb and confuse the mind— all such matters belong to the extreme of inherent evil.
Regarding the second instance of the Buddha’s transformation of a courtesan to cause her to conceive a sense of revulsion toward suffering through the contemplation of the Buddha:

the *Buddha-samādhi-sūtra* states that the Buddha told Ānanda, "In the past, during my summer retreat (*varṣā*), there was a courtesan in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī named Māyāvatī who had a karmic affinity with the Buddha. The Buddha, together with Nanda, went to that courtesan."
He departed. Day after day he went begging for alms. This woman had never shown me respect; she had instead developed a partial attachment only for Nanda.
After seven days had passed, the woman thought to herself: "If the śramaṇa Gautama could only send away Nanda and Ānanda..."
"In accordance with my vow, I shall provide various offerings. The World-Honored One said to Ānanda and Nanda, "From this day forward, do not go to that village.
The World-Honored One went alone to the woman's tower. For one day up to three days, he emitted golden light to transform the devas and humans, yet this woman did not awaken.
On a later day, the World-Honored One again took Ānanda and Nanda and remained below the tower.
As they were walking along, because the courtesan felt love and reverence for the two bhikṣus, she scattered a multitude of flowers from afar over the Buddha and the two bhikṣus.
Ānanda said to her, "You should pay homage to the Buddha. The woman loved Ānanda, so she immediately prostrated herself.

The Buddha manifested three youths, all fifteen years of age, with handsome and upright features. When the woman saw them, she was filled with joy; to transform these youths, she threw herself to the ground in reverence.
She paid her respects and said to the young man, "O noble sir, this house of mine is like the Goddess of Merit (Puṇyavatī);
it is wealthy, independent, and adorned with every kind of treasure. I now offer my own person, along with my servants and maidservants, to you, noble sir, to serve as your attendants.
If you would deign to accept me, I shall provide for all your needs according to your wishes, withholding nothing. [The transformed man] sat upon the couch."

After the duration of a meal, the woman approached him and said, "I pray you fulfill my wish. The transformed man did not refuse her, and for one day and one night his mind was neither weary nor disenchanted.
When the second day arrived, his feelings of love gradually subsided. On the third day, she said to him, "O noble sir, please arise and eat and drink.
The transformed man then arose; yet as they continued their lingering intimacy without end, the woman became weary and regretful, and said to the noble sir:
