Now, this strange man was such that the transformed being told her: "According to the laws of my former lives, whenever one has intercourse with a woman, one must wait twelve days before resting.
When the woman heard these words, she was like a person choking on food—unable to spit it out and unable to swallow it down.
Her body suffered pain as if being pounded by a pestle; by the fourth day, it felt as if she were being crushed by a chariot wheel; by the fifth day...
At that time, it was as if iron balls were piercing her body. By the sixth day, every joint and limb ached as if an arrow had struck her heart.
The woman thought to herself, "I have heard that Prince Śuddhodana rescues those in suffering; why does he not come to save me today?
Having had this thought, she was overcome with grief and reproached herself: "From this day until the end of my life, I shall no longer crave sensual desire. Rather—"
"To dwell in the same room as tigers, wolves, lions, and other fierce beasts, yet not undergo such suffering!

Having spoken these words, she rose again to eat and drink, moving about and sitting together with them; there was nothing she could do. The transformed woman also became angry and spat at her, saying, "You wicked, evil woman!"
"It ruins my livelihood. Now that I am joined with you as one body, it would be better for me to die early.
If my parents and kinsmen come searching for me, where shall I hide myself? I would rather hang myself than endure such shame. The woman said, "You wretched thing, I have no use for you.
If you wish to die, do as you please. The transformed man took a knife and pierced her throat; blood stained the woman's body as she slumped down.
It spread across the ground; the woman could not bear it, yet she could not escape it. After two days had passed, [the corpse] was livid, bruised, and black with a foul stench.

On the third day, it became bloated and swollen. On the fourth day, it began to rot and slough off, with excrement, urine, and various foul insects, along with spurting blood and pus, smeared all over the woman’s body.
The woman felt extreme loathing and revulsion, yet she could not leave it. By the fifth day, the skin and flesh were gradually decaying. Upon reaching...
At the sixth day, the flesh had completely fallen away. By the seventh day, there remained only stinking bones, as sticky as glue or lac, adhering to the woman’s body.

The woman made this vow: "If the devas, the ṛṣis, or the son of King Śuddhodana can free me from this suffering, I shall take all these precious jewels and give them as alms. While she was thinking thus, the Buddha—

With Ānanda and Nanda leading the way and Śakra holding a precious incense burner (*dhūpakaṭacchuka*) and burning priceless incense before him, and Brahmā following behind holding a great precious parasol (*ratnacchattra*), immeasurable devas performed celestial music. The Buddha emitted his constant radiance, illuminating heaven and earth.
The entire great assembly all saw the Tathāgata approach this woman’s tower. When the woman saw the Buddha, she felt shame and remorse;
having no place to hide her bones, she took various white woolen cloths and immeasurable varieties of incense to wrap her putrid bones, yet the stench remained as it was before.
It could not be concealed. When the woman saw the World-Honored One, she immediately prostrated herself in salutation. Out of shame and remorse, her body became transparent, revealing her bones;
suddenly, a stinking bone appeared upon her back. The woman wept and said, "The Tathāgata’s merit and compassionate mercy are immeasurable.
If you can enable me to be free from this suffering, I pray to become your disciple; my mind shall never waver. By the Buddha's spiritual power—

Therefore, the stinking bones did not appear. The woman was filled with great joy and prostrated before the Buddha, saying to him, "World-Honored One, I now offer all that I hold most precious as a gift to the Buddha.
The Buddha offered a blessing for her, his Brahma-voice flowing smoothly. Hearing this, the woman rejoiced, and at that very moment she attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
Third, the account of subduing the wilderness *yakṣa*.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Good son, at one time I was traveling through that wilderness village among the groves of trees.
Beneath those trees there was a *yakṣa* named Wilderness (*Āṭavaka*), who subsisted solely on flesh and blood and frequently killed sentient beings. Furthermore...
In that assembly, one person was eaten every day. Son of good family, at that time, I extensively expounded the essential teachings of the Dharma for those spirits;
yet, being violent, evil, foolish, and lacking wisdom, they did not accept the instructions.
I then manifested as a spirit of great power, shaking their palace so that they could find no peace therein. At that moment, those spirits, along with their retinues, emerged from it.
The palace was about to come forth to resist and oppose me. When the ghost saw me, it immediately lost its mental composure;
struck with terror, it fell to the ground, fainting and gasping until it was like one dead. Out of compassion, I stroked its body with my hand, whereupon it rose up and sat back down, saying:
"How wonderful! Today I have regained my life. This great divine king possesses immense majesty and virtue, and is endowed with compassion."
With a compassionate heart, he pardoned my transgressions and immediately conceived a virtuous faith toward me.
I then restored myself to the body of a Tathāgata and further expounded various essential teachings for him, causing that spirit to receive the precept against killing.
On that very day, there was an elder in the village of Kāṣṭhavāṭa whose turn it was to die; the villagers had already delivered him to that spirit.
"O ghost! Once the ghost had received it, he immediately gave it to me. Having accepted it, I then established another name for the elder, naming him 'The Elder with Hands.
At that time, the ghost addressed me, saying: 'World-Honored One, I and my retinue...'"
"I rely solely on blood and flesh to sustain my life. Now that I have received the precepts, how shall I support myself? I replied to him:
"Henceforth, I shall command my śrāvaka disciples that wherever they practice the Buddha-dharma, they must all provide you with food and drink.
"Noble son, for this reason, I have established such a precept for the bhikṣus: you..."
From this day forward, you must always provide food to those wilderness spirits (*kāntāra-bhūta*).
If there are those who dwell [among us] and yet cannot provide it, you should know that such people are not my disciples; they are merely the followers and retinues of the celestial Māras.
Son of good family, the Tathāgata manifests these various skillful means (*upāya*) for the sake of taming sentient beings; it is not with the intention of causing them to feel fear.
He struck him in fear. Fourth, he struck the Dharma-protecting ghost with a wooden club.
Fifth, atop a mountain, he pushed the goat-headed ghost so that it fell down the slope. Sixth, at the top of a tree, he dashed the monkey-protecting ghost.
Seventh, he caused the wealth-guarding elephant to see five lions. Eighth, he had the Vajra deity terrify Saccaka Nigaṇṭha. Ninth, likewise, with...
The Tathāgata pricked the bodies of the arrow-hair demons with needles. The Tathāgata further said: "Even though he acts in this way, he does not cause those various demons to suffer destruction;
rather, he intends only to cause them to abide securely in the True Dharma, and thus he manifests such various skillful means."
The fourth [account], the occasion of subduing the intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Good son, I say that this loving-kindness has immeasurable gateways, namely, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Good son, for example, Devadatta instructed Ajātaśatru, desiring to harm the Tathāgata. At that time, I entered Rājagṛha..."
In the great city, as I went on my alms-round in due order, King Ajātaśatru immediately released the mad and intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla, intending to harm me and my disciples.
At that time, the elephant trampled and killed countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings;
after these beings died, there was much blood and scent, which the elephant sniffed and his madness and intoxication became twice as great as usual. Seeing my attendants and their attire...
It was red; they called it blood. Furthermore, among my disciples who had not yet abandoned desire, they fled and scattered in all directions, with the sole exception of Ānanda.
At that time, all the people within the city of Rājagṛha simultaneously raised their voices, wailing and shedding tears, saying:
"How strange! The Tathāgata passes away today. How can this be for a Perfectly Awakened One?"
Once it was shattered and destroyed, at that moment Devadatta’s heart was filled with joy, thinking, "It is most excellent that the Śramaṇa Gautama has passed away;
from this day forward he will truly no longer appear. How wonderful is this plan! My wish has been fulfilled.

Son of good family, at that time, desiring to subdue the elephant Dhanapāla, I immediately entered the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) and extended my hand to show him. Immediately—
Upon my five fingers, I manifested five lions. When the elephant saw them, fear arose in his heart;
he voided excrement and urine and threw his entire body to the ground, prostrating at my feet. Good son, at that time there were actually no lions on my fingers;
rather, it was through the power of the roots of goodness cultivated through compassion and kindness that I tamed him.
Regarding the fifth story, the account of King Śaṅkha killing a brāhmaṇa, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"I recall that in the past, in this Jambudvīpa, I was a great king named Śaṅkha.
I cherished and revered the Mahāyāna sūtras; my mind was purely virtuous, free from coarseness, evil, envy, or stinginess."

[He was] stingy. Yet his mouth constantly proclaimed kind and virtuous speech, and his body constantly protected the poor and the solitary. He practiced giving and diligence without rest or cessation.
At that time, there were no Buddhas, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas in the world. During that period, I took delight in the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras;
for twelve years, I served a Brāhmaṇa, providing him with all his necessities. After those twelve [years had passed...]
Having completed the distribution of gifts and comforted them, he spoke these words: "You all should now resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The brāhmaṇas said: "Great King, the nature of bodhi is non-existent;
the Mahāyāna sūtras are likewise so. Great King, why do you cause people and things to be made identical to empty space? O virtuous sons..."
"Son, at that time, my mind was set upon the Mahāyāna. When I heard the brahmins reviling the Vaipulya sūtras, as soon as I heard it, I immediately severed their life-faculties.
After those brahmins passed away, they were reborn in the Avīci Hell. There, they immediately had three thoughts:
first, they wondered from where they had come to be born here; then they immediately knew for themselves that they came from among humans."
First, they come from within the path. Second, they reflect to themselves, "Where have I been born now?
and immediately know for themselves that it is the Avīci Hell. Third, they reflect to themselves, "By what karmic conditions have I come to be born here?
and immediately know for themselves that they were killed by a sovereign ruler because they slandered the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras and did not believe in causes and conditions.
Having reflected on this matter, he immediately conceived a heart of faith and reverence toward the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras.
At that very moment, his life came to an end, and he was reborn in the world-system of the Tathāgata Amṛtadundubhi. There, his lifespan was a full ten kalpas.
Good son, for this reason, I previously granted this person a lifespan of ten kalpas; how could this be called killing? Good...
"Good man, for this reason, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva never takes the life of any sentient being.
Good man, regarding what you have asked: 'When you killed the Brahmin, did you obtain this stage? Good man, I had already obtained it at that time;
I severed his life-force out of affectionate concern, not out of an evil mind. Good man, it is just as with a father..."
Mother, suppose one has an only son whom they love very deeply. If he violates the laws of the state, at that time the parents, out of fear, might exile him or put him to death;
yet they harbor no ill will toward him. It is the same for a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who seeks to protect the True Dharma:
if there are sentient beings who slander the Mahāyāna, he shall immediately punish them with the infliction of whips and lashes, or even deprive them [of their lives].
Regarding their lives, he wishes to cause them to reform their past ways and follow and cultivate wholesome dharmas. A bodhisattva should constantly reflect in this way:
"By what causes and conditions can I cause sentient beings to give rise to faith? Through whatever skillful means are appropriate, I must act for their sake."
The sixth [account] concerns the circumstances in which the Tathāgata, while still in the causal stage, saved a group of merchants.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: During the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there were five hundred merchants who went to sea to seek treasures.
Among them was one with a wicked mind who thought, "I shall now kill all these merchants and take the precious treasures for myself. At that time, there was a great guide in Jambudvīpa...
The Master was named Mahākaruṇā (Great Compassion). At that time, while he was sleeping in a dream, a sea deity spoke to him:
"Among the merchants is a thief who intends to kill five hundred companions and seize their treasures for himself alone. If his plan succeeds, he will fall into hell.
Now, you, O virtuous leader, must employ skillful means to ensure that the merchants do not die and the thief does not incur guilt. The leader reflected upon this for seven days.
There is no other expedient; I must simply kill this man. If I inform the assembly, they will surely all become enraged and kill him together, whereby we would all fall into the evil realms.

If I kill him alone, I shall receive the punishment; yet I would rather endure suffering for hundreds of thousands of kalpas myself than allow these merchants to be universally harmed and cause even a single thief to fall into hell. First, [I shall act] for their sake...
He preached the Dharma, causing their minds to be joyful and exultant as they lay down to sleep. The Buddha said:

"The Great Compassionate Guide, on account of those merchants, gave rise to great compassion and, through skillful means, eliminated this one thief. After his life ended, he was reborn in the twelfth heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
At that time, the one of Great Compassion was none other than my own self. By these skillful means, I transcended a thousand kalpas of birth."
[They] died. The five hundred merchants who were on the same ship are those who, within this Bhadrakalpa, will arise as the five hundred Buddhas.
This is the second section: the Dharma-gate of the True Nature of Evil. (The miraculous manifestations and deeds of Mañjuśrī and the other great Bodhisattvas are extremely numerous.

Here, I cite one or two instances related to the Dharma-gate of the Nature of Evil to prove that [this teaching] is not false. These are recorded extensively in the Great Canon; in truth, they exceed these.)
Regarding the causal conditions for Devadatta’s association with evil friends:
in the past, during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, Śākyamuni was a young brahmin student (*maṇava*) who went to study under the Rishi Ratnakaṇḍa.

Having completed his studies, he reflected on how to repay his teacher's kindness. Considering himself to be poor, he thought that at that time Yaśoda was about to give away his daughter in marriage. At that moment, there was...
Sumati sought to become his son-in-law; he was clever and wise, yet his physical appearance was ugly.
When the Māṇava encountered him while debating, Sumati was defeated in argument. Yaśoda rejoiced and bestowed upon him great treasures, giving him his daughter as a wife.
Sumati became resentful and made a vow that in future lives he would constantly cause him distress. Due to these causes and conditions, he was always [afflicted].
He was also called Nanda. From that time onward, as he passed through the six realms of existence, they constantly vexed one another; these accounts are numerous and not recorded here in full.
Devadatta, in this world, was known by the causes and conditions of his name:
he was also called Tianre (Heavenly Heat) and Tianshou (Heaven-Conferred). He was the son of King Kṛkī and thus the younger cousin of the Buddha.

Ānanda was his own biological brother. Devadatta possessed thirty of the marks of a great man. Having left the household life, he recited sixty thousand dharma-aggregates and mastered the twelve Vedas.
For the sake of gain and offerings, he went to the Buddha’s presence and requested to learn supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

The Buddha did not teach them to him, instead instructing him that he could attain the Way by contemplating impermanence himself. He then went to Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and even to the abodes of a hundred other disciples.

He did not preach the methods of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) to any of them. Although Ānanda was his own biological younger brother, because he had not yet attained the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), [the Buddha] did not bestow the methods of supernatural power upon him.

When Devadatta entered the mountains and had mastered the five supernatural powers, he thought to himself, "Who can act as my patron (*dānapati*)? Prince Ajātaśatru possessed the marks of a great king;
therefore, Devadatta transformed himself into an elephant or a horse treasure and, in the presence of the prince, embraced him and kissed him on the mouth. He then went further...
In the heavens, he took celestial flowers and celestial food and said to the prince, "I shall become a new Buddha, and you shall become a new king;
would this not be delightful? At other times, he transformed himself into a small child, and King Ajātaśatru placed him upon his lap and fed him from his own mouth with saliva.
Later, he requested the assembly [of monks] from the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked him, saying, "Foolish man, you lack understanding! You do not even entrust the assembly to Śāriputra."
"If even Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were so, how much more so you, a foolish man who eats the spittle and snot of others!
Because of this, he harbored resentment and separately devised five points to entice the Buddha’s assembly. These five points were: first, wearing rag-robes; second, always begging for food.
3. Eating while seated; 4. Always sitting in the open air; 5. Not accepting salt or the five flavors. This differs from the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states: 1. Not accepting the five flavors; 2. Abstaining from meat; 3. Abstaining from salt; 4. Not accepting cut-and-sewn robes; 5.
Not residing in a monastery on the outskirts of a village. When the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, he assembled the Saṃgha for a specific reason. Devadatta...
Rising from his seat, he cast five voting sticks (*śalākā*), saying: "Those who accept these five points shall follow the Vinaya.

At that time, five hundred newly ordained monks who lacked wisdom took up the sticks. Devadatta said to them, "There is no need for the Buddha or the Saṃgha," and he led them away to Mount Gayā, where they performed formal acts (*karmavācanā*) among themselves.
When the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said: "Foolish men, you are unworthy."

He extinguished his wholesome mind and fell into hell, where he could not be saved for an entire kalpa. Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana went to Gayāśīrṣa Mountain. Devadatta said to Śāriputra, "Preach the Dharma to the assembly;
I am now suffering from back pain," and he lay down on his right side. Maudgalyāyana displayed his supernormal powers while Śāriputra preached the Dharma.

Consequently, Devadatta took five hundred newly ordained disciples and returned to the Buddha’s presence. Having lost his followers upon rising from his recumbent position, [Devadatta was cast into hell].

He gave rise to hatred and pushed a mountain to crush the Buddha. Guhyaka Vajrapāṇi raised his vajra-staff against him; as the mountain crumbled and fragments flew forth, they wounded the Buddha’s toes.
The Bhikṣuṇī Puṣpavarṇā rebuked him, and he struck her with his fist until her eyes popped out.

Having thus committed three of the five *ānantarya* sins, he further incited Ajātaśatru to kill his father—which was accomplished—and to harm his mother—which remained at the stage of preparation. Because he both committed and incited others to commit these five *ānantarya* sins, he was born alive [in the Avīci hell].
He fell into the Avīci Hell.

The *Bao'en jing* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness) states: "At that time, the Tathāgata immediately dispatched Ānanda to go to the hell to inquire after Devadatta, asking whether his suffering could be endured.
At that time, having received the Tathāgata’s instruction, Ānanda arrived outside the gates of the hell and asked.
The ox-headed *āpānaka* said, "Call for Devadatta for me. The ox-headed *āpānaka* asked, "Whose Devadatta do you mean?
[Ānanda] replied, "All Buddhas of the past had their own Devadattas.
Ānanda said, "I am calling for Devadatta of Śākyamuni Buddha. At that time, the *āpānaka* immediately spoke to Devadatta. Ānanda...
The difficulty lay outside. Desiring to see him, Devadatta said, "Welcome, Ānanda! Does the Tathāgata still hold me in his compassionate regard?
Ānanda replied, "The Tathāgata has sent me to inquire after you: can your suffering be endured?
Devadatta said, "Though I dwell in the Avīci Hell, it is like the bliss of a bhikṣu who has entered the third dhyāna."
The Buddha said: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice great skillful means to guide and receive sentient beings;

though they undergo immeasurable great suffering within birth and death, they do not regard it as a calamity. If someone were to say that Devadatta was truly an evil person who entered the Avīci Hell, such a thing is impossible.
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately manifested Devadatta for the sake of the great assembly."

At the time when Dàduo (Datta) performed his subtle, secret, and wondrous practices of great skillful means, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* up to that of *arhat*. The celestial beings of the void rained down various heavenly flowers.
It completely covered the great assembly, performing celestial music and emitting great radiance, while praising him, saying, "Excellent! What the Tathāgata has spoken is unprecedented.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, the entire assembly bowed their heads to the ground in prostration and departed with joy.

Regarding the causal conditions for Devadatta as a spiritual friend, the "Devadatta Chapter" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, as well as the fourfold assembly of devas and humans.
Throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, I sought the Lotus Sūtra without weariness or fatigue.
During many kalpas, I constantly served as a king, making vows to seek unexcelled bodhi with a mind that never regressed.
Desiring to fulfill the six pāramitās, I diligently practiced giving, my heart free from stinginess, bestowing elephants, horses, the seven treasures, kingdoms, cities, wives, and children.
He gave away his slaves, servants, and attendants; his head, eyes, marrow, and brain; and his body’s flesh, hands, and feet, not sparing even his own life.

At that time, the people of the world possessed immeasurable lifespans; for the sake of the Dharma, he renounced his royal throne and entrusted it to his legitimate crown prince, then beat the drum to proclaim a decree.
He traveled in all four directions seeking the Dharma, saying, "Who can preach the Mahāyāna for me? I shall serve as his attendant and provide for him for the rest of my life.
At that time, there was a rishi who came and said to the king, "I possess the Mahāyāna, titled the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. If you do not oppose me, I shall proclaim it for you.
Upon hearing the rishi's words, the king was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he immediately followed the rishi, providing for his needs.
He gathered fruit, drew water, collected firewood, and prepared food; even using his own body as a seat and bed, he never grew weary in body or mind.
Thus he served him for a thousand years, diligently attending to him for the sake of the Dharma, ensuring that he lacked for nothing.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
I recall a past kalpa when, for the sake of seeking the Great Dharma, though I was a king of the world, I did not crave the pleasures of the five desires.
Ringing a bell, I proclaimed to the four quarters: "Who possesses the Great Dharma?
If you can explain it to me, I shall become your slave. At that time, there was an Ṛṣi named Asita.
He came and addressed the Great King: "I possess a subtle and wondrous Dharma, rare in this world.
If you are able to practice it, I shall explain it for you. When the King heard the words of the seer, his heart was filled with great joy;
he immediately followed the seer and provided him with all that was required.
Gathering firewood and fruits and melons, he offered them with respect at all times;
because his heart was set upon the wondrous Dharma, his body and mind were free from weariness.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he diligently sought the Great Dharma, neither for his own sake nor for the pleasures of the five desires; therefore, he became a great king.
"By diligently seeking, I obtained this Dharma, and thus eventually attained Buddhahood; for this reason, I now speak it for you.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "The king at that time was none other than myself. The rishi at that time is now Devadatta.
It was because of the spiritual friend Devadatta that I was enabled to fulfill the six pāramitās."
The [Buddha’s] qualities of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics; the purple-golden hue;
the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four means of integration, and the eighteen unique attributes; his supernatural powers and spiritual strength; his attainment of perfect enlightenment;
and his vast deliverance of sentient beings—all these were due to the spiritual friend Devadatta. He addressed the fourfold assembly: "Devadatta..."

After the passing of immeasurable kalpas, he shall attain Buddhahood, to be named Tathāgata Devendra, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha Bhagavān.
His world shall be named Devamārga. At that time, the Buddha Devendra shall remain in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas, extensively benefiting sentient beings.

He preached the sublime Dharma, whereby sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the fruit of Arhatship; immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon the path of Pratyekabuddhas;
and sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path, attaining the patience of non-arising and reaching the stage of non-retrogression.
After the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Devendra, the True Dharma remained in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas.
A stūpa made of the seven precious jewels was erected over his entire bodily relics; it was sixty yojanas in height and forty yojanas in length and breadth.
All the devas and human beings offered various flowers, powdered incense, burning incense, ointment incense, robes, necklaces, banners, flags, precious canopies, and music and song.
Verse: By prostrating to and making offerings to the wondrous stūpa of the seven jewels, immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of arhatship;
immeasurable sentient beings realized the state of a pratyekabuddha; and inconceivable numbers of sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta and reached the stage of non-retrogression.

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "In a future age, if there are good men or good women who, upon hearing the 'Devadatta Chapter' of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, believe and revere it with a pure heart and do not give rise to doubt or confusion, they shall not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
They shall be born before the Buddhas of the ten directions, and in every place where they are born, they shall constantly hear this sūtra. If they are born among humans..."
One will experience supreme and wondrous bliss among the devas; if one is before the Buddha, one will be born through transformation upon a lotus flower. The Treatise says:
Generally, that which is favorable is perfected through adversity, and wholesome causes are sustained by evil. It is like fire being able to temper gold; gold is not refined without fire.
It is like stone being able to grind jade; jade is not polished without stone. Thus, the nature of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni is the Dharma of goodness.
The gate is ultimately perfected entirely through the dharma-gate of Devadatta’s inherently evil nature, which was cultivated through manifold means.
Thus, the Lotus Sūtra says: "It is because of the spiritual friend Devadatta that I have come to be fully endowed with the six pāramitās."
Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; the purple-golden hue; the ten powers and four fearlessnesses;
the four methods of attraction and the eighteen unique qualities; the power of the divine paths and superknowledges;

the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment, and the vast deliverance of sentient beings. It is further said: "Devadatta, after the passing of immeasurable kalpas, shall attain Buddhahood, and his name shall be Tian (Heaven)."

The Tathāgata is endowed with the ten titles. Now, if Devadatta had indeed committed evil because of his own inherent evil, he would have been a wicked friend forever, sinking eternally into the ocean of the three sufferings and never receiving the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.
Furthermore, if Śākyamuni Tathāgata had truly regarded Devadatta as an adversary and acted toward him as an adversary, it should not be said that [the Buddha’s merit] arose from Devadatta’s goodness.
Because of his wisdom, he enabled me to fulfill the six *pāramitās* and so forth, thereby attaining Buddhahood.
Since I sought its profound meaning, had there not been this subtle dharma-gate of the inherent goodness and evil, there would have been no means by which to propagate it;

therefore, it is placed at the head of the dharma-gates concerning the true nature of inherent goodness and evil. By this, one can understand why it is ranked above Śākyamuni and crowned with Mañjuśrī below. Nevertheless, the Tathāgata...

Thus, one fully realizes inherent goodness (*prakṛti-kuśala*) to give rise to cultivated goodness (*bhāvanā-kuśala*), and through cultivated goodness, one reaches the ultimate limit of inherent goodness.

Now, as for Devadatta, could it not be said that he fully realized inherent evil (*prakṛti-akuśala*) to give rise to cultivated evil, and through cultivated evil, reached the ultimate limit of inherent evil?
In this regard, Devadatta’s fundamental nature and his manifested traces are both profound; indeed, they cannot be [fathomed].
This is beyond the scope of discursive thought.

Regarding the circumstances of the lay practitioner Vimalakīrti subduing the celestial Māra, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states: The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Lokadhara: "Go to Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness. Lokadhara...
He addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness. Why is this?

I recall that in the past, while I was staying in a quiet chamber, Māra Pāpīyān—accompanied by twelve thousand celestial maidens appearing like Śakra, with the beating of drums and the singing of lutes—came to where I was.
Together with his retinue, he bowed his head at my feet and, with palms joined in reverence, [stood] before me."
He stood before me. I thought he was Śakra, and I said to him, "Welcome, Kauśika! Although you possess merit, you should not be self-indulgent.
You should contemplate the impermanence of the five desires and seek the root of goodness, cultivating enduring dharmas through your body, life, and wealth.
He then said to me, "Virtuous man, accept these twelve thousand celestial maidens; they may serve as your attendants."
I said, "Kauśika, do not offer these things that are contrary to the Dharma to me, a śramaṇa son of the Śākyas;
this is not appropriate for me. Before I had finished speaking, Vimalakīrti arrived and said to me, "This is not Śakra;
it is Māra who has come to harass and trouble you. He then spoke to Māra, saying, "You may give these maidens to me. As I...
He should accept them. Māra was immediately struck with fear and thought, "Vimalakīrti will surely trouble me. He wished to vanish from sight and depart, but he could not vanish;
he exhausted all his supernatural powers, yet still could not leave. Then he heard a voice in the air saying, "Pāpīyān, give these women to him, and only then may you depart.
Out of fear, Māra reluctantly gave them to him. At that time, Vimalakīrti said:
The women said, "Māra has given you all to me; now you must all resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
He then preached the Dharma to them according to their needs, causing them to give rise to the aspiration for the Way.

He further said, 'Now that you have resolved upon the Way, there is the joy of the Dharma with which you may find delight; you should no longer take pleasure in the delights of the five desires. O Deva!

The woman then asked, "What is called the joy of the Dharma? He replied: "It is the joy of constantly having faith in the Buddha; the joy of desiring to hear the Dharma; the joy of making offerings to the Saṃgha;

the joy of being detached from the five desires; the joy of viewing the five aggregates as enemies and thieves; the joy of viewing the four great elements as venomous snakes; the joy of viewing the internal sense bases as an empty village;
the joy of following and protecting the resolve for enlightenment; the joy of benefiting sentient beings; and the joy of making offerings to one's teacher."

They delight in extensively practicing giving; they delight in firmly upholding the precepts; they delight in patience, gentleness, and flexibility; they delight in diligently accumulating roots of goodness;
they delight in meditative concentration without distraction; they delight in stainless, luminous wisdom; they delight in expanding the bodhicitta; they delight in subduing all māras;

they delight in severing all afflictions; they delight in purifying buddha-fields; and they delight in adorning [themselves] by cultivating all meritorious virtues for the sake of accomplishing the primary and secondary marks.

To adorn the site of practice; to delight in hearing the profound Dharma without fear; to delight in the three gates of liberation; not to delight in improper times; to delight in associating with fellow students;
to delight in having no anger or obstruction toward those who are not fellow students; to delight in protecting against evil associates;
to delight in drawing near to virtuous friends; to delight in a joyful and pure mind; and to delight in cultivating the immeasurable factors of the path—these constitute a bodhisattva.
The Joy of the Dharma. Thereupon, Pāpīyān said to the daughters, "I wish to return with you all to the celestial palace.
The daughters replied, "We have been given this householder; we possess the joy of the Dharma and find it most delightful. We no longer take pleasure in the joys of the five desires.
Māra said, "Householder, you should relinquish these women and give them all away as a gift to him. This is...
"Bodhisattva," Vimalakīrti said, "I have already relinquished them; you may take them away so that all sentient beings may have their aspirations for the Dharma fulfilled.
Thereupon, the goddesses asked Vimalakīrti, "How shall we dwell in the palace of Māra?"
Vimalakīrti said, "Sisters, there is a dharma-gate called the 'Inexhaustible Lamp. You should study it. As for the Inexhaustible Lamp:
it is like a single lamp that ignites hundreds of thousands of lamps; those in darkness all become bright, yet the light is never exhausted.
In this same way, sisters, when a single bodhisattva guides and instructs hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
The bodhicitta; its aspiration for the Way shall never be extinguished. According to the Dharma one preaches, one increases all virtues within oneself;

this is called the "Inexhaustible Lamp. Although you dwell in the palace of Māra, by means of this Inexhaustible Lamp, you cause countless sons and daughters of the gods to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is how you repay [your debt].

The Buddha’s grace likewise brings great benefit to all sentient beings. At that time, the goddess prostrated herself at the feet of Vimalakīrti and, following Māra back to her palace, suddenly vanished from sight.
Regarding the account of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva spending the summer retreat in three locations, the *Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra* states:
At that time, the Venerable Kāśyapa said to Śāriputra, "I too have witnessed the rare supernormal powers of Mañjuśrī.
Śāriputra, at that time the World-Honored One had not long attained Buddhahood, whereas I had been a renunciant for a long time.

At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī had first arrived in this Sahā world from the presence of the Buddha Ratnaketu in the world-system Ratnavyūha, desiring to see the Buddha Śākyamuni and to pay him honor and respect.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Monastery, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, observing the three-month summer retreat. It was then that I—
I did not see Mañjuśrī, whether before the Tathāgata, among the assembly of monks, at the time of eating, on the day of the recitation of the precepts, or while the monks were walking in procession;
I saw him nowhere at all. Only after three months had passed, when the time for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony approached, did I finally catch sight of his face.
I immediately asked him, "Mañjuśrī, where did you spend the summer retreat? He replied to me, "Venerable sir..."
"Kāśyapa, I stayed for one month in the royal harem of King Prasenajit in this great city of Śrāvastī;
for another month, I stayed in the school for young boys; and for yet another month, I stayed in the quarters of various courtesans.
Having heard of these things, my mind was deeply displeased, and I immediately thought: 'How can I perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony together with such impure people? I then departed."
The Elder then struck the *gandi* bell, intending to expel the youth Mañjuśrī. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
"Go and see why this Mahākāśyapa is striking the *gandi* now.
Mañjuśrī replied to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, I have already seen him; he intends to expel me. The Buddha said to the youth Mañjuśrī:

"Son, you may now manifest your sovereign spiritual power and the realm of your supernormal knowledges, so that the minds of those śrāvakas may become pure and they do not conceive impure thoughts toward you.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī entered a samādhi called "Manifesting All Buddha-lands. Once Mañjuśrī had entered this samādhi, throughout the ten directions...
In each of as many Buddha-worlds as there are sands in the Ganges River, there was a Mahākāśyapa foremost in dhūta practices.
They all struck their ghaṇṭās. At that time, the World-Honored One asked me: "Mahākāśyapa, for what reason have you now struck the ghaṇṭā?
I replied to the World-Honored One: "Mañjuśrī has himself said this: 'During the three months of the summer retreat...'"
Because King Candraprabha resided in the royal harem and the houses of courtesans, the gong was struck to expel him.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted light from his body that illuminated the ten directions and said to me: "Now, look throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
what do you see? I then looked everywhere throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
In every world-system, there was a Mahākāśyapa striking a *gandi* bell, intending to expel Mañjuśrī.
Yet in all those places, Mañjuśrī was also seated before the Buddha. The Buddha said to me, "Which Mañjuśrī do you wish to expel now?
Is it the one in this world-system, or the ones in the worlds of the ten directions? At that time, I immediately prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and spoke thus:
"Please, World-Honored One, hear my confession. This Mañjuśrī, the son of the Dharma King, has accomplished such inconceivable bodhisattva merits.
Having attained only limited wisdom from the Buddha, I nevertheless desired to ferry across those of immeasurable wisdom;
out of ignorance, I struck the ghaṇṭā. The Buddha said to me: 'Mahākāśyapa...'"
The Mañjuśrī whom you see in the worlds of the ten directions likewise dwelt for the three months of the summer retreat in the royal harem and in the houses of courtesans.
This very Mañjuśrī-kumāra here has caused five hundred women in the palace of King Prasenajit not to regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and he has likewise caused five hundred...
Five hundred courtesans and youths attained the irreversible path to supreme enlightenment.
Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of sentient beings were tamed through the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, and immeasurable sentient beings attained rebirth in the heavens. At that time, I said:
"Venerable World-Honored One, what Dharma did Mañjuśrī teach that he was able to thus transform and guide sentient beings?
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa, you may now ask Mañjuśrī himself; he will answer you.
At that time, I immediately asked Mañjuśrī, "What Dharma did you teach to transform and subdue such sentient beings? He replied to me, saying:
Not only does he teach the Dharma to instruct sentient beings, O Venerable Kāśyapa, but there are some sentient beings whom he tames through entertainment;
or by means of protection; or by means of awe-inspiring power; or by means of gathering them through wealth; or by appearing as one who is poor and lowly;

or by manifesting great adornments; or by manifesting supernatural powers; or by manifesting the body of Śakra; or by manifesting the body of Brahmā; or by manifesting the body of a World Protector (Lokapāla).
He may manifest in the body of a universal monarch (cakravartin), or he may manifest in the form of whichever deity each being serves.
He may employ gentle speech, or harsh speech, or both; he may employ punishment, or secret benefit;
or he may manifest as a son. Why is this, Venerable Kāśyapa? Because sentient beings possess various kinds of conduct, and by means of these various [means]...

I plant the seeds of the Dharma and subdue them. Venerable Kāśyapa, I transform the realm of sentient beings through skillful means, and only thereafter do I preach the Dharma, so that they may ultimately achieve definitive subdual.
Regarding the circumstances of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva manifesting supernatural transformations, the *Ratnakaranda Sūtra* states: "At that time, the Venerable Ānanda again addressed Śāriputra:
'I too have witnessed the supernatural transformations of Mañjuśrī. Venerable Śāriputra, once in the past, when the World-Honored One was here...'"
In the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍika Monastery at Śrāvastī, together with a great community of eight hundred bhikṣus and a multitude of twelve thousand bodhisattvas, a cloud of great compassion arose.
At that time, it rained for seven days and seven nights without ceasing. Among the venerable śrāvakas, those who had attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and liberation (*vimokṣa*), or...
He entered meditative concentration and did not eat for seven days. The other ordinary persons and those still in training (śaikṣa) abstained from food for five days;
they became so hungry, exhausted, and emaciated that they were unable to go and visit the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to pay their respects and make offerings.

At that time, I thought to myself: "These bhikṣus are undergoing great suffering; I should go and inform the Buddha. I then proceeded to where the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying and bowed my head [to his feet].
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the community of bhikṣus has been without food for five days;
they are extremely emaciated and are unable to rise from their beds or attend to themselves. The World-Honored One instructed me, 'Ānanda, you should now report this matter.'"
"Go and speak to Mañjuśrī; he shall provide sufficient food for the community of monks.
Having received the Buddha's instruction, I went to the chamber where Mañjuśrī was staying. Upon arrival, I related these matters in detail.
At that time, Mañjuśrī was preaching the Dharma for Śakra, Brahmā, and the World Protectors. He replied to me, saying: "Ānanda, go and spread [the mats]."

"Prepare the seats. When the time has arrived, strike the *gandī*. Having heard these words from Mañjuśrī, I immediately prepared the seats and stayed in one place, watching for the time when Mañjuśrī would emerge from his room.
This Mañjuśrī was extensively expounding the Dharma for the sake of Brahmā, Śakra, and the World-Protecting Heavenly Kings; the teaching was titled "The Differentiation of All Bodies."
[He remained] in samādhi and did not leave his room. I thought to myself: "Mañjuśrī will surely not cause the bhikṣus to miss their meal.
At that time, Mañjuśrī manifested various forms of himself as Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors, and preached this "Samādhi of the Differentiation of All Bodies.
Mañjuśrī also immediately entered this "Samādhi of the Differentiation of All Bodies."
Having finished his meal, he emerged from his room and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to wander for alms, collecting flowers along the way; at that time, I did not see him.
Then Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself: "Mañjuśrī has finished his lion’s roar and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
I shall now obscure all the brahmins, elders, and householders within the city of Śrāvastī."
"No one was entering or leaving; no one was allowed to offer food. At that time, wherever the youth Mañjuśrī went, all the gates were closed and no one came or went.
Mañjuśrī immediately perceived through his insight that the Māra Pāpīyān had concealed all the people.
"I shall now make a vow of truthful speech," he thought. Thereupon, he made this sincere declaration:
The merit and wisdom gathered by me within a single pore are such that they do not exist even among all the Māras filling as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
These words of mine are true; the demonic obscurations shall depart.
Let the Māra himself take the form of a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*) and, at the crossroads and in the midst of the streets and lanes, proclaim these words: "One should practice giving."
One should especially give to Mañjuśrī. If one gives to him, one will obtain a great fruit and reward.

Even if one were to provide all manner of articles of pleasure for every single sentient being throughout the trichiliocosm for hundreds of thousands of billions of years, it would not equal the merit produced by giving even a single fingertip’s worth to this Mañjuśrī; the latter is far superior. Mañjuśrī, [this is true] in an instant.
After this vow had been established, all the devas opened every gate within the city, causing the multitude of people to flock toward the youth Mañjuśrī.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, assuming the guise of a householder, went through the crossroads, streets, and lanes, crying out these words: "One should give to Mañjuśrī! One should give to Mañjuśrī! If one gives to him..."

One who does so shall obtain a great karmic reward. Even if one were to provide all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm with delightful articles of worship for a hundred thousand years, the merit generated by giving even a single fingertip’s worth to this Mañjuśrī would be superior.
At that time, through his supernatural powers, Mañjuśrī caused the alms bowl he held to receive all manner of exquisite and wonderful offerings.
The food, drink, cakes, fruits, and so forth were not mixed together, as if they had been placed in separate vessels.
The food consumed by eight hundred bhikṣus and twelve thousand bodhisattvas was contained within a single bowl; yet this bowl appeared neither full nor depleted.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī, having finished his alms-round in the great city of Śrāvastī, departed from the city.
He placed the bowl on the ground and said to Māra Pāpīyas, "Act as my attendant; you may take this bowl and go ahead.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas was unable to lift the bowl and felt shame.
He said to Mañjuśrī, "I am now unable to lift this bowl from the ground. Mañjuśrī said to Pāpīyas, "You have now attained great majestic power."

Power. Why was he unable to lift even a small bowl? At that time, Māra Pāpīyān exhausted all his supernatural powers, yet he could not lift the bowl even as much as a hair’s breadth. Wondrous and unprecedented, he said to Mañjuśrī:
"With my supernatural power, I can lift Mount Īṣādhara, place it upon the palm of my hand, and hurl it into the midst of space; yet now I cannot lift such a small bowl."
[The bowl was] about the size of a hair-tip. Mañjuśrī said to Pāpīyas:
"If there were a great being, a great person of great power, the bowl held by him would not be something you, Pāpīyas, could lift.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī took up the bowl on the ground with a single finger and placed it in Pāpīyas’s hand, saying to him: "Hold this as a *karmadāna* (pure attendant)."
The bowl went ahead. Then Māra Pāpīyān exerted all his strength to carry the bowl and proceeded in front.
At that time, the Devaputra Īśvara, surrounded by a retinue of twelve thousand devaputras, approached the youth Mañjuśrī and prostrated at his feet.
Having completed the circumambulation to the right, he spoke to Pāpīyān, saying: "You are not a servant; for what reason do you carry the bowl?"
He proceeded forward. Māra said, "Son of Heaven, I am now unable to contend with one who possesses such power.
The Son of Heaven replied, "Pāpīyān, you too have accomplished great majestic spiritual power.

At that time, because Pāpīyān was sustained by the power of Mañjuśrī, he answered, "Son of Heaven, the power of delusion is what constitutes the power of Māra; the power of the clarity of wisdom is [the power of the Buddha]."
The power of pride is the power of Māra; the power of great wisdom is the power of a bodhisattva.
The power of all false views is the power of Māra; the power of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness is the power of a bodhisattva.
The power of all inversions is the power of Māra; the power of the true and correct reality is the power of a bodhisattva. The power of "I" and "mine" is the power of Māra.

The power of strength; the power of great compassion—these are the powers of a bodhisattva. The power of greed, hatred, and delusion—this is the power of Māra. The power of the three gates of liberation—this is the power of a bodhisattva.

The power of birth and death—this is the power of Māra. The power of the patience of non-arising, which is without birth, without cessation, and without all conditioned formations—this is the power of a bodhisattva.
When the Māra Pāpīyān spoke these teachings, in the midst of the great assembly...

Five hundred devaputras among them resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and twelve hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

At that time, Mañjuśrī, together with Māra Pāpīyān, took this bowl of food and placed it within the Kālika-puṣpa garden; having done so, they both departed. At that moment, I no longer saw Mañjuśrī. Then...
When the time for the meal arrived, he still had not emerged from his room. I thought to myself: "Perhaps Mañjuśrī is causing the assembly of bhikṣus to miss the proper time for the meal.
I shall go to the Buddha's presence and report this matter in detail. I immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
"World-Honored One, the time for the meal has already arrived, yet Mañjuśrī still has not emerged from his room. The Buddha—
He said to me, "Ānanda, did you not go into this Kāliṅga Garden to look at it?
I replied to the Buddha, "Venerable Blessed One, I saw a small bowl, its contents filled with food. The Buddha said to me, "Quickly strike the ghaṇṭā and assemble the community of bhikṣus.
I said to the World-Honored One, "The community of bhikṣus is large; to whom should this single bowl of food be given?"
"Who is it? I asked. The Buddha said to me, "Do not worry about this.
Even if all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm were to eat the food from this bowl for a hundred thousand years, they still could not exhaust it.
Why is that? This bowl is sustained by the power of Mañjuśrī. Mañjuśrī possesses various pāramitās."
To measure his merit: Having heard the Buddha’s words, I struck the *gandi* and assembled the community of bhikṣus. At that time, this food in the bowl was not mixed together;
its fragrant and exquisite flavors could not be exhausted as they filled the great assembly, yet the food in the bowl did not diminish.
Then the Māra Pāpīyas, wishing to vex the youth Mañjuśrī, immediately manifested by transformation four thousand bhikṣus wearing robes...

His robes were tattered and worn; his deportment was coarse and unrefined; he carried a broken alms bowl; his nose and eyes were askew; his hands were clenched into fists and his feet were lame; his form was hideous.
He sat in the lower row, and [the Buddha] filled his alms bowl with food until it was full.
Then Māra Pāpīyas caused a manifested bhikṣu to appear, who ate the thousand varieties of food from the kingdom of Magadha at every person's place; yet this alms bowl remained as full as before.
The food remained full and did not diminish, yet it caused those gardeners and laborers who were serving the meals to become exhausted.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, through his supernatural power, sustained the bowls of the bhikṣus emanated by Māra Pāpīyas so that the food did not decrease, even though their hands and mouths were both filled.
They were unable to swallow; their breath was stifled and their eyes rolled back, and they all collapsed to the ground.
Mañjuśrī said to Pāpīyas: "O Bhikṣus, why do you not eat further? The evil Māra replied:
"Mañjuśrī, these bhikṣus lie on the ground near death. Have you not given them poisoned food? Mañjuśrī said to Pāpīyas:
One who has already exhausted all poison—what poison could they possibly have? One who possesses poison within bestows poison upon others;
one who lacks poison within does not bestow poison upon others. Pāpīyān, that which is called "poison" refers to greed, hatred, and delusion.
For one who is well-praised and disciplined within the Dharma, it is impossible for them to bestow poison upon others. Furthermore, Māra Pāpīyān, that which is called "poison" is ignorance.
There are views of craving; views of "I" and "mine"; views of no cause or condition; views regarding name-and-form; views of attachment, aversion, and hatred;

Pride. Increasing disputes and litigation. Perceiving the real as unreal, and perceiving the unreal as real. Conceiving the idea of merit within sensual pleasures.

Giving rise to madness and delusion within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). Failing to see the faults in the activities of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Conceiving a sense of terror toward *nirvāṇa*.
Pāpīyān, such dharmas as these are called "poisons" within the Sublime Dharma. The Buddha [said]: *Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available fragment.*
Within the Dharma, there is no such thing, Pāpīyan. The nectar-like Dharma is called the Buddha-Dharma. The Dharma of peace and security is called the Buddha-Dharma.
The Dharma free from conceptual proliferation is called the Buddha-Dharma. The Dharma free from faults and evils is called the Buddha-Dharma.

The dharma that is free from fetters and proclivities is called the Buddha-dharma. The dharma of the definitive exit [from suffering] is called the Buddha-dharma. The dharma that is without fear is called the Buddha-dharma.
The dharma that is without conceptual discrimination is called the Buddha-dharma. The dharma that does not grasp at self or other is called the Buddha-dharma.
The dharma that is without reproach or censure is called the Buddha-dharma. It acts as a shelter, a refuge, an island, and a protector.
The Dharma. This is called the Buddha-dharma. The Dharma of subduing and tranquility; this is called the Buddha-dharma. The Dharma of self-purification, stainlessness, and illumination;
this is called the Buddha-dharma. The Dharma of right direction and right progression; this is called the Buddha-dharma. The Dharma free from all false conceptualization and well-subdued;
this is called the Buddha-dharma. The Dharma of skillful instruction, the skillful path, and accordance with suitability; this is called the Buddha-dharma. Thus he spoke of himself.
To teach the Dharma of others is called the Buddha-Dharma. To tame all non-Buddhist teachings according to the Dharma is called the Buddha-Dharma.
To subdue the teachings of Māra is called the Buddha-Dharma. To sever the stream of birth and death is called the Buddha-Dharma. It is the Dharma of right mindfulness.

These are called the Buddha-dharma, because they abide in the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). The dharma of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) is called the Buddha-dharma, because they sever all evils.

The dharma of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) is called the Buddha-dharma, because they contemplate the lightness of body and mind. The dharma of the faculties (*indriya*) is called the Buddha-dharma, because faith is their foremost [faculty].
The dharma of the powers (*bala*) is called the Buddha-dharma, because they cannot be overcome. The dharma of the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*) is called the Buddha-...
The Dharma is called the Buddha-Dharma because it is the sequential awakening. The Dharma of the Right Path is called the Buddha-Dharma because it is the entry into the right stream.
The Dharma of Samādhi is called the Buddha-Dharma because it is ultimate tranquility. The Dharma of Wisdom is called the Buddha-Dharma because it penetrates all noble methods of liberation.
The Dharma of the True Truths is called the Buddha-Dharma because it is free from anger and resentment. The Dharma of all eloquence is called the Buddha-...
The Dharma. Because the words and meanings of the Dharma are eloquently expounded without obstruction, one clearly understands the dharmas of impermanence, suffering, and non-self;
this is called the Buddha-dharma. Because it reviles and destroys all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), the dharma of emptiness is called the Buddha-dharma.
Because it subdues all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the dharma of tranquility is called the Buddha-dharma. Because it leads toward *nirvāṇa*, the dharma of the *pāramitās* is...
The Dharma of the Buddhas is so called because it reaches the further shore. The Dharma of skillful means is so called because it skillfully gathers [beings].
The Dharma of loving-kindness is so called because its wisdom is faultless. The Dharma of compassion is so called because it is free from oppression.

The Dharma of sympathetic joy is so called because it extinguishes dissatisfaction. The Dharma of equanimity is so called because what was to be done has been accomplished. The Dharma of meditative concentration...
This is called the Buddha-dharma, because it extinguishes arrogance. To not sever the dharmas of the Triple Gem is called the Buddha-dharma, because it gives rise to the bodhicitta.
All dharmas of peace and happiness, free from suffering and affliction, are called the Buddha-dharma, because they do not seek after the various realms of existence.

Written by the Śramaṇa Chuandeng of Youxi at Mount Tiantai:
The Account of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s Subjugation of Māra (This belongs to the fifth account of the Dharma-gate of the True-Participation-in-Reality and the Innate Evil).
The *Māravijaya-sūtra* states: "Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva was expounding the Great Dharma together with the Devaputra Mahāprabha. Heaven...
Having heard this, the son replied, "It is difficult to fathom... (and so forth)... it is truly unprecedented.
Mañjuśrī, that which you have now spoken is subtle, sublime, and of infinite wisdom; its transcendence is such as this. Yet Māra Pāpīyān has not come here.
Is he seeking to obstruct and disrupt your practice? No sooner had these words been spoken than, before long, at that moment, Māra Pāpīyān—
For ten days he remained in the void, raising great clouds and rain, and emitting a great sound. That sound was heard everywhere, and at all times the assembly thought to themselves:
"What kind of sound is this that flows forth so extensively? Then the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī:
"Do you see the disturbances raised by Māra? He replied: "Indeed, O God among Gods. Mañjuśrī said:
Then, just as in that vision, he entered into meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and contemplated it, causing Māra to spontaneously find himself bound at his five limbs.
He immediately fell to the ground, crying out in lamentation and resentment, angrily reviling Mañjuśrī: "Now you shall place my body in stocks and fetters!"
Mañjuśrī replied, "Ho! Māra Pāpīyān, there is another bondage, firm and difficult to untie, even more so than this one you currently bear, which you do not perceive.
What is called 'firm bondage'? It is the bondage of the self, of inversion, of affection, and of false views;
it is the bondage of causes and conditions. You are constantly bound by these shackles, yet you do not realize it yourself. Māra then addressed him again.
He said, "I pray only that you grant me pardon and allow me to attain liberation. Mañjuśrī replied, "You must initiate the performance of Buddha-works;
I can then cause you to be released from your bonds. Māra immediately responded, "Within the Buddha-dharma, I have committed no obstruction or neglect, nor have I caused any destruction.
For what reason, then, should I perform Buddha-works? Mañjuśrī replied, "Pāpīyān, you desire..."
Knowing that the performance of Buddha-works is actually the transformation of a bodhisattva’s wisdom, it would not be difficult for a Tathāgata to perform such Buddha-works;
rather, for Māra to perform Buddha-works is truly marvelous.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī entered a samādhi corresponding to that form and caused the Māra Pāpīyān to transform himself into the likeness of a Buddha, adorned with the thirty-two marks.
Adorning his body, he sat upon a lion throne. With wisdom and eloquence, his speech was like that of a Buddha, and he proclaimed these words:
"Whatever you wish to ask, whatever doubts all sentient beings may have, feel free to inquire; I shall resolve them for you. Then Mahākāśyapa asked Māra Pāpīyas:
"In the practice of a bhikṣu, what constitutes bondage? Māra immediately replied: "It is conceptualization (*parikalpa*)."

"I practice meditative concentration and my mind is tranquil; thus, there is the notion of 'having thought' and 'not having thought. Taking the emptiness of conceptual categories as essential, I destroy all notions of views.
I contemplate the notion of 'wanting to think,' give rise to various reflections, and govern the notion of 'wishlessness' by destroying all wishes.
I form the notion of *nirvāṇa* and delight in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), while destroying the notion of birth and death. This, Kāśyapa, is the fetter of a bhikṣu who practices in this way."
Why is this? Kāśyapa, you should know that one must not destroy various individual views in order to practice emptiness.
As for what is called "emptiness," it is that all views are empty; one must not destroy mindfulness in order to dwell in the signless.
Why is this? Whatever is conceived of is entirely signless. One must not destroy aspiration in order to seek the wishless. Regarding that which...
As for vows, they are all likewise vowless. One should not seek nirvāṇa by destroying birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
To clearly understand that birth-and-death is unattainable is itself nirvāṇa. Kāśyapa, you should know this: one who practices nirvāṇa does not give rise to conceptual thought.
Among all attachments, one should cause nothing to arise. When [birth-and-death] is destroyed and extinguished, nirvāṇa is fundamentally pure and has no arising or production. Thus...
Regarding the conditioned and the unconditioned: when these words were spoken, the minds of five hundred bhikṣus attained purity.
In this manner, even down to Subhūti, Śāriputra, and Maudgalyāyana—those five hundred noble disciples and others—each asked themselves about what they knew.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas distinguished and articulated each of their thoughts. Thereupon, the various devas...
In the assembly, there was a son of heaven named Susīma who asked Māra Pāpīyān: "Mañjuśrī has just now expounded upon the various activities of Māras.
Are you, O Benevolent One, able to take up this heavy responsibility once again to explain the principles? What are called the Māra-activities of a Bodhisattva?"
Then Māra replied: "O Son of Heaven, you should know that there are twenty demonic deeds of a bodhisattva.
What are these twenty? To fear birth and death; to desire liberation; to follow, practice, and cultivate the Buddha’s true Dharma;
and to prostrate, take refuge, and harbor expectations—these constitute demonic activities. Thus, the demonic deeds of a bodhisattva are altogether twenty; they are fully explained as follows."
As the Sūtra says: At that time, the World-Honored One praised Māra Pāpīyān, saying, "Excellent, excellent! You have well explained these demonic deeds of a bodhisattva.

If there should be someone who discusses this Dharma matter, listens to it, reflects upon it, and practices accordingly, rather than following the teachings of Māra, that person will establish the Great Way of the Buddha’s Dharma and preach the sūtras, thereby attaining twenty matters. What are these twenty? First, [Great...]"
"Great compassion and great pity—thus there are twenty such items, as fully explained in the sutra.
Thereupon, the Devaputra Susīma asked Māra Pāpīyas, "How timid you are, O Śubhavyūha! You have been skillfully praised by the Tathāgata. At that time, Māra replied:
"It is a great joy and a sublime benefit that my own person is not used [for self-aggrandizement]. It is, for example, like a man possessed by a spirit;
whatever he says should be reckoned as not his own, for what that person speaks is the speech of the spirit.
In the same way, O virtuous one, what I have now spoken was prompted by Mañjuśrī; it should not be proclaimed, saying, 'This is my own teaching. Thus spoke the Devaputra."
He said: "Now that you, O Benevolent One, have transformed into the body of a Buddha, are you not joyful?
Furthermore, with your physical form adorned by the marks and signs of excellence, sitting upon the lion throne and preaching the Dharma, are you not happy? Māra replied again:

"While you all see my body adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, I look upon myself as being bound by shackles and fetters. The Son of Heaven told him: "Pāpīyan, you yourself have surrendered!"
The Text of Repentance and Submission: "Mañjuśrī, by the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī, may you grant pardon to Pāpīyān.
Pāpīyān replied: "One should not repent for having studied under Mahāyāna Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. Why is this?

One who practices as a Bodhisattva does not perceive realms of deficiency, flaw, or impurity. As for one who gives rise to anger, even if they destroy resentment, it is only then that [one should...]"
They bowed their heads in repentance and took refuge [in him]. The Devaputra asked again, "What kind of patience does a bodhisattva possess?
The Māra replied, "A bodhisattva’s patience consists of twelve matters. What are these twelve? They are the patience of one's fundamental nature, which is free from blemish;
thus there are twelve kinds. This is as explained in detail in the sūtra. Thereupon, the Devaputra Susīma questioned the Māra.
“Pāpīyān, if you were to recount these twenty matters up to the twelve patiences (*kṣānti*), would you not leap for joy?
He replied, “I would be filled with joy. Suśīma then addressed Mañjuśrī: “Virtuous One, please grant pardon for the offense of the Māra Pāpīyān.
Mañjuśrī asked the Māra, “Who has bound you? He replied, “I do not know who has bound me. Mañjuśrī said, “Pāpīyān, you have not...”

Bound, they imagine themselves to be bound. All foolish, ordinary worldlings are likewise thus: their minds are fundamentally pure and free from all conceptualization, yet their will becomes attached to thoughts;
they do not know impermanence, but conceive the notion of permanence; they perceive suffering as pleasure; where there is no body, they reckon it as a body;
where there is impurity, they conceive it as purity; where there is no form, they conceive it as form; and where there is no sensation, they give rise to the thought of sensation.
He dies with consciousness and perceives the five aggregates. Just as Pāpīyān now fears being bound, by what cause could he be liberated?

He further asked: "Shall I not attain liberation now? He replied: "It is so, Pāpīyān. One who has already attained liberation does not need to be liberated again. By what cause would one be liberated?
It is because of conditions arising from false perceptions that one incurs bondage; [only by] eliminating them..."
To eliminate these defilements is called liberation. Thereupon, Mañjuśrī withdrew the majestic spiritual power he had established, causing Māra Pāpīyas to immediately return to his former state.
As Mañjuśrī was about to finish preaching the Dharma to the Devaputra Susīma, at that time Māra Pāpīyas, harboring grief and sorrow in his heart, wept with tears like rain and spoke these words:
Wherever this sutra is circulated, the various Māras, including Pāpīyān, shall find no opportunity. Should anyone receive and uphold it, they will sever the activities of Māra;
when Māra utters such words, he will immediately vanish and depart.
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*, concerning the introduction to the bodhisattva’s practice of unsoiled conduct within the realm of Māra, states:
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, it is unprecedented!
Now that you have preached the Śūraṅgama-samādhi, these evil Māras have not come to cause disturbance. The Buddha told Śāriputra: “You...”
"Do you wish to see the misfortune and affliction of Māra? "Yes, indeed; I have already seen it.
At that time, the Buddha emitted a ray of light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, and the entire assembly saw the Evil Māra bound by fivefold fetters, unable to free himself.
The Buddha asked Śāriputra, "Do you see the Evil Māra bound by the five fetters? "Yes, indeed; I have already seen him. "For whose sake was this Evil Māra bound?"
[The assembly] was bound [in wonder]. The Buddha said, "This is the power of the majestic spiritual authority of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Unstained by Conduct in the Realm of Māra, who addressed the Buddha, saying, "Indeed, World-Honored One, I shall now manifest within the realm of Māra a sovereign spiritual power, causing Māra to abide in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. At that time, the Bodhisattva Māragocarānupalipta suddenly disappeared from the midst of the assembly and appeared in the palace of Māra.
He spoke to the evil Māra, saying: "Have you not heard the Buddha preach the Śūraṅgama Samādhi?
Immeasurable sentient beings have all resolved their minds toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they have departed from your realm, and you shall likewise deliver them."
When others emerged from his realm, Māra immediately replied, "I have heard the Buddha speak the name of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi;
because I am bound by five fetters, I am unable to go there—namely, my two hands, two feet, and head. He further asked the evil Māra, "Who has bound you?
Māra then answered, "Just as I resolved my mind, desiring to go and destroy those who listen to and receive the Śūraṅgama..."
Regarding the "rigorous samādhi," it is that which is bound by the five fetters. I have further reflected: "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess great majestic power and virtue;
they are difficult to disturb or disrupt. If I were to go there, I might perhaps destroy myself. It would be better for me to remain here in this palace."
Having formed this thought, he immediately attained liberation from the five bonds. The Bodhisattva replied:

"In this way, all ordinary beings have bonds because they engage in recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination, and grasp at signs through inversion; they have bonds because of the movement of thought and frivolous proliferation;
they have bonds because of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. Within this, there is in reality neither one who is bound nor one who is liberated. Why is that?"

Why is this? All phenomena are without bondage; they are primordially liberated. Because all phenomena are without bondage and primordially without liberation, they possess the characteristic of constant liberation.

The world is deluded; it is for this reason that the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma through this gateway of the teaching. If there are sentient beings who come to understand this meaning, [they shall attain liberation].
Desiring to seek liberation, he applied himself with diligent and vigorous effort, whereby he attained release from all bonds.

At that time, seven hundred celestial maidens from the host of Māra scattered divine flowers, powdered incense, unguents, ointments, and various necklaces over the Bodhisattva Māradharṣaṇa (Unstained by the Practice of the Realm of Māra), and spoke these words: "When shall we be liberated from the realm of Māra? The Bodhisattva...
Sā replied, "If you are able not to destroy the bonds of Māra, then you will attain liberation. What is meant by the 'bonds of Māra'?
It refers to the sixty-two views. If a person does not destroy these various views, they will thereby attain liberation from the bonds of Māra.
The goddess spoke again, "What is meant by attaining liberation without destroying the various views? She answered:
All views fundamentally come from nowhere and go nowhere. If all knowledge and views lack the characteristics of coming and going, one attains liberation from the bonds of Māra.
All views are neither existent nor non-existent; if one does not discriminate between existence and non-existence, [one is liberated].
One thereby attains liberation from the bonds of Māra. If there is nothing seen, this is the view of a mound (*stūpa*).
Such right view is neither right nor wrong. If a phenomenon is neither right nor wrong, and is without action or reception, one thereby attains liberation from the bonds of Māra.
These various views are neither internal, nor external, nor in between; such views are likewise [non-existent].

Without dwelling on them, he attained liberation from the bonds of Māra. Upon hearing this teaching, seven hundred celestial maidens attained the *anulomikī-kṣānti* (receptive patience) and spoke these words:
"We, too, shall practice within the realm of Māra without being defiled, and we shall deliver all those bound by Māra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Māragocarānupalipta addressed the Evil Māra, saying: "You..."
"All these attendants have already resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
they shall attain liberation from these bonds. At that time, out of compassion for Māra, the goddesses all spoke these words:
"You should resolve your mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Do not conceive thoughts of fear regarding what is secure, nor [seek] within pleasure..."
They conceive the perception of suffering; they do not conceive the perception of bondage within liberation.
At that time, Māra the Evil One conceived a deceitful and crooked mind and spoke these words: "If you were to abandon the bodhicitta, I would then resolve to attain it.
Then, the celestial maidens, through their skillful means, said to Māra: "We have all already abandoned this mind; you may now resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
The mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. If one bodhisattva gives rise to the bodhicitta, all bodhisattvas likewise share this same mind.
Why is this? Because the mind is without differentiation; toward all sentient beings, the mind is entirely equal.
At that time, the evil Māra addressed the Bodhisattva Māragocarānupalipta, saying: "I shall now give rise to *anuttara*..."
"By this root of goodness, may I be liberated from my bonds. Having spoken these words, he immediately saw his own body released from its fetters.
Then, the Bodhisattva Māragocarānupalipta, by means of his supernormal powers, [acted].

He emitted great rays of light and manifested a pure and wondrous body that illuminated the palace of Māra. When Māra saw his own body, it was devoid of majestic radiance, appearing like a mass of ink.
At that time, among the host of Māras, two hundred celestial maidens were deeply attached to sensual desire;
seeing the upright and handsome form and color of this Bodhisattva, they conceived lustful and affectionate thoughts and each said: "If this man would only engage with us in amorous affairs..."

"We shall all comply with his instructions. At that time, this bodhisattva, knowing that the celestial maidens were destined for deliverance through their past karmic conditions, immediately manifested two hundred devaputras, whose features were handsome and majestic, no different from his own body.
He also created two hundred jeweled pavilions with latticed canopies, surpassing the palace of Māra. All these celestial maidens saw themselves within these jeweled pavilions.

Each one thought to themselves, "I am sporting with this bodhisattva. Their aspirations were fulfilled, their lustful thoughts ceased, and they all gave rise to a profound mind of love and reverence for the bodhisattva.
