Thereupon, the bodhisattva immediately preached the Dharma to them according to what was appropriate for each.
All of them resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. At that time, the Bodhisattva Māragocarānupalipta addressed the Evil Māra, saying, "You should go to the Buddha.
The Māra thought to himself, "My bonds have been severed; I shall go to the place where the Buddha is to disrupt his preaching of the Dharma.
Then the Evil Māra, surrounded by his retinue, went to the place where the Buddha was and said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One..."
He did not speak this Śūraṅgama Samādhi again. Why was this?
Because when he spoke of this samādhi, his body was immediately bound with the fivefold bonds. "I only pray that the Tathāgata will speak of other matters.
Then, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati said to the evil Māra, "Who has released your bonds? He replied, "The Bodhisattva Māragocarānupalipta has released my bonds. You..."
"What do you grant? he asked. "I grant that you shall resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*," the Māra replied.
At that time, the Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Resolute Mind (*Dṛḍhamati*): "Now this evil Māra has resolved his mind on *bodhi* for the sake of being released from his bonds;
it is not with a pure intention. Thus it is, Resolute Mind: after my parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years, there will be many..."
"Monks, there are those who resolve upon the mind of enlightenment for the sake of gain and offerings, not with a pure intention.
Śrīghoṣa, you should observe the power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and the majestic spiritual authority of the Buddha-dharma.
There are these monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who, with a frivolous mind, a mind greedy for gain and offerings, and a mind following after others, hear of this samādhi and yet resolve upon it."
The bodhicitta—I know that all such minds serve as the causal conditions for attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
How much more so for one who hears this Śūraṅgama Samādhi and, with a pure mind, resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
You should know that such a person has already attained definitive certainty within the Buddha-dharma and possesses firm resolve in their bodhicitta.

Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, now that this evil Māra has heard the exposition of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, he has resolved his mind on Bodhi for the sake of liberation from his bonds.
Will he also obtain the causes and conditions for the full realization of the Buddha-dharma? The Buddha said, “It is as you have said.”

By virtue of the causes and conditions of hearing this samādhi and the causes and conditions of having resolved for bodhicitta, that evil Māra will, in future ages, be able to abandon all demonic activities, demonic behaviors, the deceitful and crooked mind of Māra, and the afflictions caused by Māra.
From this time forward, he shall gradually attain the power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and achieve the Buddha-way. Thus it was said by the Bodhisattva Firm Resolve.
[Sā] said to the Evil Māra: "The Tathāgata has now bestowed a prediction upon you. Māra replied:
"Good son, I did not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* with a pure mind. Why, then, does the Tathāgata bestow a prediction upon me?
As the Buddha has said: "From the mind comes karma; from karma comes retribution. I myself have had no mind that sought awakening..."

Dharmodgata asked, "For what reason has the Tathāgata bestowed a prediction of enlightenment upon me? At that time, wishing to sever the doubts of the assembly, the Buddha addressed Dṛḍhamati, saying:
"There are four kinds of predictions bestowed upon bodhisattvas. What are these four? There is the bestowing of a prediction before one has yet resolved to attain awakening;

there is the bestowing of a prediction at the very moment one resolves to attain awakening; there is the secret prediction; and there is the prediction for those who have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
The prophecy of presence—these are called the four. Only a Tathāgata can know this matter;
it is something that no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas can know, as explained at length in the sūtra. At that time, the Bodhisattva Māragocarāsaṃkliṣṭa...
The celestial maidens who had been converted were inspired to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Each scattered heavenly flowers over the Buddha and addressed him, saying: "World-Honored One, we do not delight in receiving a secret prediction of enlightenment.

We pray that you may grant us a manifest prediction of the realization of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). We only wish, World-Honored One, that you would now grant us this prediction."

[The Buddha gave] the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. At that time, the Buddha smiled, and from his mouth issued various kinds of wondrously colored light that illuminated all the worlds, then returned and entered the crown of his head.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, for what reason do you smile?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Do you now see these two hundred goddesses who, with palms joined, pay respectful homage to the Tathāgata?
"World-Honored One, I have seen them," [Ānanda replied]. "Ānanda, these goddesses have already planted deep roots of goodness in the presence of five hundred Buddhas in the past.
From this point forward, they shall again make offerings to countless Buddhas for seven hundred asaṃkhyeya kalpas."
...they shall all attain Buddhahood, named King Pure (Jingwang).

Ānanda, after these goddesses have ended their lives, they will transform out of their female bodies and all be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where they will make offerings to and serve Maitreya Bodhisattva.
At that time, having heard that the goddesses had received their predictions, the evil Māra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I myself now..."
All their retinues will lose their autonomy because they have heard this exposition of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; how much more so for others who hear it?
If a person hears the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they will immediately attain definitive certainty and abide within the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the goddess, with a heart free from fear, said to the evil Māra: "Do not grieve so greatly; we now..."
"Depart from our realm! Why is this? The suchness (*tathatā*) of the realm of Māra is identical to the suchness of the realm of the Buddha.

The suchness of the realm of Māra and the suchness of the realm of the Buddha are non-dual and not distinct. We do not depart from this suchness. The characteristics of the realm of Māra are identical to the characteristics of the realm of the Buddha.
The dharma-realm of Māra and the dharma-realm of the Buddha are non-dual and not distinct. Regarding these dharma-characteristics, we neither exit nor transcend them. Māra—
The realms have no fixed dharma that can be pointed out; even the Buddha-realm has no fixed dharma that can be pointed out.
The realm of Māra and the realm of the Buddha are neither two nor distinct. We do not go beyond, nor do we transcend, these characteristics of phenomena.
Therefore, you should know that all dharmas are without determination. Because they are without determination, there are neither followers nor non-followers. At that time, the evil Māra...
Distressed and sorrowful, he wished to return to his celestial palace. The Bodhisattva Māradharṣaka said to the Evil Māra, "Where do you wish to go?
The Māra replied, "I now wish to return to the palace where I dwell. The Bodhisattva said, "Without leaving this assembly, this itself is your palace.
At that moment, the Evil Māra saw himself standing within his own original palace. The Bodhisattva...
The Bodhisattva said, "Māra, what do you see? Māra replied, "I see myself dwelling in my own original palace, with its beautiful groves, gardens, and ponds—all of which are my property.
The Bodhisattva said, "You may now offer these to the Tathāgata. Māra said, "So be it.
As soon as he had spoken these words, he saw the Tathāgata, along with the entire assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, all present there.

Within that [assembly], the Śūraṅgama-samādhi was expounded. At that time, Ānanda said to the evil Māra, "You have gained great benefit in being able to offer this palace to the Buddha for him to dwell in.
Māra replied, "This is due to the power and grace of the Bodhisattva Māradharṣaṇa-asaṃkliṣṭacaryā (Unstained by Conduct in the Realm of Māra).
Then the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, this Bodhisattva Māradharṣaṇa-asaṃkliṣṭacaryā dwells..."
"Is the sovereign power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi truly like this? The Buddha said, "It is as you have described.

Now, this bodhisattva, dwelling in this samādhi, is able by means of his supernormal powers to manifest all manner of activities within the realm of Māra with complete mastery according to his will, yet he remains untainted by those demonic deeds. He manifests enjoyment with celestial maidens, yet in reality..."

This son of good family does not succumb to the evil dharma of sexual desire. Abiding in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, he manifests entry into the realm of Māra, yet his body never leaves the assembly of the Buddha.
He manifests engaging in the play and entertainment of the realm of Māra, while using the Buddha-dharma to teach and transform sentient beings.
Regarding the account of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva transforming the hungry ghost Mārīci,
the *Yankou Jing* (Flaming Mouth Sūtra) states: At that time, the World-Honored One was at the Nyagrodha Monastery in the city of Kapilavastu,
surrounded on all sides by bhikṣus, bodhisattvas, and countless sentient beings, as he preached the Dharma for them.
The Dharma. At that time, Ānanda was dwelling alone in a quiet place, focusing his mind with single-minded attention.
Then, after the third watch of that night, he saw a hungry ghost named Mūrdha-jvala (Face-Ablaze) standing before him. The ghost addressed Ānanda: "Three days from now..."
"Your life is about to end; you shall immediately be reborn among these hungry ghosts.
When Ānanda heard these words, his heart was filled with terror, and he asked the hungry ghost: "Regarding this calamity of mine, what plan should I devise to escape from such suffering?"
At that time, the hungry ghosts replied to Ānanda: "If, at dawn,
you can provide alms to as many hungry ghosts as there are grains of sand in hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Ganges Rivers, as well as to hundreds of thousands of brahmins and sages,
giving each one *droṇa* of food and drink measured by the Magadha *droṇa*, and furthermore make offerings to the Triple Gem on our behalf, you shall obtain increase."
"May my life-span be such that I may leave behind the suffering of the hungry ghosts and be reborn in the heavens.
Ānanda saw this hungry ghost with a blazing face, his body emaciated, withered, and extremely hideous;

fire blazed upon his face, his throat was like a needle, his hair was disheveled, his fur and claws were long and sharp, and his body was as if burdened by a heavy load. Furthermore, hearing such discordant words, he was greatly startled.

Terrified, his body hair standing on end, he immediately rose from his seat and hurried to where the Buddha was. Prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he bowed at the Buddha’s feet;
trembling in both body and mind, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "Save me, World-Honored One! Save me, Sugata! In three days my life will come to its end.
Last night I saw a hungry ghost with one side burning, who spoke to me, saying: 'In three [days]...'"
"Your life will surely end today, and you shall be reborn among the hungry ghosts. I then asked, "By what means or stratagem may this suffering be avoided?
The hungry ghost replied, "If you were to give alms to as many hungry ghosts as there are grains of sand in hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Ganges Rivers..."
"and hundreds of thousands of brahmins, as well as the various sages and others, eat. You shall obtain increased longevity.
"World-Honored One, how may I now escape this suffering? At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda: "Do not fear now.
There is an alternative skillful means by which you may obtain the food given to such hungry ghosts, the brahmins, and the sages, so that it does not arise [as suffering for you]."
“Ānanda, the Buddha said, ‘There is a dhāraṇī called “Infinite Power of All-Virtue Light.
If anyone recites this dhāraṇī, it is as if they have already made offerings to a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of hungry ghosts,
as numerous as the sands of a hundred thousand Ganges Rivers, as well as to six hundred and eighty koṭis of nayutas of brahmins, and furthermore— ’”
Before each of the sages, there were four *droṇas* and nine *āḍhakas* of food and drink, measured by Magadha measures.

The Buddha said to Ānanda, "In a previous life, when I was a brahmin, I received this dhāraṇī from the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and the Tathāgata Lokeśvararājadeva. By the power of this dhāraṇī, I shall [now]..."
I have obtained the fulfillment of providing food for immeasurable and innumerable hungry ghosts, as well as for brahmins and sages.
Because I gave food to these hungry ghosts, I shall cast off this body and be reborn in the heavens.
Ānanda, you should now receive and uphold this dhāraṇī to protect yourself. Then he spoke the mantra:
Then, *sarvatathāgatapūjite oṃ svāhā svāhā hūṃ*.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda, if one wishes to perform this rite of offering food, first take food and drink and place them in a clean vessel.
Recite this dhāraṇī mantra seven times over the food, stand within the doorway, and extend your arms through the opening."
Outside, place the tray on a clean spot of ground and snap your fingers seven times.
Having performed this offering, there will be hungry ghosts numbering in the hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in each of the four directions.
Before each and every hungry ghost, there shall be four *magadha* bushels and nine pecks of food and drink. In this way, all these hungry ghosts shall be completely satiated. These hungry ghosts...
After the ghosts had consumed this food, they all cast off their ghostly bodies and were entirely reborn in the heavens. He spoke again:

"Ānanda, if bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās are able to constantly recite this dhāraṇī and offer them food and drink, they will thereby fulfill immeasurable merit, their lives will be prolonged, and they will immediately achieve the offering of hundreds of thousands of koṭis."
...the *koṭi*. The Tathāgata’s merits consist of a complexion that is fresh and pure, as well as majestic power and a powerful memory.
All non-humans—such as the *bhūta*, *piśāca*, *yakṣa*, and *rākṣasa*, along with all the *preta*—fear such a person; they cannot bear to look upon them.
Such a person immediately achieves and possesses great strength, diligence, and progress. Furthermore, Ānanda, if one wishes to give to a *brāhmaṇa* or...
Regarding the food for the sages (*ṛṣi*): one should take food and drink, fill a bowl with it, and recite this *dhāraṇī* mantra over the food seven times.
Then, pour it into flowing water as a complete offering to countless *koṭis* of hundreds of thousands of *Ganges-sand* Brahmans, as well as the sages and others.
Having consumed this food, they shall have their faculties restored, attain perfect auspiciousness, and each give rise to [a pure resolve].
This is his vow: he praises those who give; those who give food attain purity of mind and swiftly realize the majestic power of Brahmā.
Constantly practicing pure conduct, they fully accomplish the merit of making offerings to hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Among all enemies, they always achieve victory. If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, [or upāsikās...]
Sai Upāsikā, if one wishes to make offerings to all the Triple Gem, one should prepare incense, flowers, food, and drink,
and recite this dhāraṇī mantra twenty-one times over the food, incense, flowers, and other offerings being presented. By making these offerings to the Triple Gem,
these sons and daughters of good family will fully accomplish the wondrous offerings of the devas, as well as the [unconditioned...]
Make offerings above. Honor and praise the Three Jewels of all the Tathāgatas’ lands.
All Buddhas will keep you in mind, proclaiming and praising you, and the devas will protect you. The Buddha said: "Go, Ānanda!

You must protect yourself and also extensively explain this for the sake of all sentient beings, so that all sentient beings may achieve and be fully endowed with immeasurable merit in every lifetime they are born."
Constantly encountering hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas.
Third, the "Simile of the Nature of Evil" Dharma-gate:
the account of the Venerable Śāriputra subduing the six teachers.
The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states: When the six heretical teachers heard that the Tathāgata intended to come to Śrāvastī, they went to inform the king, saying:
"The elder Sudatta has purchased Prince Jeta’s garden, intending to build a vihāra for Gautama.
Allow us and our disciples to compete in supernatural arts. If the śramaṇa prevails, then let him proceed with the construction; if he does not, he shall not be permitted to build it."
The King summoned Sudatta and questioned him, saying, "Now these six teachers claim that you have purchased this grove with the intention of erecting a vihāra for Gautama.

They have come to compete in their respective skills with the śramaṇa and his disciples; if they are victorious, you shall be permitted to build the vihāra, but if they are not, you shall not be allowed to do so.
Sudatta returned home, put on soiled and greasy clothes, and was filled with grief and distress.
"I am unhappy. Then, when the time had come the following day, Śāriputra donned his robes, took up his bowl, and went to the house of Sudatta.
He immediately asked him, "For what reason are you unhappy? Sudatta replied in detail: "These six teachers have been renunciants for a long time;

they have long possessed sincerity and integrity, and there is no one who can equal them in the skills and arts they have studied. I do not know if your venerable self’s arts and skills can compare with theirs."
“Shall we compete? Śāriputra said, “Even if these six heretical teachers were to fill Jambudvīpa, as numerous as a grove of bamboo, they could not move even a single hair on my foot.
What do you wish to compete in? Go ahead and do as you please. Su-datta was delighted;
he changed into new clothes, bathed in scented water, and so forth, and immediately went to inform the King, “I have questioned him; let him do as he pleases.”
Heeding their intent, the King informed the six masters: "Now I grant you permission to compete in arts and skills with the śramaṇa. The six masters proclaimed to the people of the country:
"Seven days hence, we shall compete in arts and skills with the śramaṇa outside the city. At that time, there were eighteen hundred million people in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
According to the custom of that country, they would strike a drum to assemble the multitude; if a bronze drum was struck, eight hundred million people would gather. If...
When the silver drum was struck, fourteen billion people gathered; if the golden drum were struck, everyone would gather.
When the seven-day period was complete, they went to a level and open place and beat the golden drum, and everyone assembled. The followers of the six teachers numbered three hundred million.
At that time, the people all prepared high seats for the king and his six teachers. Then, Sudatta prepared a high seat for Śāriputra.
At that moment, Śāriputra was beneath a tree, having entered into various meditative concentrations.
He then had this thought: "The great assembly in this gathering has practiced heterodoxy for a long time;
they are arrogant and self-exalting, regarding all living beings as mere weeds and chaff. By what virtue shall I subdue them? Having reflected thus, he immediately made a vow:
"If throughout countless kalpas I have been compassionate and filial toward my parents, and have revered and honored śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, then as I first enter this assembly, may all..."
“Great assembly, act as my witnesses. When the six teachers saw that the assembly had already gathered, yet Śāriputra alone had not yet arrived, they said to the king:
“The son of the Śākya, Gautama, knows himself to be without skill; now that the assembly has gathered, he does not come out of fear.”
The King informed Sudatta: "The time has arrived; it is fitting that the Buddha’s disciples come for discussion.
Then Sudatta went to where Śāriputra was and, kneeling with his right knee on the ground, said: "Venerable One, the great assembly has already gathered. I pray that you will come to the meeting.
At that time, Śāriputra arose from meditative concentration, adjusted his robes, placed his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) over his left shoulder, and proceeded with slow and dignified grace.
He walked like a lion king and approached the great assembly.

At that moment, the great assembly and the six heretical teachers suddenly rose up, bowing their heads in salutation without realizing it, like grass bent by the wind. Then Śāriputra ascended the seat prepared by Sudatta.
Among the followers of the six teachers was a disciple named Raudrākṣa, who was skilled in the arts of illusion. Before the great assembly...
Previously, he had used incantations to create a single tree that naturally grew tall and wide, providing shade for the entire assembly.
Its branches and leaves were lush and dense, and its flowers and fruits were each distinct. Everyone said, "This transformation was surely wrought by Raudrākṣa.
Then Śāriputra, employing his supernatural powers, conjured up a whirlwind that blew up and tore out the roots of the tree, casting it to the ground and pulverizing it into fine dust. The people—
Everyone said, "Śāriputra is superior. He then created another pond;
its four sides were all made of the seven precious gems, and within the waters of the pond grew various kinds of flowers. Śāriputra further manifested a great six-tusked white elephant.
Upon each tusk there were seven lotus flowers, and upon each flower there were seven jade maidens. The elephant proceeded with slow and dignified grace.
He went to the edge of the pond and sipped its water; the pond immediately vanished.
He then created a mountain adorned with the seven treasures, where the various ponds, trees, flowers, and fruits were lush and flourishing.

Śāriputra further manifested as a Vajrapāṇi, who pointed at it from afar with his vajra-pestle; the mountain was instantly destroyed, leaving nothing behind. He then manifested as a dragon with ten heads.
In the midst of the void, various kinds of jewels rained down; thunder and lightning shook the earth, startling and agitating the great assembly.
Śāriputra further manifested as a golden-winged bird king (*garuḍa-rāja*), who tore it apart and devoured it. He then manifested as an ox, its body immense and tall.
It was fat and powerful, with coarse legs and sharp horns; it pawed the ground and roared loudly as it charged forward.
Śāriputra again transformed himself into a lion and tore it apart to eat it. He then changed his form once more, becoming a yakṣa ghost with a massive body.
A fire blazed upon his head, making it as red as blood; his four fangs were long and sharp, and fire issued from his mouth and eyes.
As he leaped and rushed forward, Śāriputra transformed himself into King Vaiśravaṇa. Terrified by the yakṣa, [the yakṣa] immediately sought to retreat and flee.
Flames erupted on all four sides; there was no place to flee. Only at the side of Śāriputra was it cool and free of fire.
Immediately, [Lokāṭṭha] prostrated himself, casting his body to the ground, seeking mercy to escape with his life. Once a sense of shame had arisen within him, the fire was instantly extinguished.
The assembly all cried out, "Śāriputra has triumphed; Lokāṭṭha is defeated. Then Śāriputra ascended into the air and manifested the four majestic postures.
He performed eighteen miraculous transformations. Having performed these transformations, he withdrew his supernormal powers and sat upon his original seat.

When the great assembly witnessed his spiritual power, they were all filled with joy. Then Śāriputra preached the Dharma for them; according to their respective roots of merit, each attained the fruits of the Path.
Three hundred million disciples from the following of the Six Heretics went forth as monastics under Śāriputra.
Regarding the study of the Way:
the *Jianglong jing* (Sutra on Subduing the Dragon) relates the conditions under which Maudgalyāyana manifested two supernormal powers to subdue the two dragon kings.
It says that the Buddha commanded the elder Anāthapiṇḍada to practice giving; he immediately rose, knelt with his right knee to the ground, and [responded].

With palms joined, he addressed the Buddha, saying, "I pray that the Buddha and the community of monks will deign to visit my home tomorrow. I wish to provide a simple meal. The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "Tomorrow morning we shall ascend to the heavens and descend at noon; we shall gather at the house of Puṇyavanta for the meal.
On the following morning, the Buddha and the bhikṣus ascended into the void in the time it takes to snap one's fingers. At that time, there was a rākṣasa...
A man named Sīta straightened his robes and, from within the void, addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have ascended to heaven many times, yet never before has it been as dark as it is now.
The Buddha said: "There are two dragon kings who, being greatly enraged, have spat forth mist; for this reason, it is so dark."
There was another Arhat named Śubha who addressed the Buddha, saying, "I wish to stop them. The Buddha said, "These two nāgas possess great majestic power;
if you go there, they will surely manifest evil and vomit forth water, drowning and killing the people and all crawling creatures.
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha, "I wish to go and admonish them. The Buddha said, "Very well. Maudgalyāyana immediately went to the place where the nāgas were. The nāgas—
Upon seeing Maudgalyāyana, the dragon immediately emitted smoke from its mouth, and in a moment, it burst into flames, surrounding Maudgalyāyana in a single layer.

Maudgalyāyana, through his spiritual power, likewise manifested fire that surrounded the dragon in three layers. He then transformed his body to enter the dragon’s eye, exiting from the left and entering from the right.
It entered from the right and exited from the left; in this manner, it successively entered and exited through his ears and nose, or flew into his mouth.
The nāga said to Maudgalyāyana, "You are within my belly! Maudgalyāyana again transformed his body and circled the nāga fourteen times, using his body to threaten the two nāgas.
The nāgas were struck with great terror; their bristling hair fanned the ocean waters and shook Mount Sumeru. From afar, the Buddha addressed Maudgalyāyana: "This..."
"Even a dragon can spew forth water and drown all the people in the world; you must be cautious. Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:

'I possess the supernormal power of the four dhyānas and have always practiced them with faith. I am able to take this Mount Sumeru and the two dragons, place them in the palm of my hand, and hurl them to another realm.
Furthermore, I can grasp Mount Sumeru with my hand and grind it until it is as fine as dust.'"

None of the devas or humans were aware of this. When the two nāgas heard it, they immediately submitted. Maudgalyāyana returned to his status as a śramaṇa, and the nāgas transformed back into human form.

They prostrated themselves in worship and repented before Maudgalyāyana, saying, "We were foolish, deluded, and confused; we did not recognize your venerable divinity. We have offended you by disturbing the clouds and mist.
We beg for your compassion and pardon for our transgressions. After the two nāgas had repented, they received the five precepts and prostrated themselves before the Buddha.
Having paid homage, he departed.
Regarding the circumstances of Upagupta’s renunciation and his subduing of Māra, the *Aśokarāja-sūtra* states:
"Śāṇakavāsin built a monastery on Mount Mahātakra. A merchant selling incense..."
The merchant leader was named Gupta. Through the power of skillful means, Śāṇakavāsin converted him and inspired him to practice with diligence.
At that time, Śāṇakavāsin entered his house alone. Gupta asked, "Noble one, why do you travel alone without any disciples?
I delight in living at home and cherish the pleasures of the five senses; I have no desire to leave the household life. If I were to have a son..."
He should follow the Elder. Eventually, Guptā gave birth to a son named Apagupta.
When he had grown up, Śāṇakavāsin went to Guptā’s place and said, "You previously made a vow that if I were to have a son, you would give him to me as a novice.
Now that a son has been born, you should permit him to follow me and go forth. Guptā replied, "I now only..."
He had a son. [The father said: "If a second son is born, I shall give him to you, Elder. Eventually, a second son was born, named Anagha.
He requested him again from the father, but the father would not grant it. A third son, Upagupta, was also requested from him. The father replied:
"I shall make a vow that Upagupta shall manage my livelihood; whether he prospers or declines, he must not be given to you."
"If he leaves the household life, he will neither advance nor regress; therefore, permit him to leave the household life.
At that time, the Māra-king caused all the people of the kingdom of Mathurā to purchase his goods so that he might obtain profit. Then Upagupta was selling incense himself.
Then the Elder Śāṇakavāsin said: "How are your mind and mental factors wholesome? How are they unwholesome?
He replied: "I do not know. The Elder spoke again: "If the mind and mental factors are associated with greed, hatred, and delusion, these are called unwholesome.
If they are associated with non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, these are called wholesome. At that time, the Elder—
He prepared nine heaps each of black earth and white earth, and said to him: "If a dark thought arises, take a black ball;
if a pure thought arises, take a white ball. Then Upagupta followed these instructions; as long as no wholesome thought arose, he did not obtain even a single white ball.
Thus he gradually proceeded to take the balls, [until there was] one part black balls and one...
He divided them into white pills. He then reflected further on the half-black and half-white pills, contemplating the wholesome in succession, so that evil thoughts did not arise.
When he took a white pill, there was a courtesan in the kingdom of Mathurā named Bhavāvatī, who had a maidservant.
He went to Upagupta’s place and purchased a great quantity of incense. The owner asked him, "Where did you obtain this much incense?
Are you not stealing it? He replied, "There is a merchant named Upagupta, who is endowed with perfect physical form."
Her speech was subtle and artful. She used the Dharma as a pretext to sell herself; when her master heard this, a lustful desire arose within him.
He then sent his maidservant to Upagupta’s place, instructing her: "You should say to him, 'I wish to enjoy myself with you.
Upagupta replied, "The time for such a meeting has not yet come. This was repeated three times, yet he still would not consent. At that time—
He summoned the son of a householder and went to his location. The merchant leader had come from Northern India, bringing five hundred horses and various goods, and arrived at the kingdom of Mathurā.
Having arrived, he asked the people of Mathurā, "In what part of this country is there a woman who is foremost in beauty?
The people replied, "There is one woman who is foremost in beauty."
"His name was Bhavatrāta. The merchant leader said, "I now wish to go to that place with five hundred silver coins and various goods.
At that time, because the courtesan was greedy for his wealth, she killed the son of the elder, took his body, and placed it in an impure location.
She then enjoyed herself together with the merchant leader. This was known by the son of the elder’s close friends.
The *vijñāna* (consciousness) sought out a corpse in an impure place and went to inform the king, saying:
"You may take that Vasavadatta, cut off her hands, feet, ears, and nose, and scatter them in the wilderness. They did exactly as the king commanded.
At that time, Upagupta thought to himself: "In the past, I did not wish to see her; together we experienced the five [desires]..."
He wished to see and examine his hands, feet, ears, and nose, so he went to look at him and spoke these verses.
Having heard these words, Vāsavadatta was deeply terrified of birth and death; hearing of the Buddha’s virtues, his mind was transformed and he took pleasure in *nirvāṇa*.
He then spoke a verse in response to Upagupta. Upagupta then spoke four [verses].
He contemplated his own body with intense focus. He attained revulsion for the realm of desire and realized the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
Vāsavadatta realized the fruit of *srotāpanna*. Not long after Upagupta had departed, Vāsavadatta passed away and was reborn in the heavens.
At that time, the Elder Śāṇakavāsin went to Upagupta’s dwelling and said to him, "You should listen to Upa..."
"Upagupta, follow me and renounce the householder's life. Upagupta replied, "I have previously made a vow that I shall now engage in trade;

only if it is neither profitable nor unprofitable will I permit myself to renounce the world. Śāṇakavāsin then used his supernormal powers to cause his trade to be neither profitable nor unprofitable.
At that time, Upagupta reflected within himself, weighing and calculating whether it was profitable or not.
Śāṇakavāsin went again to Guptā and said to her, "This son of yours has been prophesied by the Buddha that, one hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, he shall perform the work of a Buddha.
You should permit him to follow me and go forth into the religious life."
Guptā consented immediately. Śāṇakavāsin took Upagupta to the Nandika Monastery and granted him the going forth and the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Upon reaching the fourth *karmavācanā*, he severed all fetters and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
At that time, Śāṇakavāsin said to Upagupta, "O son of noble family, you were prophesied by the Buddha; I have entered [the state of parinirvāṇa]."
One hundred years after the Parinirvāṇa, there will be a bhikṣu named Upagupta who shall perform the work of a Buddha. Later, he shall become a Buddha named Asaṃjñika (The Nameless).
He shall preach the Dharma in this manner. At that time, the Māra King will rain down pearls amidst the great assembly to distract the minds of the people.
Because the multitude is thus distracted, not a single person will be able to realize the Truth (*dṛṣṭi*). Then, he [the bhikṣu] will reflect to himself:
He reflected: "I know this is the King of Māras. On the second day, even more people came; the King of Māras rained down gold, again disturbing the minds of the assembly.
On the third day, twice as many people arrived; the Māra rained down pearls and gold and produced celestial music.

At that time, the multitude had not yet attained freedom from desire; upon seeing the forms and hearing the sounds, their minds were shaken, and they no longer listened to the Dharma. Then the Māra...
The king then fastened a flower garland around Upagupta’s neck. Upagupta reflected, "Who has done this?
and immediately recognized it was Māra. Upagupta then thought, "Why did the World-Honored One not convert him?
He further reflected, "He is one whom I shall convert; the Buddha prophesied that I would be a Buddha without marks (animitta-buddha) and taught me [this duty]."

To convert the people, Upagupta took three corpses—a dead snake, a dead dog, and a dead human—and by means of his supernatural powers, transformed these three corpses into flower garlands. He went to the abode of Māra and fastened them around his neck.
At that time, Māra went to Maheśvara, Śakra, and the other gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
The gods of the Four Great Kings sought to release him from the corpse, but they were unable to do so. He then went to the abode of Mahābrahmā.
Mahābrahmā said, "O son of good family, this is a feat produced by the supernatural power of a disciple of the One of Ten Powers;
who can release it? It is like the great ocean shore, which water cannot breach. The Māra King then spoke, saying, "How shall I instruct you? I shall now take refuge [in you]."
“Who? the Great Brahmā asked. “Go now quickly and take refuge in Upagupta,” he replied. “Just as a person who falls to this ground rises from that very spot.
At that time, the Māra King realized for the first time that the supernatural power of the Buddha’s son was great;
he then spoke a verse in praise of the Buddha and in self-reproach. The Māra King of the Desire Realm immediately abandoned his arrogance and confessed his past transgressions.
Regarding the account of a seven-year-old śrāmaṇera subduing non-Buddhists, the *Aśokarāja-sūtra* states:
"In the past, King Aśoka had deep faith in the Triple Gem and constantly made offerings to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, as well as to various brāhmaṇas and non-Buddhists.
These [latter] all conceived feelings of jealousy and gathered together. They selected those who were long-established..."
There were five hundred men who all recited the four Vedas and were profoundly learned in astronomy and geography.
They gathered together and deliberated, saying, "King Aśoka provides offerings to nothing but those who have shaved their heads. We are long-established elders and have never been consulted;
what expedient means should we employ to turn his mind? Among them was a skilled Brahmin priest who spoke to the others...

The brahmin said, "Virtuous ones, simply follow me. Seven days from now, by the power of my incantations, I shall assume the form of Maheśvara and fly to the gate of the royal palace. You all must follow behind me on foot;
I am able to cause a great offering to be made, and you shall all receive it. All the brahmins agreed, and seven days passed.
Sūrya, the Brahmin Sādhucitra, immediately transformed his own body into that of Maheśvara.
He flew through the air to the king’s gate, and all the other Brahmins likewise followed as attendants to the king’s gate.
He sent a messenger to inform the king, saying, "In the sky there is Maheśvara, leading four hundred and ninety-nine Brahmins."
He descended from the sky and is now outside the gate. Other brahmins stand upon the ground, wishing to see the king.
King Aśoka then called him forward and had him sit upon a couch in the side chamber. The king said, "Sit for a moment; let us exchange greetings.
He then spoke to him, saying, "Maheśvara, how could you deign to lower yourself to come and meet me? What is it that you desire?"
“Do you wish for it? he asked. He replied, “I wish for food and drink. The king immediately issued an order, and five hundred trays of food and drink were brought forward and placed before him.
Maheśvara and the others all pushed them away with their hands, saying, “Since birth, we have never eaten such food as this.
King Aśoka replied, “It was not previously agreed that we would eat; I did not know what we should eat, or what to eat. Maheśvara and the others all [said the same].
They spoke with one voice, saying, "Our food is the consumption of shaven-headed men. King Aśoka immediately commanded an official to go to the Kukkuta Monastery and say to the Venerable Yaśas:
"Within the royal palace there are five hundred brāhmaṇas, one of whom claims to be Maheśvara.
We do not know whether he is a human or an evil rākṣasa; we pray that you will explain the reason for this."
The Ācārya arrived and, for my sake, dispatched a messenger. This person was a disciple of a heretical Brahmin.
Upon reaching that assembly, he did not report the facts as they truly were, but spoke to the monks according to what the King had said:
"Of all the five hundred Brahmins belonging to King Aśoka, their appearance is that of humans, but their speech is that of rākṣasas; they do nothing but this."
He said, "I specifically wish to have you, Śramaṇa, prepare the meal. The Elder Yaśas then spoke to the Karmadāna: "Strike the gong to assemble the Saṃgha.
Rising to address the assembly, he said, "I am old and decrepit. For the sake of the Saṃgha, I shall attend to such matters as these;
may the Saṃgha remain at ease and protect the Buddha-dharma. Grant me leave to depart. The Second Elder said, "The Elder should not go."

"My body has no capacity; it is only I who should go. Thus they passed the word in succession, until among the assembly of one hundred and sixty-eight thousand monks, the very youngest—a seven-year-old śrāmaṇera—arose from his place, went into the midst of the monks, knelt with palms joined, and spoke these words:
"The entire great assembly need not be disturbed; as I am but a child, I am unable [to go]."
"You are capable of protecting and upholding the Buddha-dharma. I pray only that the Great Assembly will surely grant me leave to depart.
The Elder Yaśas was filled with great joy; he stroked the śrāmaṇera’s head and said, "It is fitting for you to go. Without waiting for his attendants, the śrāmaṇera departed first.
King Aśoka said, "Has anyone come? The messenger replied, "They have passed the responsibility to one another until the junior-most śrāmaṇera was sent.
The King remarked, "The elders were ashamed, so they sent the youth to respond.
Upon hearing that the śrāmaṇera had arrived, the King immediately went out to meet him and seated him upon the royal throne. All...
The brahmins were all greatly incensed, saying, "King Aśoka is utterly lacking in discernment," and so forth.
The śrāmaṇera asked the king, "Why did you call him? The king replied, "This Maheśvara wishes to have the ācārya as his food."
The śrāmaṇera said, "I am young and have not eaten since this morning. Your Majesty, please give me food first; only then shall I give it to him.
The king immediately commanded his cook to bring food and give it to him. He ate one tray of food until it was completely finished.
When five hundred trays of food were brought and given to him in this manner, he was still not satisfied. The king again commanded his cook, saying, "Whatever remains..."

Having finished eating, he took the food and brought it to him. When the śrāmaṇera had finished the food, it suddenly vanished entirely. He asked, "Is it enough? He replied, "It is not enough; my hunger and thirst remain as they were.
The kitchen supervisor informed the king, saying, "The food and drink in the storehouse are completely exhausted;
there is no more food. The śrāmaṇera said, "Take the head of that brahmin down here; I wish to eat it. Immediately, he devoured it all.
In this manner, he completely devoured all four hundred and ninety-nine brahmins until none remained.
Only Maheśvara was left, who was struck with extreme terror; he flew up into the void, seeking to escape. At that moment, the śrāmaṇera raised his hand from his seat.
From the midst of the void, he seized their heads and devoured them until they were all gone. The King was immediately struck with terror as he watched them being eaten.
Seeing that the brahmins had been consumed, he asked, "Will you not eat me as well? The śrāmaṇera, knowing the King's thoughts, spoke to him, saying:
"The King is a patron (dānapati) of the Buddha-Dharma; you shall never suffer harm or destruction. Do not be afraid. He then said to the King: "The King may come with me."
"Is it not so at Kukkutārāma Monastery? The King said, "Ācārya, whether you lead me to heaven or into the earth, I shall follow you in all things.
The śrāmaṇera immediately went with the King to the monastery. When the King saw the food that the śrāmaṇera had eaten, he [asked] about the various monks.
They all shared and ate together. Those five hundred brahmins who had eaten all had their hair and beards shaved off and were clad in dharma robes;
they sat at the end of the row among the assembly of monks. As for the first to eat, he was seated at the very head of the assembly—the seat of Maheśvara.
Standing at the very end of the procession, the five hundred men saw King Śrāmaṇera and were filled with extreme shame and remorse.
"We are not even able to contend with this śrāmaṇera," they thought, "let alone compete in strength against this great multitude.
They were like herons waiting beside glowing coals, like mosquitoes competing in flight speed with a garuḍa, or like small rabbits [facing a lion].

They contended their power against that of the Lion King; in such a manner, these five hundred brahmins, who had failed to measure themselves, felt shame and remorse in their hearts and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

According to the *Nei Zhuan* (Inner Biography) concerning the circumstances of the two great venerable masters, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna, who subdued the Daoist practitioners of the Five Peaks:
on the first day of the first month of the fourteenth year of Yongping, the Daoist practitioners of the various mountains of the Five Peaks...
Following the sequence of the New Year’s audience, they addressed one another, saying: "The Son of Heaven has abandoned our Way and the Dharma to seek afar for barbarian teachings.
Now, taking advantage of this imperial assembly, we may present a memorial to oppose him. Their memorial read roughly as follows:

"Chen Xin and others, six hundred and ninety disciples of the Three Caverns (Sāndòng) of the Most High (Tàishàng) from the Five Peaks and eighteen mountains, submit this with the gravity of death. We, your servants, have heard that originally there is no [higher] above..."

Formless and nameless, it is the ultimate; the unsurpassed, void, and spontaneous Great Way. It emerged before the creation of the cosmos and was followed by the ancient sovereigns, whose primary rule remained unchanging.
Today, Your Majesty’s Way surpasses that of the Emperor of Righteousness (Yihuang), and your virtue exceeds that of Yao and Shun.

Yet I have heard, in private, that Your Majesty has abandoned the fundamental to pursue the peripheral, seeking instruction from the Western Regions. That which you serve is but a barbarian deity, and what is preached therein does not accord with [the Way].
"O Great China! We pray that Your Majesty will forgive the offenses of your servants and grant us permission for our trials.

Among us, the Daoist masters of the various mountains, many have listened to the teachings throughout the night and possess a broad mastery of the classics. Since the time of Emperor Yuan, there is nothing among the various records of the Most High, nor the talismans and incantations of the Great Void, that we have not thoroughly studied and mastered.
We have reached the furthest limits of these arts; some command ghosts and spirits, while others swallow the mists and drink the vital breath."
Entering fire, he is not burned; treading upon water, he does not drown; at times he ascends to heaven by day; at times he conceals his form beyond measure.

Regarding such arts and techniques, there is nothing he cannot do. I wish to have him compared with you, for this would serve four purposes: first, it would bring peace of mind to Your Majesty; second, it would allow for the discernment of truth from falsehood;
third, it would ensure that the Great Way has a clear destination; and fourth, it would prevent the confusion of the refined and the vulgar. If we were to compare them...
It is not so. We shall leave it to you to decide the matter definitively. Should you prove superior, we beg that our false claims be expunged.

By imperial decree, Song Xiang, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, was dispatched to escort [the Emperor] into the Changle Palace. On the fifteenth day of this month, the Daoist masters of Baima Monastery and others are to be assembled.
He then established three altars. On these altars were arranged twenty-four gates. There were the Daoist practitioners of Mount Nanyue, Chu Shanxin;
Mount Hua, Liu Zhengnian; Mount Heng, Zu Wendu; Mount Dai, Jiao Dexin; Mount Song, Lü Huītong;
and those from the eighteen mountains, including Mount Huo, Mount Tianmu, Mount Wutai, and Mount Bailu.
Qi Wénxìn and others each brought five hundred and nine scrolls, including the *Língbǎo Zhēnwén*, the *Tàishàng Yùjué*, and the *Sānyuán Fúlù*,
which they placed upon the western altar. They also placed two hundred and thirty-five scrolls of the various *Zǐshū* (Books of the Masters),
such as those by Dì Chéngzǐ, Xǔ Chéngzǐ, Huángzǐ, and Lǎozǐ, upon the central altar, where they prepared sacrificial food and made offerings to the hundred deities.
They were placed upon the eastern altar. The Emperor resided in the mobile palace at the south gate of the monastery. The Buddha’s relics, scriptures, and images were placed to the west of the path.

When the fifteen-day fast concluded, the Daoist masters took firewood and reeds, mixed them with agarwood and sandalwood, and fashioned them into torches. They circumambulated the scriptures and wept, saying:
"We, your subjects, hereby address the Great Ultimate, the Great Dao, the Primordial Celestial Honored One, the myriad immortals, and the hundred spirits: Now, this barbarian deity..."
In the chaotic summer, the sovereign believed in heterodoxy; the orthodox teaching vanished from sight and the profound influence of the Dharma fell into ruin.

Your servants dared to place the scriptures upon the sacrificial altar and employ fire as a test, desiring to enlighten the minds of the ignorant so that they might distinguish the true from the false. Thereupon, we set fire to the scriptures.
When the scriptures were cremated by fire, they were completely reduced to ashes. The Daoist practitioners looked at one another with pale faces, filled with great terror.
They intended to ascend to heaven and conceal their forms, but they lacked the power to do so. Those who practiced the prohibitions and invoked spirits called upon [Zhu Fa]ce, but he did not respond;
each felt deep shame and remorse. The Daoist Fei Shucaī of Mount Nanyue died of his own accord. The Grand Tutor Zhang Yan spoke thus to Chu Xin.
[Dao’an] said: "What you have tested has yielded no results; this is therefore false and delusory. You ought to follow the true Dharma that has come from the West. Chu Xin said:
"Mao Chengzi stated that the Supreme One (Taishang) is the Celestial Venerable of Numinous Treasure (Lingbao Tianshun).

The work of creation is called the Great Primal (Taisu); how could this be false? Daoyan said: "The Great Primal possesses the name 'Noble Virtue,' but it has no designation for verbal teaching. Now..."
If one says there is verbal teaching, that is immediately false. Faith is silent. At that time, the light of the Buddha’s relics was five-colored;
it rose straight into the air and circled like a canopy, covering the entire assembly and eclipsing the sunlight. Dharma Master Mātanga—
He leaped high into the air and sat or lay amidst the sky, extensively manifesting supernatural transformations. At that time, celestial jewel-flowers rained down upon the Buddha and the Sangha.
Furthermore, the sound of heavenly music was heard, moving the hearts of men; the great assembly was filled with joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

All circumambulated Dharmarāta to listen to his exposition of the essential Dharma, while simultaneously chanting the *Brahmā-śīrṣa* and praising the virtues of the Buddha, causing the entire multitude to join in extolling them as well.
The Three Jewels teach that all good and evil karmas have their respective retributions, and explain that the various characteristics of the three vehicles are not identical.
Furthermore, they state that the merit of leaving the household life is the highest; its blessings are equal in measure to those of the five original Buddhist temples.

Liu Jun, the Marquis of Yangcheng and Minister of Works, along with over a thousand officials, scholars, and commoners, left the household life at the monasteries of the Four Peaks and various mountains.

Six hundred and thirty individuals, including the scholar Lü Huītōng and others, entered the monastic order. Yin Fūrén, Wáng Jiéyǔ, and two hundred and thirty palace attendants also entered the monastic order.
Ten monasteries were subsequently established: seven were located outside the city to accommodate monks, and three were located inside the city to accommodate nuns.
There is a five-fascicle biography of these events, which has not been recorded here in full detail.
Regarding the account of National Teacher Nanyue’s conversion of the Daoist, the *Fozu tongji* states:
When the Great Master first resided at Mount Nanyue, there was a Daoist named Ouyang Zheng from Jiuxian Guan.
Then, observing that the mountain possessed an extraordinary aura, he consulted with the assembly, saying, "This aura belongs to the Dharma King in brown robes.
When his influence flourishes, our own Dharma will decline. He then pierced the heart of the mountain peak and drove in stone bolts as a fraudulent act of sorcery, burying weapons upon the mountain.
He then submitted a deceptive memorial, claiming that a northern monk had accepted a recruitment from the Qi state to perform this deed. Emperor Xuan dispatched an envoy to investigate; at first—
As they were crossing the Stone Bridge, two tigers roared; the messenger retreated in alarm. The following day he returned, and the Master said, "The donor should proceed ahead;
I shall follow shortly. Seven days passed, yet the messenger had still not arrived, so the Master finally traveled there by flying his mendicant's staff.
He was seen entering through all four gates of Jinling. When the messenger finally arrived, they proceeded together to have an audience with the Emperor, who was seated at ease.

The Emperor saw the Master descend from the air; his appearance was that of a Brahmā, extraordinary and beyond the ordinary. Startled and realizing he was a divine being, the Emperor asked nothing at all.

Instead, because the Daoist had falsely accused him of subverting the sovereign, he ordered the case to be investigated. The charge carried the penalty of execution by public beheading. The Master pleaded, saying, "It was not my intention to harm another's life.
I beg only to be released so I may return to the mountains and serve the monastic community; this would suffice as a small punishment. The Emperor granted his request.
The Emperor commanded the relevant authorities to mint fourteen coins and inscribe the names of fourteen Daoist masters around their circumference.

He sealed them with an imperial decree and ordered that they accompany the Master back to the mountain. As he was about to depart, the Emperor honored him with exceptional rites, bestowing upon him the title "Great Chan Master" (Tài Chánshī).
It was from this point that the fame of Sita (Tiantai) truly began. Initially, the Emperor had decreed that he reside at Qixuan Temple; he once visited Waguan Monastery and encountered...
The rain did not wet him; he walked through the mud without being soiled. When the monk Lihui Gao encountered him on the road, he sighed and said, "What a person of divine wonder!
How could such a one have come here? From that time on, the entire court, both monastics and laypeople, turned their hearts toward him in devotion and reverence. The Grand Commander Wu Mingche—

Whenever he attended the Master’s discourses on the Way, he wished to offer him a rhinoceros-horn pillow but did not dare speak of it. The Master said, "If you wish to give me a pillow, you may do so.
Mingche was greatly astonished by this. After the Master returned to the mountains, he continued to preach the Dharma as before.

When the assembly of practitioners informed him that he was old and ill, they requested to offer several *qǐng* of fields to provide for the incense and lamps, thereby redeeming their own aging bodies. The Master said, "If you wish to leave these fields behind, you may do so."
The place was named Liutiang (Retained Field) in accordance with your wish. The iron warrant that was granted to you has been fully preserved;
its events were engraved upon stone and titled "Record of the Iron Warrant Granted by the Emperor of the Chen Dynasty to the Great Meditation Master Sida of Nanyue for Subduing Daoist Practitioners."

The Peak of Huading, where the Great Master Zhiyi subdued the demons, is a separate peak to the north of the temple known as Huading. From its summit, one cannot see the surrounding mountain ranges; its climate is forever different from other places.
The Great Master left the assembly and went alone into the forest for dhūta practice. Suddenly, during the latter part of the night, a great wind uprooted trees and thunder shook the mountains.
Ten groups of malevolent spirits appeared in a hundred forms; some had dragons and snakes upon their heads, others spat sparks from their mouths.

Their shapes were like black clouds and their voices like crashing thunderbolts. They shifted and transformed in an instant beyond counting—just as they are depicted in paintings of the Subjugation of Māra.

These transformations were but slight; yet the signs of what is truly fearsome exceed even these. Nevertheless, one is able to settle the mind in profound stillness and emptiness, so that the circumstances of oppression naturally dissipate.
Furthermore, one may manifest in the forms of parents, teachers, or monks, sometimes resting upon them or embracing them, weeping with choked sobs.
Yet, by deeply contemplating the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and realizing that all things are fundamentally non-existent, the signs of sorrow and suffering vanish instantly.
It was extinguished once more. Neither strong nor weak conditions could move him. When the morning star appeared, a divine monk manifested and said:
"To overcome an adversary and conquer an enemy—this may be called valor. To be able to surmount such a hardship as this, none is like you.

Having offered these words of consolation, he further preached the Dharma for him. The words of his preaching can be grasped through the meaning; they cannot be fully recorded in writing. One must understand them from the context of the speech itself.
The meaning of each phrase was clearly understood. Like parting the clouds to drink from a spring, he realized that even water and the sun are inadequate metaphors for it.
He then asked, "Great Sage, what is this Dharma-gate? How should one study it? How should one propagate and proclaim it? He replied, "This is called the Single Truth of Reality (Ekayāna-satya).
Study it through Prajñā (wisdom); proclaim it through Mahākaruṇā (great compassion). From this day forward, whether for yourself or for others, all shall be my echoes and shadows."
Regarding the Master of Great Wisdom’s karmic conditions for subduing Māra at Mount Yuquan:
when the Master first arrived in Dangyang, he gazed toward the Ju and Zhang regions, where the mountain colors appeared as deep as indigo.

He wished to select a clear stream to establish as his place of practice, but finding it too cramped and confined, he proceeded northward about a hundred paces from Jinlong Pond. There, a large tree stood spreading its branches in a lush, drooping canopy.
He covered himself with a canopy, its interior as empty as a hut, and sat cross-legged there to enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*). One day, heaven and earth grew dark and murky;
wind and rain howled in fury, and strange monsters of diverse forms suddenly underwent a thousand transformations. A giant python over ten *zhang* long appeared, its mouth agape and turned inward.
Demonic spirits arrayed themselves in ranks, raining down cannonballs and arrows like a torrential downpour. For seven days, the Master showed no sign of fear. Out of compassion for them, he...
He said to them, "What you have done are the various karmas of birth and death; you cling to mere worldly blessings and do not feel sorrow or repentance.
As he finished speaking, the host of demons vanished. That evening, the clouds parted and the moon shone bright. Two men appeared, their majestic bearing like that of kings:
the elder had a fine beard and was robust, while the younger wore a cap and was strikingly handsome. They came forward and paid their respects, saying, "I am Guan Yu of Han..."

The realm fell into chaos; the Nine Provinces were split like melon seeds. Cao Cao was unkind, and Sun Quan sought only self-preservation. I, a righteous minister of Shu-Han, vowed to restore the imperial house.
However, the times were adverse and my ambitions were not fulfilled. My death leaves behind a legacy of enduring brilliance; therefore, I am buried here on this mountain.

"Virtuous and Holy Master, why have you deigned to employ your supernatural powers [to come here]? The Master said, "I wish to establish a site for the Way (bodhimaṇḍa) in this place to repay the virtue of my physical birth.
The spirit said, "I pray that you will take pity on my ignorance and graciously accept me. One *śā* from here,"

The mountain was shaped like an overturned boat, and its soil was deep and thick. The disciples said, "We shall build a temple with you, Master, to provide for the offerings and sustain the Buddha-dharma.
We pray that you will remain in meditative absorption for seven days to await its completion.

Once the Master emerged from his concentration, he saw that the thousand-fathom deep pool had transformed into level ground, and the buildings were magnificent and radiant, their exquisite craftsmanship surpassing the eye of man. It was as if wrought by divine power and ghostly labor, accomplished with such speed.

The Master led the assembly to take up residence there and expounded the Dharma day and night. One day, the spirit said to the Master, "Today, as a disciple, I have been fortunate enough to hear the world-transcending Dharma.
I pray that you will cleanse my heart and transform my thoughts, allowing me to receive the precepts so that they may forever serve as the foundation for Bodhi.
The Master immediately took up the incense burner and conferred the Five Precepts upon him. Thereupon, the spirit’s majestic virtue shone forth across a thousand li. Far and wide...
Everyone looked on with solemn reverence as he prayed.
A guest said, "If it is truly as the Master has cited, then [how do you account for] the battle between the Confucian Yellow Emperor and Chiyou, or the expulsion of Jie by Tang the Successful?"
When Yi Yin exiled Tai Jia; when the Great Yu executed the Lord of Fangfeng; when King Wu campaigned against Zhou;
and when Confucius put Shao Zheng Mao to death—could these alone not be called the Dharma-gate of the inherent evil of human nature? I replied:

"To commit rebellion against obedience and to use depravity to interfere with rectitude is called 'cultivated evil. To execute the rebellious through obedience and to eliminate the depraved through rectitude is called 'cultivated [good].'"
Excellent. Now, as for Chiyou, Jie, Taijia, Zhou, the Lord of Fangfeng, and Shaopengmao:
in their present lives, they created the causes for the three miserable realms, thereby receiving the "glorious" retributions of being punished, exiled, executed, or put to death.

In the future, they will surely fall into the three miserable realms to receive the karmic fruits of being crushed, burned, pounded, and ground—all of which are the results of cultivating evil. Yet the Sage, by means of the Way of Great Publicity and Ultimate Rectitude...
To subdue them, release them, execute them, attack them, or punish them—all these are practices for cultivating virtue within the Way of human relations.
As for the emperors of successive dynasties, some used royal armies to crush rebels, while others slew a single man to stabilize the realm.
Whether one slays tens of millions of people to bring peace to the common folk, it is all for the cultivation of goodness.

If, however, there were even a hair’s breadth of private intent within such acts, thereby obstructing the Way of Heaven, then whether one fortunately possesses the empire or unfortunately loses it, [the fault remains].

All are practices of evil. Should the Way of the King and the Way of the Hegemon be practiced concurrently, and benevolence, righteousness, deceit, and force be employed in a mixed fashion, then good and evil will become confused, and the heterodox and the orthodox will be muddled.

As for the Dharma-gate of the inherent evil of nature (*xing-è*), it is like a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*) who can destroy all enemies, yet there is nothing that is actually destroyed. Therefore, all things are as such.
Although he manifests killing, in reality he has never killed anyone;
rather, it is through the power of the roots of goodness cultivated over immeasurable kalpas that he causes all sentient beings to see such events and thereby obtain various benefits.
Furthermore, this principle was something the Tathāgata had never previously expounded in past ages, but at this present time—
That which Tiantai has never before propagated—how could the Confucian sages of this land be sufficient to know it?
Much less could they practice it by fully realizing their inherent nature.
*Treatise on the Good and Evil of Human Nature*, Volume Four.
*Treatise on the Innate Goodness and Evil*, Fascicle Five.
Written by the Śramaṇa Chuandeng of Youxi on Mount Tiantai.

A guest says: "I have already heard the teaching that at the stage of fruition, when perfect realization is attained, there is nothing whatsoever that is altered. Why, then, is it called 'following purity'?"

"Complete cultivation and total cultivation reside within the gate of nature. I said: "In the previous section explaining the gate of the ten realms' distinctions as True Suchness responding to conditions, two meanings were generally distinguished:
first, responding to pure conditions; second, responding to defiled conditions. Master Ciyun’s *Tushuo* (Illustrated Exposition) treated these meanings somewhat briefly.
Now, wishing to explain these meanings extensively, I shall once again bring forth the point that the causal mind is inherently complete and lacks nothing whatsoever."

To clarify this: the term "perfect cultivation" (*yuánxiū*) is used in contrast to the cultivation of the nine realms that follow defilement, for the latter cannot be called cultivation that accords with the nature (*chēngxìng*).
Furthermore, one should know that the cultivation of the nine realms is likewise nothing other than the arising of cultivation from the entirety of the nature;

they are each perfectly interfused (*yuánróng*), differing only in that one is deluded and the other is enlightened. Therefore, they are designated as "perfect" or "not perfect. Thus, the Venerable Ziming [Zhiyi] in the *Miaozong* [Chanyuanji] says:

The Commentary explains that the mind is divided into the defiled and the pure, while conduct is opened into the wholesome and the unwholesome. It states: "Mind" refers to the two minds of delusion and enlightenment; "conduct" refers to the two types of conduct, contrary and compliant.
Within the six realms and the three teachings, one is deluded regarding the nature of the three virtues and is stained by the three delusions; therefore, it is called the "defiled mind.

All bodily and vocal karmas that exist in violation of principle and are performed [with such intent] are termed "unwholesome conduct. Only the Perfect and Sudden Teaching realizes the nature of the three virtues and is free from...

Only when the three delusions are purified can it be called a "pure mind. When the various actions of body and speech accord with principle and are without deliberate effort (*anabhisamskāra*), they are termed "wholesome conduct.

Thus we know that the partiality or completeness of cultivation, and the opposition or conformity of practice, are entirely distinguished based on whether one’s understanding is superficial or profound.

This is because within the nine realms of phenomena, the Dharma-realm of sentient beings arises from the full manifestation of inherent evil through cultivated evil; whereas within the Dharma-realm of the Buddha, there is the full manifestation of inherent goodness.
One cultivates goodness by means of its arising. Since it arises fully from the nature, what single dharma is not itself the Buddha-dharma?
It is like seeing water through the waves, or seeing space through the vessel; even so, one sees the warm spring through the myriad phenomena.

Therefore, among the various Mahāyāna sūtras of the Perfect and Sudden teaching, there are few that observe the inherent goodness of the nature by means of cultivated goodness, while those that observe the inherent evil of the nature by means of cultivated evil are many.
This is frequent [in the scriptures]. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa; afflictions are themselves bodhi.

Birth-and-death and afflictions are the evil of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), whereas bodhi and nirvāṇa are the evil of nature (*prakṛti*). Although the good and evil of cultivation are distinguished, there is no distinction between the good and evil of nature.
This is what the teaching refers to as the "interfusion of the evil of nature," wherein there is no dharma that does not partake in it, spontaneously encompassing and attaining the Buddha-realm.
This is what is meant by "inherent goodness. Furthermore, it is said: "Lust, anger, and delusion are themselves liberation. It is also said: "The sixty-two views are the seeds of the Tathāgata.
It is further said: "The six sense faculties are all the Pure Land. And it is said: "There is no liberation to be taught apart from words and letters.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Lust is itself the Way; so too is anger. Within these three dharmas..."

Possessing all Buddha-dharmas, there is nothing that does not cause the practitioner to reach the point where no shifting or turning is required. One realizes that practicing evil is precisely the realization of the inherent nature of evil.
Furthermore, the teachings of the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* (*Léngyán jīng*) are supremely perfect and sudden;

their methods of cultivation likewise lead one to realize the inherent nature of evil through the very practice of evil. Although this is not explicitly stated in the texts, their essential meaning is in complete accord. Now, regarding the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*:
I have merely set forth the essential outline; however, in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he extensively cites scriptural evidence to elucidate it.

In the Mañjuśrī Chapter of the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*, it clarifies the Tathāgata’s original ground for practice, stating: "Only by permanently severing ignorance does one attain the Buddha-way.
What is this ignorance? It is that all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have undergone various inversions and have falsely identified the four great elements as a self.

Characteristics. The shadows conditioned by the six sense-objects are the characteristics of one's own mind. Thereafter, one uses *śamatha* to examine the body and returns it to the four great elements, realizing that the body has no characteristic of a body.
One examines the mind and returns it to the shadows conditioned by the six sense-objects, understanding that the mind has no characteristic of a mind.

Even to the point of [knowing] that these are like empty flowers, there is no cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). The ignorance of body and mind is the illusory cultivation of evil; one must penetrate this.

It is fundamentally empty. To contemplate and cultivate evil is precisely the cultivation of the nature of evil. Therefore it is said: "To know illusion is to be detached from it; no expedient means need be employed. To be detached from illusion is awakening;

this is likewise not a gradual process. As for the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, where the twenty-five sages each set forth their methods of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), there is not one that does not involve the full cultivation of evil.
This is because the nature of evil encompasses the six sense organs, the six sense objects, the six consciousnesses, and the seven elements—all of which are the six [realms].
The Way takes the cultivation of evil extremes as its object; it is that which is contemplated by the Three Vehicles and the partial teachings.
In some cases, one takes the cultivated evil itself and, by partially entering the "evil" of the *tathāgatagarbha* of emptiness, brings it into harmony with the "good" of nature.

In other cases, one takes the cultivated evil itself and, by partially entering the "evil" of the *tathāgatagarbha* of non-emptiness, brings it into harmony with the "good" of nature. Or, one enters entirely into the three kinds of [tathāgatagarbha].
The *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) is precisely the cultivation of the evil nature of phenomena (*dharmas*) in order to harmonize with the good nature of the essence (*dharmatā*).

As for those who have partially entered [the stage], it is impossible to cite them all in detail. Here, I shall elucidate this by taking the seven great Bodhisattvas, such as Ucchuṣma, who have fully entered, so that those engaged in the Perfect and Sudden Teaching may have a clear path to follow.
First, clarifying that the cultivation based on the fire element—whether partial or complete—is inherent in its nature:
the Sūtra states, "Ucchuṣma, before the Tathāgata, joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'I constantly recall that in the distant past, during many kalpas, my nature was characterized by much greed. At that time, a Buddha appeared in the world named..."

"O King of Emptiness, you have taught that those who indulge excessively in lust become a mass of fierce fire. You instructed me to contemplate the hundred-fold limbs and all the cold and warm vital energies throughout my body.
As the divine light coalesced within, it transformed my lustful mind into the fire of wisdom.
From this point on, all Buddhas have called me by the name 'Fire-Head. By the power of the Samādhi of Fire-Light, I have attained Arhatship. Thus he spoke from his heart.
Great Vow: When all Buddhas attained the Way, I served as a powerful warrior and personally subdued the demonic adversaries. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied:

"By clearly observing that the sensations of warmth within my body and mind flowed unimpeded through my channels, all outflows were extinguished and a great jewel-flame arose, whereby I realized supreme enlightenment.
This is the foremost method."
The commentary states: A nature characterized by excessive desire is the lowest among the nine realms of cultivated evil and is the cause for rebirth in hell.
When the Tathāgata, the King of Emptiness, says that those with much lust become a mass of fierce flames, he is indicating their "flower-retribution" (the immediate manifestation).

This includes ailments such as futile exhaustion, phlegm-fever, and wasting diseases; as for the "fruit-retribution," there is the suffering of being scorched by fierce flames throughout kalpas in hell.

When I was instructed to observe everywhere the hundred startling sensations and the various cold and warm energies throughout my four limbs, it meant that by correctly observing the fire of cultivated evil, one takes the fire of cultivated evil as the fire of the original nature.

When the divine light is internally obstructed and transforms a mind of much lust into the fire of wisdom, this occurs because after long observation, the fire of cultivated evil is transformed into the fire of the original nature;
when the original nature and evil are interfused, there is no dharma that is not [transformed].
Gati. This refers to the spontaneous attainment of the virtuous nature of the Buddha-realm (*buddhadhātu*). From this point on, all Buddhas have called me by the name Agnīśikha.
Through the *Agniprabhā-samādhi*, I attained the state of an Arhat. I made a great vow:

"When the Buddhas attain the Way, may I serve as a powerful attendant to personally subdue their demonic adversaries. It was precisely because I cultivated great evil through fire that I attained awakening; it was by means of the fire-light...
Performing Buddha-work through samādhi and practicing the bodhisattva path is the dharma-gate of the nature of evil.

This is because, from time immemorial, within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of fire is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true fire; it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
The three virtues manifest as the three paths of karma, afflictions, and suffering. Since these three paths are themselves the three causes, therefore now—

One may observe that the fire of cultivated evil is precisely the fire of inherent evil. Therefore it is said: "Instruct me to observe throughout my hundred skeletal members, my four limbs, and all sensations of cold and warmth.
When the spiritual light coalesces within, it transforms a mind of excessive lust into the fire of wisdom.

This is what is meant by 'remaining unchanging amidst conditions'—to be differentiated yet without differentiation. Indeed, when one contemplates the warm touch of body and mind, it flows through without obstruction.
To abide in the realization of reality is to cease [delusion]. To universally observe the hundredfold terrors of the four limbs is to cease through skillful means in accordance with conditions.
To transform a mind of excessive lust into the fire of wisdom is to cease by ending the dualistic discrimination of the two extremes.

When the realization of reality is perfected, the virtue of pure *prajñā* is restored; when skillful means are perfected, the virtue of primordial liberation is realized. Thus, the cessation of the two extremes is accomplished.
Since the virtues of the Dharma-body are perfect, is it not because the cultivation toward perfection follows purity, such that the entire cultivation resides within the nature?
Second, to clarify how the cultivation toward perfection follows purity and the entire cultivation resides within the nature based on the element of earth, the Sūtra says:
Bodhisattva Earth-Holder immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying, "I recall..."
In the past, when the Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa appeared in the world, I was a bhikṣu.
I constantly repaired all major roads, ferry crossings, fields, and narrow passes that were improper or obstructed the passage of carts and horses;
I leveled them all, or built bridges, or carried sand and earth. Through such diligent toil, immeasurable Buddhas appeared in the world, yet there were some...
When sentient beings in the marketplace required someone to carry their goods, I would first carry them for them;
