having reached their destination, I would set down the goods and depart without taking any payment. During the time when Vipaśyin Buddha was present in the world, there was widespread famine;
I served as a porter, accepting only one coin regardless of whether the distance was far or near. Or, if there were carts or horses stuck in the mud, I [would rescue them].
By his supernatural power, he pushed the wheel for him and extracted his suffering and affliction. At that time, the Great King of the country invited the Buddha to provide a vegetarian feast.
I, at that moment, leveled the ground to await the Buddha. Vipaśyin Tathāgata touched my head and said to me: "You should level the mind-ground; then the ground of the world will all become level.
My mind was immediately opened, and I saw that the minute particles of my own body and all that constitutes the created world [are one].
"Fine dust particles are equal and without distinction; the self-nature of fine dust particles does not touch one another, and even weapons do not come into contact with them.

Regarding this nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), I realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and became an Arhat. Having turned my mind back, I now enter the stage of a Bodhisattva.
Hearing the Tathāgatas proclaim the ground of the Buddhas' wondrous Lotus wisdom and vision, I was formerly their witness and served as..."
"O World-Honored One, when asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I observed with clarity that the two objects—the body and the realm—are equal and without distinction;

they are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha. These objects arise through false delusion. When the objects are dissolved, wisdom becomes perfect, and one achieves the Unsurpassed Way. This is the foremost."
The commentary states: "As for my waiting for the Buddha upon level ground at that time," this Bodhisattva took leveling the ground as the condition for attaining awakening.
"When one levels the mind-ground, then all the grounds of the world become level. Now, leveling the ground refers to the body; leveling the mind-ground refers to wisdom.
The ground is the illusory form that follows conditions (*pratyaya*), while the mind is the form of the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*); it is the following along with true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

As for conditions: when the ground is level, one passes through a thousand differences with a single thought without changing; when the mind is level, one brings a thousand differences back to the single nature.
When passing through a thousand differences, ten thousand thoughts race about in confusion; thus they become afflictions and birth-and-death.
When returning to the single nature, there is the One Path, and all is serene; thus it becomes Bodhi and Nirvana. Therefore, when the great earth is leveled, the mind...
The earth, conversely, results in inequality. This is what is meant by "no difference, yet there is difference.
When the mind-ground is leveled, then the entire world-ground becomes level. This is what is meant by "difference, yet no difference. Thus, before long after observing this, my mind was opened;
I saw that the subtle particles of my own body and all the subtle particles that constitute the world are equal and without distinction. This...
Thus, it is not only that the entire world created is entirely level; even the earth—the basis for both the primary and secondary retributions—is equal and without distinction, being entirely level.

If it were not for the fact that the nature of the evil nature is entirely such that its "nature-form" (xing-se) remains unchanging yet follows conditions to manifest as differentiated, thereby constituting the form of the basis and the primary retribution of the nine realms, how could the body and the sensory dusts be equal and without distinction in their reliance upon form?
There is differentiation, yet they do not touch one another; even weapons do not come into contact with them. Following conditions without changing or differing—how truly non-different!

It is precisely because one can realize that the form of cultivated evil is itself the form of inherent evil, and that through the interpenetration of inherent evil, there is no phenomenon that does not enter [the realm of reality], that one spontaneously attains the inherent goodness of the Buddha-realm.
Thus, as defilements dissolve and wisdom becomes perfect, one achieves the state of *amala* (stainless).

This is the superior path. To speak in terms of the three types of cessation: it refers to the state where appearances exist within the realm of sensory dusts, like the resonance of a bell within a vessel that issues forth externally.
With the *dhyāna*-body as its sovereign, it is that which simultaneously negates and illuminates, contemplating the three truths together.
Third, clarifying that the cultivation based on the water element—whether partial or complete—is inherent in its nature:
the Sūtra says, "The youth Candraprabha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'I recall that in the past, as many kalpas ago as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Jaladeva. He taught all the bodhisattvas to practice...'"
The contemplation of water. Entering samādhi, he contemplates that the watery nature within the body cannot be displaced.

Beginning with mucus and saliva, he thus exhaustively examines the lymph, essence, blood, and the large and small excretions; as they circulate and return within the body, the watery nature is identical throughout.
Seeing the water within his own body, he perceives it to be no different from the various fragrant oceans of the Floating Banner King Buddha-land outside the world. Thus I...
At that time, when he first accomplished this contemplation, he saw only the water and had not yet attained the state of bodilessness.
While he was practicing dhyāna in his room as a bhikṣu, a disciple of mine peered through the window to observe the room; he saw nothing at all except clear water filling the entire space.
Being young and ignorant, the boy picked up a piece of tile or gravel and threw it into the water, causing the water to splash and make a sound. He then looked around in surprise.
He departed. After I emerged from samādhi, I suddenly felt pain in my heart, as if Śāriputra had encountered the "Harmful Ghost.
I reflected to myself: "I have now attained the path of Arhatship; I have long since been free from the conditions of illness.
Why has this heart-pain suddenly arisen today? Could it be that I am falling away? At that moment, the youth came quickly before me and related the aforementioned events. I then...
He said, "If you see water again, you may open the door and enter this water to remove the tiles and debris. The youth followed these instructions.
Later, when he entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he saw the water once more, with the tiles and debris still clearly present. He opened the door and removed them.

When I later emerged from concentration, my physical body was as it had been before. In this manner, he encountered immeasurable Buddhas, continuing thus until he reached the Buddha King of Sovereign Power over Mountains and Seas.

"O Tathāgata, it is only now that I have realized that my own body and all the fragrant water-oceans throughout the worlds of the ten directions are of a single nature with true emptiness, being neither two nor distinct.
Now, from the Tathāgata, I have received the name 'Childlike Purity' and am admitted into the assembly of Bodhisattvas. When the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration of the Way, I say:
through the single flavor of the flowing nature of water, I have attained the patience of non-arising and perfected Bodhi; this is the foremost."
The commentary states: "To contemplate that the water-element within the body cannot be displaced" means to realize that the water of evil nature is the gateway of non-duality (*advaya-dvāra*).
Beginning with mucus and saliva, and extending thus to the end of all secretions, essences, blood, excrement, and urine, these circulate and revolve within the body;

the water-element is identical throughout. Contemplating this water of the primary retribution (*vipāka*), one realizes that cultivated evil is itself innate evil. Thus, one perceives the water within the body.
"Being non-different from the fragrant water seas of the Floating Banner King lands outside the world" means that one has attained a semblance realization of the water of the dependent retribution;
this is the inherent evil of cultivation (the evil of nature). Because one has not yet emerged from the stage of segmented existence (*pariccheda*), one cannot yet transcend the body.

It is only upon reaching the Tathāgata of Sovereign Penetration over Mountains and Seas that one can transcend the body; it is only upon reaching the stage of partial truth and the transformation of rebirth (*parivṛtti*) that one truly attains it.
It is of one essence with the waters of the fragrant oceans throughout the worlds of the ten directions, being non-dual and indistinguishable from true emptiness.
Is this not a profound realization that the nature of water is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true water—pure and fundamental by nature, pervading the entire Dharma-realm?

Indeed, within the single suchness of the Tathāgata-garbha, True Suchness is unchanging; the nature of water is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true water, pure and fundamental by nature.
Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, it accords with the minds of sentient beings and manifests according to the measure of their cognitive capacity, appearing in accordance with their karma.

Though undifferentiated, it appears as differentiated, serving as the water for the two retributions—the environment and the inhabitants—of the nine realms of existence. If it were not the case that it remains unchanging while following conditions, how could the nature of these two waters—the environment and the inhabitants—remain inseparable?
Having contemplated this for a long time, one can cause the nature [of the mind] to merge with true emptiness, such that there is neither duality nor distinction.

This is to initiate cultivation from within the perfection of nature, employing the Middle Way *dhyāna*. Just as when a gong within a vessel produces a sound that resonates outward, this serves as the primary principle.
Thus, one attains the uniform flow of the essence of water and achieves the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Fourth, clarifying that the cultivation based on the wind-element, following the pure and perfect [nature], consists of the complete cultivation existing within the nature:
the Sūtra says: "The Dharma Prince Vaidūryaprabha immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:"
I recall that in the past, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Immeasurable Sound (*Anantaghoṣa*).

He revealed the wondrous clarity of the Bodhisattva’s fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), observing that this world and the bodies of sentient beings are all driven by the power of the winds of delusive conditions.

At that time, I contemplated the establishment of the realms, contemplated the movement of the world, contemplated the movement and stillness of the body, and contemplated the movement and thoughts of the mind.
All movements were non-dual and equally without distinction. At that time, I clearly realized the nature of these manifold movements: they come from nowhere.
There is nowhere to which one goes. The sentient beings throughout the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, are all equally illusory.

Thus it is even within a single trichiliocosm: all the sentient beings therein are like the mosquitoes and gnats within a single vessel, chirping and clamoring in confusion, creating a frantic noise within a mere fraction of space.
Having encountered the Buddha for but a short time, they attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that moment, my mind was opened, and I beheld the land of the Buddha Akṣobhya in the eastern direction. I became a Dharma Prince, serving the Buddhas of the ten directions;

my body and mind emitted light, penetrating all things without obstruction. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied: "By observing that the power of wind has no dependence, I have attained this state."
Awakening to the bodhicitta and entering samādhi, one unites with the Buddhas of the ten directions and transmits this single wondrous mind; this is the foremost [method].
The commentary states: Tathāgata Immeasurable Sound revealed the wondrous luminosity of the Bodhisattva’s fundamental awakening (mūla-awakening).

One should contemplate it from the perspective of the unmoving nature of fundamental awakening. Now, however, we observe that this world and the bodies of sentient beings are all merely false conditions.
That which is turned by the power of wind is precisely the wind of cultivated evil. Observe how this power of wind, following conditions, appears to differ yet remains without difference.
Now, within the single *tathāgatagarbha*, true suchness is unchanging; the nature of wind is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true wind.
Pure and fundamental from the beginning, it pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*. While its essence is without differentiation, it follows the minds of sentient beings across the nine realms.

According to the measure of what is known, it manifests as the wind that serves as the environmental retribution (*pariṇāma-vipāka*) of the world, and as the wind that constitutes the individual retribution (*vipāka-phala*) of sentient beings, appearing in various distinctions.
Nevertheless, there is nothing that does not arise from cultivation through the totality of the nature, nor anything that exists within the nature apart from cultivation.

Therefore, one may observe the undifferentiated through the differentiated. Thus it is said: "At that time, I observed the establishment of the elements, observed the movement of the world, observed the movement and stillness of the body, and observed the movement and thoughts of the mind; all movements were non-dual and equal, without distinction. This is indeed the realization of the non-differentiation of the nature of wind. Regarding the statement that "wind is fundamentally pure and pervades the entire dharma-realm," it says:

"At that time, I realized that this nature of collective movement comes from nowhere and goes nowhere... (and so forth). Not only did I perceive that wind and emptiness are of one nature, but I also understood that movement is itself non-movement.
This is because by means of the unmoving, one awaits the moving; one realizes that within movement there exists that which is unmoving.
This still involves dependence on something external. When one moves with the realization that coming has no origin and going reaches no destination, one is indeed without dependence.

Thus, not long after meeting the Buddha, he attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). At that moment his mind opened, and he beheld the Land of Akṣobhya Buddha in the East, becoming a Dharma Prince.
This was because movement and stillness were understood to be entirely without opposition; it was through total cultivation that this was realized.
Regarding "nature":
the fifth section clarifies that based on the great element of space (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*), through the cultivation of purity and perfection, the entirety of cultivation resides within nature.
As the sutra says: The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I..."
Together with the Tathāgata, he attained the Boundless Body from Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
At that time, he held four great precious jewels in his hands, which illuminated the Buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, transforming them into empty space.

Furthermore, within his own mind, he manifested a great round mirror, from which ten kinds of subtle and wondrous jewel-light radiated forth, flowing and filling all the realms of the Sovereign Banners at the very limits of empty space throughout the ten directions. They came...
Entering within the mirror, it penetrates my body; the body is identical to empty space, with no mutual obstruction.
The body is able to skillfully enter lands as small as motes of dust, extensively performing Buddha-works, and attaining great accordance.

This great supernormal power arises because I have contemplated that the four elements have no basis, that false thoughts arise and perish, that empty space is non-dual, and that Buddha-lands are fundamentally the same. By illuminating this sameness, I have attained...
"Regarding the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), when the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I attained samādhi by contemplating that space is boundless;
its wondrous power is perfectly luminous, and this is the foremost."
The commentary states: This boundless body attained by the Bodhisattva is the contemplative cultivation of the dark and obscured emptiness as the true emptiness of inherent evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*).
This emptiness of inherent evil and the emptiness of inherent goodness are non-dual within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Because the Dharma-realm is boundless, the body is likewise boundless. Furthermore, it is not only this: that very emptiness of inherent evil is itself the form (*rūpa*) of inherent evil.
The three elements of fire, wind, and water are likewise thus. When the Bodhisattva realizes this wondrous emptiness, he is immediately endowed with its sublime functions.
At that time, he holds four great precious jewels in his hands, which illuminate the Buddha-fields as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, transforming them into empty space.

This is to demonstrate it: this not only clearly reveals the realization of the boundlessness of empty space, but also the realization of the boundlessness of the nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

It is not only that one enters the gate of the evil dharmas regarding the nature of the element of space, but also that one enters equally into the gate of the evil dharmas regarding the nature of the four great elements.
It is not only that one realizes the boundlessness of the five great elements, but also that one realizes the five aggregates (*skandha*) within the ten dharma realms.
This is the reality-dharma (*dharmatā*). Because the lands of the supported realm are boundless, one further manifests a great round mirror within one's own mind.
From within it, ten kinds of subtle and wondrous jewel-lights are emitted, flowing and filling all the banner-king lands throughout the reaches of space in the ten directions.
These lights enter back into the mirror and penetrate my body; my body becomes identical to space, without mutual obstruction, skillfully able to cause the body to enter the subtle.
Throughout the lands of the dust motes, they extensively perform Buddha-activities and attain great accordance.

Is this not so because the realms of mind are interfused, the dependent and the primary are non-dual, the one and the many are unimpeded, the small and the large are mutually inclusive, and wondrous function manifests before us, all while the essential nature remains undivided?

Originally, from within the true awakening of the unchanging nature of True Suchness (tathatā) and emptiness, following the mind and conforming to karma, it manifests according to the measure of what is known as the "obscured emptiness" and the "emptiness of the four great elements. Thus, though there is no difference, a difference arises.

The emptiness now realized, however, follows the pure and perfect cultivation wherein the entire cultivation is contained within the nature; thus, while appearing as differentiation, there is no differentiation. Therefore, it is said: "This Great Spirit..."

Power. Through my earnest contemplation that the four great elements have no basis, that deluded thoughts arise and perish, that empty space is non-dual, and that Buddha-lands are fundamentally identical, I have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas by realizing this identity.
Sixth, clarifying that the great element of consciousness, depending on purity and perfection, is fully cultivated and resides within its own nature:
the Sūtra says, "Maitreya Bodhisattva immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'I recall that in the past, after the passing of atoms of kalpas, a Buddha appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa. From that Buddha, I..."
I left the household life, yet my mind remained heavy with worldly fame, and I delighted in visiting noble families.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught me to practice the samādhi of the consciousness-only mind and enter into *samādhi*. Throughout kalpas since then, by means of this samādhi, I have served Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
my pursuit of worldly fame has ceased and vanished. When Dīpaṃkara Buddha appeared in the world, I then attained the realization of non-arising.
The supreme, wondrous, and perfect samādhi of the mind-consciousness extends throughout all the lands of the Tathāgatas as far as the limits of space;

whether pure or defiled, existent or non-existent, all are manifestations produced by the transformations of my own mind. World-Honored One, because I have realized that all is but the mind-consciousness, the nature of consciousness has flowed forth as immeasurable Tathāgatas.
I have now received the prediction that I shall succeed the Buddha in his place. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration [of the senses], I replied with this truth.
Contemplating the ten directions as mere consciousness, the conscious mind becomes perfectly luminous and enters the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Remaining far removed from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); this is the foremost.

The commentary states: The preceding sutra clarifies that the fundamental *tathāgatagarbha* is "inherently conscious and luminously knowing; its awakened luminosity is the true consciousness; its wondrous virtue is brilliantly pure, pervading and encompassing the dharma-realm.
This refers to the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) in its unchanging state. "According to the minds of sentient beings, responding to the measure of what they know;
following karma, it manifests"—this means that according to the pure mind and wholesome karma, it becomes the ninth consciousness, the *amala-vijñāna*, which is white and pure.
This consciousness, following the defiled mind and its evil karma, becomes the eight consciousnesses of Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles;

it becomes the eighth, seventh, or sixth consciousnesses of ordinary beings in the six realms. This is what is meant by "the unchanging following conditions," where there is no differentiation yet there is differentiation.
This is precisely what this scripture refers to when it says: "The mind values worldly fame and delights in wandering among the noble families. At that time, the World-Honored One instructed me.

One cultivates the samādhi of mind-only consciousness and enters into samādhi; thus, one takes the three impure consciousnesses as the object of cultivation to contemplate the true suchness (tathatā) of their intrinsically evil nature.
By seeking to extinguish the worldly mind of seeking fame until it no longer exists, one destroys the pervasive conceptual grasping of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
Eventually, one achieves the unsurpassed, wondrously perfect samādhi of the consciousness-mind, thereby destroying the eighth consciousness.

One attains the realization of the ninth consciousness, the true, eternal, and pure consciousness. This is none other than awakening to the fact that True Suchness (Tathatā) is unchanging; though it is without differentiation, it appears as differentiated.

Therefore, one may take these very differences and return to their state of non-differentiation. Since at that time one takes the entirety of the nature (xing) as cultivation (xiu), one can likewise take the entirety of cultivation as being within the nature.
To be able to thoroughly comprehend this is what is meant by relying on the Great Consciousness (shidak) for the practice of following purity and perfection.
"Complete cultivation resides within the nature.
The seventh section clarifies that "complete cultivation resides within the nature" based on the great faculties and following the pure, perfect cultivation.
The Sūtra says: Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Prince of the Dharma, together with fifty-two bodhisattvas of his same rank, immediately rose from their seats...

He rose, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “I recall that in the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there appeared a Buddha named Immeasurable Light (*Amitābha*).
Twelve Tathāgatas succeeded one another throughout that single kalpa, the last of whom was named Surpassing the Sun and Moon (*Sūryacandraprabhābhibhū*).
That Buddha taught me the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha (*Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*). It is like a person who, with single-minded focus, thinks of another person.”
[The first] is single-mindedly forgetful. Thus, whether these two people meet or not, or see one another or not, they remember each other;
their mutual remembrance is deep. In this way, from birth to birth, they are like a form and its shadow, never diverging or differing.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions pity and cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. If the child has run away, what can the mother’s remembrance do? If the child...
It is like the way a mother remembers her child; throughout successive lives, mother and child do not remain far apart.

If sentient beings, in their hearts, remember the Buddha and contemplate the Buddha, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future. They will not be far from the Buddha; without relying on expedient means, they will spontaneously attain the opening of the mind.
It is like a person who has been perfumed with incense, whose body retains the fragrance. This is what is called "Adornment of Fragrant Light. I, in my original...

In my past life, by means of the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, I entered the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Now, in this world, I gather those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha and lead them back to the Pure Land.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties, I have no preference; I simply gather all six sense organs and maintain a continuous flow of pure mindfulness, thereby attaining *samādhi*.
This is the foremost method.

The commentary states: Although the preceding sutra clarifies the faculties (*indriya*) and the great elements (*mahābhūta*), its underlying meaning explains them by taking the "greatness of seeing" as the model for the five faculties.
It fully employs all six faculties to elucidate the principle that "the unchanging follows conditions, and following conditions is the unchanging. Thus it says:

"Just as the single faculty of seeing pervades the Dharma-realm, so too do hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, the sensation of touch, and cognitive awareness—wondrous virtue is brilliantly pure, universally pervading the Dharma-realm."
The realms fill the ten voids; how could they have a specific location? For now, let us speak of the faculty of sight alone.
There is true seeing, there is the essence of seeing, and there is deluded seeing. True seeing is the nature of the unchanging *tathatā*.

It is what is called "the wondrous clarity of original awakening" and "the luminous wonder of fundamental awakening. The essence of seeing is the initial stage of responding to conditions; it is that body which, in a sudden flash, becomes obscured and darkened.

This is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). It is the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) within the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-ghana*). This is what is meant by "delusively taking [the light] as luminous awareness.

Delusive seeing is precisely the discrimination of sense-objects. This is what is meant by "relying on luminosity to establish the objective. Once the objective has been delusively established, your delusive subjectivity arises.

Within that which is devoid of identity or difference, a blazing diversity is produced; it is that which, being inherently without distinction, creates distinctions. This corresponds to the first fascicle.
The fundamental, pure essence of Bodhi and Nirvana is precisely this essential clarity of your present consciousness, which is capable of giving rise to all conditions.
That which is lost amidst these conditions is identical [to the original essence]; it differs only in that there was no beginning [to its delusion] compared to today.

If you wish to point directly to the human mind and see your nature to achieve Buddhahood, you must do so right here. Understand that while you follow defiled conditions to cultivate evil, the source remains fundamentally without distinction.
To eliminate this discrepancy, one may immediately take the present differentiation and, by means of the non-differentiated essence, realize that the cultivation of evil is itself the nature of evil.
This "seeing-essence" (*jìng*) is precisely the "consciousness-essence" (*shí-jìng*). True seeing is the fundamentally pure essence of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
When the seeing sees, that seeing is not [ordinary] seeing; seeing is already detached from seeing, such that seeing cannot reach it. Thus, one follows...

The principle that the pure, perfect cultivation and complete cultivation reside within the nature is thus understood. It is so for one faculty; it is the same for the ear-faculty and all other faculties.
By means of this very [principle], one becomes Śrī Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Through the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, one enters the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

there is nothing that cannot be accomplished. For in the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, there is mindfulness of the three bodies of one's own Buddha, and there is mindfulness of the three bodies of other Buddhas.
Regarding the "body": there are those who, through the union of self and others, contemplate the three bodies as one. When seeing the act of seeing, that seeing is not [ordinary] seeing.
If one can see in this way, then the three bodies of self-nature are simultaneously contemplated. If the capacity to see belongs to wisdom (*jñāna*), then the fruit is the *saṃbhogakāya*;

thus, within the causal stage, one contemplates the *saṃbhogakāya*. As the Sūtra says, "The path of wondrous Bodhi" refers to this. If that which is seen belongs to the realm of phenomena (*dharmatā*), then...
The fruition is the accomplishment of the Dharmakāya; during the causal stage, one contemplates the Dharmakāya.
As the Sūtra says, this is the "pure true reality" (*viśuddha-lakṣaṇa*). Master Tiantai said: "Bodhi-wisdom and the Dharma-nature correspond and merge.
'Correspondence' is like the fit between a box and its lid; 'merging' is like water and milk merging together. It is like mercury mixed with pure gold, which can coat all manner of forms."
The merit and the Dharmakāya manifest and appear everywhere; therefore, at the moment of seeing this seeing, the seeing is not [ordinary] seeing.
Seeing is already free from seeing, beyond the reach of seeing, thereby accomplishing the virtue of liberation. Upon reaching the fruit, it can further accomplish the Sambhogakāya;
is this not the efficacy of "seeing the seeing"? Are not the three bodies complete within mindfulness? Furthermore, by means of this, one mindfully contemplates the Dharmakāya of the Buddha himself.
When one contemplates the Dharma-body of other Buddhas, it is utterly traceless and devoid of boundaries; self and other are seen simultaneously, not separated by even the tip of a hair.
When contemplating the Reward-body and Response-body of other Buddhas through this [Dharma-body], there is nothing that does not abide within my own dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

There is neither subject nor object, and all relativity is severed. This is what is meant by: "the object is wondrous provisional, and the contemplation is empty"; thus, object and contemplation are both [unified].

To forget is precisely the Middle Way. When forgetting and illuminating are one, how could there ever be before or after? It is this state where the single mind is fused and severed, leaving no trace whatsoever.
If one lacks even this thought, how could one enter the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) with a mind of Buddha-remembrance?

As it is with the faculty of the eye, so it is with the ear-gate samādhi of Avalokiteśvara; as it is for others regarding the perfect penetration of the faculties, so it is for the nose, tongue, body, and mind. Thus, all faculties are observed.
This contemplation of consciousness and the contemplation of objects are likewise illustrated by analogy: it is like a king of medicines who takes poison as medicine.
Therefore, one can realize that the nature of True Suchness (Tathatā) remains unchanging whether it is good or evil, yet functions according to conditions (pratyaya).

For one who understands that the cultivation of good or evil follows conditions while the essence itself remains unchanging, they can take up a single blade of grass and manifest it as the body of Śākyamuni Buddha ten thousand feet tall, or raise a single atom...
Dust can be made into the Western Land of Purity and Peace; taking up the entire earth, there is nothing that is not the medicinal king-tree of the Snowy Mountains.

The guest said: "I have already received your teaching on the principle of 'cultivating the pure and perfect according to conditions, wherein the entirety of cultivation resides within the nature. How is this named?"
This is the "Gate of Raising One to Encompass All" regarding the sequential, pure, perfect realization. I say:

as for "sequential, pure, perfect realization," it refers to the aforementioned seven great bodhisattvas, each of whom, based on one of the seven elements, practiced the cultivation of the matter to perfection; upon reaching the fruit, they likewise each relied on one of the seven elements to achieve perfect realization.
This is roughly illustrated by the youth Candraprabha, who awakened to the Way by relying on water, yet only attained the final fruit-realization [by relying on the other elements].
The perishing of the body merges with the nature of the ocean of fragrant waters, becoming one with true emptiness, without duality or distinction.

Is this not the following of purity to perfectly realize the Great One? Yet, since it is said that the nature merges with true emptiness without duality or distinction, then the nature of form is true emptiness;

the nature of fire is true emptiness; the nature of wind is true emptiness; the nature of awareness is true emptiness; the nature of seeing is the clarity of awareness; and the nature of consciousness is clarity.
Know that the meaning of these passages is fully reconciled throughout the third fascicle;

there is nothing that does not accord with the nature of the water element as the true emptiness, being non-dual and without distinction. Is this not the case where raising one [element] completely encompasses all?

Furthermore, in these seven gates, one contemplates and cultivates defilement as being identical to inherent evil. Not only is inherent evil interpenetrating such that no phenomenon fails to enter it, but it functions spontaneously.

One attains the goodness of the Buddha-dharmadhātu-nature, which is inherently good and permeates all; yet, there is no evil that is not fully contained within it, and thus one spontaneously attains the evil of the nine dharmadhātus.
Therefore, when a practitioner of the Perfect Teaching reaches the fulfillment of the fruit, all nine are brought to ultimate perfection.
The Venerable of Siming stated that even [beings such as] dung beetles must be judged by means of the "six identities" (*liu ji*).

This is precisely the meaning of the initial and final [stages]. A guest asked again: "The purport of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching clarifies that True Suchness is unchanging yet follows conditions, and that while following conditions it remains unchanged;
this principle is exhaustive and nothing can be added to it. Why must one necessarily discuss 'inherent possession' (*xingju*)? I replied: "Tiantai..."

The fundamental tenet of our school clarifies the meaning of "following conditions" (*suiyuan*). There is that which changes while following conditions; this refers to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).

There is that which remains unchanged while following conditions; this refers to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Whether there is change or non-change is precisely what is discussed within the teachings. Regarding the presence or absence of the [True] Cause:
if it is present, then "following conditions without changing" belongs to the Perfect Teaching. If one changes while following conditions, then the True Cause is not present. This is...

Therefore, it is judged to belong to the Separate Teaching (biejiao). This is precisely the principle that "that which accords with conditions does not change," which resides entirely within the function of the inherent nature (xingju).

How can you say that it is unnecessary to discuss the inherent nature? The guest asked again: "To clarify 'that which accords with conditions does not change' by means of the inherent nature is certainly appropriate;
why must one necessarily insist on the inherent nature of the ten realms? I replied: "As for the principle of the inherent nature..."

Those who do not clearly understand the ten realms—including their environments and inhabitants, matter and mind—merely state that the Buddha-realm is inherently possessed while the nine realms are not.
If this were so, one would necessarily have to destroy the nine realms in order to realize the Buddha-realm. Why? Because the nine dharma-realms would then not be inherently possessed;
they would instead be merely the Middle Buddha-nature, constructed by the influence of defiled conditions, like a person of pure goodness whose nature...

One who does not possess evil may suddenly be coerced by an evil person and, driven by circumstances, forcibly commit various evils. Since this was not within their own power, it is said that a good person might indeed do evil.
If one wishes to restore their inherent goodness, they must undergo profound repentance, reforming their evil ways and turning toward virtue;
thus, they cannot be called a "gentleman who is not limited" (a *bùqí*). Such a person is capable of both good and evil. As for those of the Perfect Teaching (*yuánjiào*), [they are otherwise].

Because one knows that the nature is inherently endowed with the ten realms, it is able to create the nine realms according to defiled conditions—just as water in its entirety becomes waves, and water in its entirety becomes ice.
Therefore, all deluded, defiled, and evil dharmas are inherently endowed within the nature; thus, what fault could there be in merely manifesting one's own capacity?
Since they are not faults, the two types of dharmas within delusion are, in their very essence, Buddha-nature. Regarding the dharmas of cultivation...
The "entirety of the nine realms" refers to the nine realms within one's original nature (*prakṛti*). When cultivation is entirely identical to this nature, it is called "attaining Buddhahood.

There is no other Buddha apart from this that can be attained. Furthermore, a question was asked: "If the original nature is fully endowed with the ten realms, then at the time of attaining the Way, one merely attains the fruit of Buddhahood;
since the meaning of cultivated goodness and inherent goodness is already complete and sufficient, why is it necessary to further establish the dharma-gate of inherent evil?"

[The interlocutor] said, “I respond: establishing this dharma-gate of inherent evil (xing-è) is no small matter; it possesses five major causes and conditions. First, because the principle-nature (li-ti) is fundamentally complete.
Second, because by illuminating the nature, one can accomplish cultivation. Third, because the perfect realization at the stage of fruition (guo-di) is nothing other than the wondrous Dharma.
Fourth, because when manifesting wondrous function, one must bestow [benefit] upon the ten realms. Fifth, because the capacities and natures [of sentient beings] are not...”

Because the gathering of sentient beings must be universal, the remaining four meanings have already been fully explained in the preceding text. Since the capacities and natures of sentient beings differ, the gathering of them must be universal;
this shall now be clarified. There are generally two points: first, to clarify that Bodhisattvas require this Dharma-gate to deliver sentient beings;
second, to clarify that the karmic conditions of sentient beings require this to enter the Path. Regarding the Bodhisattvas delivering sentient beings, they require this Dharma-gate.
Furthermore, there are two aspects: first, the manifestation of the gate that is immeasurable and inexhaustible; second, because self-benefit serves as the cause for immediately benefiting others.
The manifestation of the immeasurable and inexhaustible gate has already been explained in the section on the "Perfect Manifestation of the Ground of Fruition, Without Any Deficiency.
Regarding the second point—how self-benefit serves as the cause for immediately benefiting others—it shall now be discussed.

This is clarified through two general meanings: first, establishing the meaning through scriptural evidence; second, establishing it through human testimony. Regarding the first, the scriptural evidence is as stated in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*:
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti, "How does a bodhisattva penetrate the path of the Buddha?"
The answer is: If a bodhisattva commits the five acts of immediate retribution yet remains free from anger and affliction, he reaches the hells without any defilement of sin;
he reaches the animal realm without the faults of ignorance, pride, and so forth; he reaches the realm of hungry ghosts while being fully endowed with merit;
and though he practices in the realms of form and formlessness, he does not regard them as superior. He manifests the practice of desire while remaining free from all attachment. He manifests...
He manifests the practice of anger, yet harbors no resentment or obstruction toward any sentient being. He manifests the practice of ignorance, yet subdues his mind with wisdom.
He manifests the practice of stinginess and greed, yet relinquishes all internal and external possessions, not sparing even his own body or life.

He manifests the practice of violating the precepts, yet dwells securely in pure morality, feeling great dread even toward the slightest transgression. He manifests the practice of anger, yet is always...
Though possessing loving patience, he manifests indolence, yet diligently cultivates meritorious virtues. Though manifesting a distracted mind, he constantly dwells in meditative concentration.

Though manifesting folly, he penetrates both mundane and supramundane wisdom. Though manifesting flattery and hypocrisy, he is skilled in expedient means in accordance with the meanings of all sutras.
Though manifesting arrogance, he serves as a bridge for all sentient beings. Though manifesting various afflictions...
Though afflicted, his mind is always pure. He manifests entry into the realm of Māra, yet accords with the Buddha’s wisdom and does not follow the teachings of others.

He manifests entry among the śrāvakas, yet expounds the Dharma never heard before for the sake of sentient beings. He manifests entry into the wisdom of the pratyekabuddhas, yet accomplishes great compassion to teach and transform sentient beings.
He manifests entry into poverty, yet possesses a jewel-hand from which merit is inexhaustible. He manifests entry into [physical] form...

Though appearing with a crippled body, he is adorned with the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha; though appearing to enter among the lowly and base, he is born into the lineage of Buddhas and possesses all meritorious virtues;
though appearing weak, inferior, and ugly, he attains the body of Nārāyaṇa, which all sentient beings delight to behold;
though appearing to suffer from old age and illness, he has forever severed the root of disease and transcended the fear of death; and though appearing to possess the necessities of life...

Constantly contemplating impermanence, he truly has nothing to crave. Though he manifests having wives, children, and concubines, he always delights in remaining far removed from the mire of the five desires.
He appears dull-witted, yet he achieves eloquence and possesses *dhāraṇī* without loss. He manifests entry into heterodox paths.
Yet, by means of the correct [path], they deliver all sentient beings. They manifest as entering all realms of existence while severing their causal conditions;
they manifest in nirvana while severing birth and death. Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva can thus practice upon what is not the path and thereby attain penetration of the Buddha-path.

The commentary states: This scriptural passage serves as proof that a bodhisattva can, by means of the dharma-gate of the inherently evil nature (*prakṛti-pāpa-dharmamukha*), transform and deliver sentient beings and attain mastery over the Buddha-way.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti asked Mañjuśrī, "What constitutes the lineage of the Tathāgata? Mañjuśrī replied, "The body of existence is the lineage;
ignorance and craving for existence are the lineage; greed, anger, and delusion are the lineage; the four inversions are the lineage; the five hindrances are the lineage;
the six sense bases are the lineage; the seven consciousnesses are the lineage; the eightfold wrong path is the lineage; and the nine afflictions..."
They are seeds. The ten unwholesome paths are seeds. To speak in brief, the sixty-two views and all afflictions are all seeds of the Buddha.

He asked: "What do you mean by this? He replied: "If one perceives the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and enters the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), they can no longer give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It is, for example, like high ground or dry land [where crops cannot grow]."
The lotus flower grows from low-lying mud; it is from such muddy mire that the lotus flower is produced.

Likewise, those who perceive unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) and enter the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) can never again give rise to the Buddha-dharma. It is only within the mire of afflictions (*kleśa*) that sentient beings can bring forth the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, just as planting a seed in empty space will never result in growth, while in soil enriched with manure it can flourish and thrive. Thus it is.
Those who have entered the unconditioned state of certainty do not give rise to the Buddha-dharma; they conceive a view of self as vast as Mount Sumeru.
Yet, even such a person can still generate the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and give rise to the Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, one should know that all afflictions are the seeds of the Tathāgata. For example, if one does not descend into the great ocean, one cannot obtain priceless jewels.
Jewel. Just so, if one does not enter the great ocean of afflictions, one cannot obtain the jewel of omniscience.
The commentary states: According to this scriptural passage, it can be proven that the very nature of evil, when cultivated through contemplation, is itself the nature of evil;
yet, by spontaneously encompassing the nature of goodness within the Buddha-realm, it can serve as the seed of the Tathāgata.
Second, regarding the citation of human testimony, three instances are briefly introduced.
First, concerning the story of the woman Vāsuladattā, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: After the youth Sudhana had seen Siṃhavijṛmbhitā, she further addressed him, saying:
"Good son, to the south of here there is a land called Durga. In this land there is a city named Ratnavyūha."
"Vimalakīrti. Within it dwells a woman named Vāsantī. Go to her and ask: 'How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with deep reverence, and took his leave.
At that time, the light of great wisdom illuminated and opened Sudhana’s mind."
With the mind, he contemplated and observed, seeing the nature of all phenomena. He attained the dharani-door of understanding all sounds and speech;
he attained the dharani-door of upholding all wheels of Dharma; he attained the power of great compassion that serves as a refuge for all sentient beings;
he attained the door of light for observing the principles and meanings of all phenomena; and he attained the fulfillment of the entire dharma-realm.
With pure vows, he attained the light of wisdom that universally illumines all dharmas throughout the ten directions;
he attained the sovereign power to universally adorn all worlds; and he attained the perfect vow to universally initiate all bodhisattva activities.
Traveling by stages, he arrived at the city of Ratnavyūha in the perilous kingdom of Bhīṣmaka, searching everywhere for the woman Vasumitrā within the city.
People did not know of this girl’s merit and wisdom, and they thought to themselves: "This youth has tranquil faculties; his wisdom is clear and lucid.
He is neither deluded nor distracted. He gazes steadily for a fathom without weariness or fatigue.
He is free from grasping and attachment; his eyes do not blink, and his mind is unmoving. It is profound and vast, like the great ocean. One should not [treat him]..."
This woman Vasumitrā possesses a mind of greedy attachment and a perverted mind; she conceives notions of purity and notions of desire.

She should not be grasped by the beauty of this woman’s form. This youth does not practice the ways of Māra, does not enter the realm of Māra, does not sink into the mire of desire, and is not bound by Māra.
He is capable of refraining from that which ought not to be done. What [fault] could there be?
As he sought this woman, there was among them one who had previously known that this woman possessed wisdom. He said to Sudhana:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! It is well that you are now able to investigate and search for the lady Vasumitrā."
"You have already obtained vast and great benefit. Son of good family, you should resolutely seek the state of Buddhahood;
you should resolutely desire to act as a refuge for all sentient beings; you should resolutely desire to extract the poisonous arrows of craving from all sentient beings;
you should resolutely desire to shatter all notions of purity regarding female forms held by all sentient beings."
"Good man, the maiden Vasumitrā dwells in her own home, located north of the marketplace within this city.
When Sudhana heard these words, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness;
he proceeded to her gate and beheld her residence, vast and magnificent, with jeweled walls, jeweled trees, and jeweled moats, each surrounded by tenfold enclosures. As for those jeweled moats:
The ponds were filled with fragrant water, and their floors were strewn with golden sand.
Various celestial jewel-flowers—*utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka*—completely covered the surface of the water. Palaces and towers were distributed everywhere;
gates, portals, and windows were aligned and interspersed one after another, all adorned with jeweled nets and bells, and furnished with banners and streamers of immeasurable treasures.
It was adorned with wonders; its ground was made of lapis lazuli, interspersed with various jewels. It burned aloeswood incense and was anointed with sandalwood.
Countless jeweled bells were suspended, producing melodic sounds when stirred by the wind. Celestial flowers were scattered, covering the entire ground.
Its manifold splendors and beauties are beyond description. Hundreds of thousands of treasuries of rare gems and ten great groves served as its adornments.
[Śāriputra: "Excellent! At that time, Sudhana beheld this woman, her countenance dignified and majestic, her physical features perfect and complete.
Her skin was golden, and her eyes and hair were deep blue. She was neither tall nor short, neither coarse nor delicate; among the humans and devas of the desire realm, none could compare to her.
Her voice was exquisite and beautiful, surpassing all the Brahma worlds, and she possessed every distinct vocal quality of all sentient beings."

He was fully accomplished; there was nothing he did not understand. He profoundly penetrated the meaning of words and was skillful in discourse. He had attained the wisdom that is like an illusion and entered the gateway of expedient means.
His body was adorned with various ornaments and necklaces of many jewels, and his head was crowned with a tiara made of wish-fulfilling *maṇi* gems.
Furthermore, he was surrounded by immeasurable retinues, all of whom shared the same conduct as Sudhana.
"May my merit, a great treasury, be fully endowed and inexhaustible.
At that time, the maiden Bhṛkuṭī emitted a vast radiance from her body, which universally illuminated all the palaces within the residence. Those who encountered this light attained purity of body.
Then, Sudhana went before her, prostrated at her feet, stood with palms joined, and said: "O Noble One, I..."

"I have already previously resolved my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct, nor how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
I have heard that the Holy One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will speak for me.
He then replied: "Good son, I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'The Limit Beyond Greed' (*vītarāgakoṭi*)."
According to their inclinations and desires, I manifest my body for them. If a deva sees me, I appear as a celestial maiden, with a form and radiance so preeminent that they are beyond compare.
Likewise, even if humans, non-humans, or others see me, I immediately manifest as a human, non-human, or other female, according to their specific wishes, so that all may behold me.
If there are sentient beings who are entangled by sensual desire, [I appear to them accordingly].
They come to me, and I preach the Dharma for them. Having heard the Dharma, they become free from desire and attain the Bodhisattva samādhi of the unattached realm.
If there are sentient beings who see me even for a moment, they become free from desire and attain the Bodhisattva samādhi of joy.
If there are sentient beings who speak with me even for a moment, they become free from desire and attain the Bodhisattva [samādhi of] non-...

The Samādhi of Obstructing Sound and Voice: If there are sentient beings who briefly grasp my hand, they shall be freed from lustful desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Universally Traveling to All Buddha-fields.
If there are sentient beings who briefly ascend my seat, they shall likewise be freed from lustful desire.
I have attained the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of Liberation.
If there are sentient beings who gaze upon me for even a moment, they will be freed from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Tranquil Adornment.

If there are sentient beings who see me stretching my limbs, they will be freed from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Subduing Non-Buddhists. If there are sentient beings who see me blink my eyes, then...
They become free from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of the Buddha-Sphere.
If there are sentient beings who embrace me, they become free from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Gathering All Sentient Beings Without Ever Abandoning Them.
If there are sentient beings who kiss my lips, they become free from desire and attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Increasing All Sentient Beings.

The Samādhi of the Treasury of Merit. "Whatever sentient beings approach me, they all dwell in the state beyond greed and enter the stage of omniscience of the Bodhisattvas, attaining the manifest and unimpeded liberation.
Sudhana said, "Noble One, what roots of goodness have you planted, and what meritorious deeds have you cultivated, that you have attained such mastery? He replied, "Good son..."
"Son, I recall that in the past there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Uccagāmin (High Conduct). His royal capital city was named Suvilokitamukha (Wonderful Gate).
Good son, out of compassion for sentient beings, that Tathāgata Uccagāmin entered the royal city;
as he stepped upon each of its gates, the entire city shook, suddenly becoming vast and expansive, adorned with various jewels and immeasurable light."
They illuminated one another with mutual radiance, and various jeweled flowers were scattered across the ground.
The celestial music of the devas played in unison, and all the devas filled the void of space. Good son, at that time, I was the wife of a householder.
Her name was Śrīmatī. Witnessing the Buddha’s supernormal power, her mind attained awakening;
she then went with her husband to the place where the Buddha was and made an offering of a single precious coin. At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī was serving as the Buddha’s attendant.
"Preach the Dharma for me, so that I may resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Good son, I know only this Bodhisattva liberation of the 'Limit of Detachment from Greed.

As for those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have accomplished boundless wisdom of skillful means, whose treasury is vast and whose sphere of activity is incomparable—how could I possibly know them or..."
To speak of his meritorious conduct:

according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, regarding the second king, Atyantāparitṛpta (The King Never-Tiring), it is said that after the youth Sudhana had visited the elder Samantanetra, the latter further addressed him, saying: "O son of good family..."
"Son, to the south of here there is a great city named Tālāṅka. In it dwells a king named Analaṃpratiṣṭhita.
Go to him and ask: how should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Samantanetra, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with deep reverence, and took his leave to depart. At that time...
The youth Sudhana recollected and reflected upon the instructions of his spiritual friends, mindful that these spiritual friends were able to sustain and protect him,
ensuring that he would never regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Reflecting in this way, he gave rise to a mind of joy, a mind of pure faith, a vast mind,

a serene and expansive mind, a mind of exultation, a sublime mind, a tranquil mind, an adorned mind, an unattached mind, an unimpeded mind, an equanimous mind, a sovereign mind, a mind dwelling in the Dharma,
a mind that travels everywhere to Buddha-fields, a mind that beholds the adornments of the Buddhas, and a mind that never abandons the ten powers. Gradually...
Next, he traveled on, passing through kingdoms, villages, towns, and settlements until he reached the city of Tāladhvaja.

He asked where King Anala was located, and the people replied, "This king is currently in the main hall, seated upon the lion throne, proclaiming the transformative teachings of the Dharma and governing sentient beings:
those who deserve punishment are punished, and those who deserve to be gathered under his care are gathered; he metes out penalties for their crimes."
He adjudicated their disputes and comforted the orphaned and the weak, causing them all to forever sever killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.

He also caused them to prohibit false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter. Furthermore, he led them to distance themselves from greed, hatred, and wrong views. At that time, Sudhana was filled with wonder;
following the words of the multitude, he immediately went to visit him. From afar, he saw the king seated upon a Vajra-Nārāyaṇa throne.
Its seat was composed of incalculable jewels, with immeasurable jeweled images serving as its adornments.
A net of golden cords covered it from above. A *cintāmaṇi* jewel served as a crown, adorning its head.
A crescent moon made of Jambūnada gold adorned its forehead. *Indranīla* jewels served as earrings, hanging down on either side.
Below, it was adorned with priceless *maṇi* jewels as necklaces to grace its neck; celestial, exquisite *maṇi* jewels served as seals and bracelets to grace its arms;
Jāmbūnada gold formed its canopy; various jewels were inlaid to form its spokes;
great *vaiḍūrya* gems formed its shaft; *prabhāsvaramaṇi* jewels formed its yoke-pole; and various miscellaneous jewels formed its bells.
It constantly emits wondrous sounds and radiates great light that pervades the ten directions. Such a jeweled canopy covers it from above.
King Anala possesses great power and majesty; he can subdue all other hosts, and none can oppose him. With a stainless silken cloth—
He bound it upon his crown. Ten thousand ministers surrounded him from front and back, jointly managing the affairs of state.

Before him were further one hundred thousand fierce soldiers, hideous in appearance and clad in coarse, shabby garments; they brandished their weapons, bared their arms, and glared with eyes full of rage.

All sentient beings who see him are struck with terror. Countless sentient beings violate the king’s commands—some by stealing the property of others, some by taking the lives of others, some by violating the wives of others, some by giving rise to false views, some by harboring hatred and resentment, and some by conceiving greed and envy.
Having committed such various evil deeds, their bodies were bound with fivefold fetters and led before the king. According to their offenses, they were punished:
some had their hands and feet cut off, some had their ears and noses sliced off, some had their eyes gouged out, and some had their heads severed.
Some have their skin flayed; some have their bodies dismembered; some are boiled in cauldrons; some are burned with fire;
some are driven up high mountains and pushed over to fall. Subjected to such immeasurable tortures and agonies, they cry out in lamentation, as if in the Saṃghāta or Mahāpralāpa hells.
Having seen this, Sudhana thought to himself: "For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings..."

"Born into this world, he sought the conduct of a bodhisattva and cultivated the path of a bodhisattva. Now, however, this king has extinguished all wholesome dharmas and committed great sinful karma;
he oppresses sentient beings, even unto taking their lives, without ever regarding or fearing the evil realms of the future.
How can one seek the Dharma here? One must give rise to the mind of great compassion to rescue and protect sentient beings. While he was thinking these thoughts, there appeared in the sky...
The deity spoke to him, saying: "O son of good family, you should remember the instruction of the spiritual friend, the elder Viśvacakṣu.
Sudhana looked up and said to him: "I constantly remember it; I have never dared to forget it from the beginning. The deity said:
"O son of good family, do not grow weary of or turn away from the words of the spiritual friend. A spiritual friend is one who can lead you to the state free from peril."
It is a place difficult to find peace and security. Good son, the Bodhisattva’s wisdom of skillful means is inconceivable;
his wisdom of gathering in sentient beings is inconceivable; his wisdom of mindful protection of sentient beings is inconceivable; his wisdom of bringing sentient beings to maturity is inconceivable;
his wisdom of guarding sentient beings is inconceivable; and his wisdom of liberating sentient beings is inconceivable.
"Inconceivable! The wisdom that tames sentient beings is inconceivable.
Having heard these words, the youth Sudhana immediately went to the king's presence, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice. How...
"How does one cultivate the bodhisattva path? I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain it to me.
Then King Anala, having attended to his royal duties, took Sudhana by the hand and led him into the palace, inviting him to sit together with him and said:

"Good son, you should observe the palace in which I dwell. Sudhana, following these words, immediately looked all around and beheld that palace, vast beyond compare, composed entirely of exquisite jewels.

It was surrounded on all sides by walls made of the seven precious substances, and featured hundreds of thousands of towers and pavilions made of various gems; its manifold adornments were all exquisitely beautiful. Not...
A net of *cintāmaṇi* jewels was spread over its surface. Ten billion handmaidens were there, exquisite and peerless in beauty;
their deportment and every movement were worthy of admiration, and all their actions were skillful and artful.
They rose before [the king] and retired after him, serving his every wish with gentle hearts. At that time, King Anala said to Sudhana: "Good son, what do you think? If I..."
"You have indeed committed such evil karma; how then could you obtain such a retribution as this—a physical body such as this, such retinues, such abundance, and such sovereignty?
Good son, I have attained the Bodhisattva liberation called 'Like an Illusion.
Good son, all the sentient beings in my land mostly practice killing, stealing, and even hold wrong views."
I employ other skillful means, yet they are unable to cause them to abandon their evil karma.
Good son, for the sake of taming those sentient beings, I manifest as an evil person who commits various sinful deeds and undergoes manifold sufferings.

When all those sentient beings who commit evil see this, their hearts are filled with terror, they develop a sense of weary detachment, and they become disheartened; thus they sever [their evil ways].
Regarding all the evil karma they have committed, they shall give rise to the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Son of good family, by means of such skillful expedients (*upāya-kauśalya*), I cause all sentient beings to abandon the ten unwholesome paths of action and abide in the ten wholesome paths of action, so that they may attain ultimate happiness, ultimate peace, and ultimately dwell upon the ground of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*). Son of good family, [this is how it is].
With my body, speech, and mind, I have never once harmed or afflicted a single sentient being.

Good son, as for my heart, I would rather undergo the sufferings of the Avīci Hell in the future than ever give rise to a single thought of causing suffering to even a mosquito or an ant, let alone a human being.
A human is a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), for they are able to give birth to all wholesome dharmas.
"Good son, I have attained only this liberation that is like an illusion.

As for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they know that all realms of existence are entirely like illusions; that all bodhisattva practices are entirely like illusions;
that all worlds are entirely like shadows; and that all dharmas are entirely like dreams. They enter the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) without obstruction."
This is the Dharma-door of practicing all manner of conduct like a celestial net, traversing the sphere of objects with unimpeded wisdom,
universally entering all samādhis of equality, and having attained mastery over dhāraṇīs.
How could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?
Treatise on the Innate Goodness and Evil of Human Nature, Volume Five;
Treatise on the Innate Goodness and Evil of Human Nature, Volume Six.
Written by the Śramaṇa Chuandeng of Youxi at Mount Tiantai.
Regarding the third story of the Brahmin Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
After the youth Sudhana had visited the spiritual friend Vimalacakra, the latter addressed him again, saying:
"Good son, to the south of here there is a village named Īśāna, where there dwells a Brahmin."
His name is Jvalanāntaratejorāja. Go to him and ask: how should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
At that time, the youth Sudhana, filled with joy and exultation, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and gazed upon him with deep reverence.
Having taken his leave, he traveled south. Then, the youth Sudhana was empowered by the bodhisattva liberation called "Inconquerable Banner."
Because of this illumination, they abide in the inconceivable spiritual power of all Buddhas; they realize the inconceivable wisdom of the supernormal powers of Bodhisattvas;
they obtain the light of wisdom of the inconceivable samādhis of Bodhisattvas; they obtain the light of wisdom of the samādhis cultivated at all times;
they obtain the light of wisdom of the samādhi that thoroughly knows all objective realms as abiding solely in conceptualization; they obtain one...
The supreme light of wisdom of all worlds manifests its body in every place;
through ultimate wisdom, it teaches the non-dual, undifferentiated, and equal Dharma. With clear and pure wisdom, it universally illumines all objects.

Regarding whatever Dharma is heard, one is able to accept, endure, and maintain pure faith and understanding. One attains definitive clarity regarding the self-nature of phenomena, and the mind never abandons bodhicitta.
Practicing sublime conduct, they seek omniscience without ever regressing. They attain the light of wisdom of the ten powers and diligently seek the sublime Dharma with constant insatiability.
Through correct practice, they enter the realm of the Buddhas and give rise to the immeasurable adornments of a bodhisattva.
Their boundless great vows are entirely purified, and by means of inexhaustible wisdom, they know infinite worlds.
The net of realms: with a mind free from cowardice, they deliver an ocean of immeasurable sentient beings; they comprehend the boundless spheres of all bodhisattva practices;
they behold the various distinctions of boundless worlds; and they behold the various adornments of boundless worlds.
They enter the subtle realm of infinite worlds; they know the various names of infinite worlds;
they know the various expressions of infinite worlds; they know the various inclinations of infinite sentient beings; they see the conduct of infinite sentient beings;
they see the conduct of infinite sentient beings toward maturation; they see the diverse perceptions of infinite sentient beings; and they are mindful and well-acquainted with them.
Vijñāna gradually traveled on until he reached the village of Īśāna. There he saw that Ugra-tapas practicing various ascetic penances in his quest for omniscience.
On all four sides were masses of fire like great mountains, and in their midst was a mountain of blades, towering and infinitely steep.
[Ugra-tapas] would climb that mountain and cast himself into the fire. At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet and stood with palms joined.

He spoke these words: "Noble One, I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct, nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me. The brahmin said: "Good son, if you are now able..."
Ascending this mountain of blades and casting oneself into the mass of fire, all the practices of the Bodhisattvas become completely purified.
At that time, the youth Sudhana thought to himself: "Difficult is it to obtain a human body; difficult is it to be free from all calamities; difficult is it to attain a state free from calamity;

difficult is it to attain the pure Dharma; difficult is it to encounter a Buddha; difficult is it to possess all the sense faculties; difficult is it to hear the Buddha’s teachings; difficult is it to meet a virtuous person; difficult is it to encounter a true and good friend."

It is difficult to gain knowledge; it is difficult to receive the correct teaching according to reality; it is difficult to attain right livelihood; and it is difficult to practice in accordance with the Dharma.

Is this not perhaps instigated by Māra? Is this not the work of Māra’s treacherous and evil faction, who falsely manifest the appearance of Bodhisattvas and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) in order to create obstacles for my roots of goodness, to create obstacles for my life, and to hinder my cultivation of omniscience?
"The Path leads me into the various evil realms and seeks to obstruct my Dharma-gate and my Buddha-Dharma.
While he was thinking this, ten thousand Brahmā devas in the midst of the void spoke these words: "Good son, do not think such thoughts;
do not think such thoughts! This noble one has attained the radiance of the Vajra-flame Samādhi and has aroused great vigor."
Advancing to deliver all sentient beings with a mind free from regression; desiring to exhaust the ocean of all craving and attachment;

desiring to sever the net of all false views; desiring to burn away the firewood of all afflictions; desiring to illuminate the dense forest of all delusions; desiring to cut off the fear of all aging;
desiring to destroy all obstacles of the three periods of time; desiring to radiate the light of all dharmas—O virtuous son!
"Son, many of us Brahmā deities are deeply attached to false views; we all consider ourselves to be autonomous and creators, thinking, 'In this world, I am the most supreme.

When we saw the brahmin performing the penance of the five fires, our hearts found no pleasure in our own palaces, nor did we find any flavor in our various meditative absorptions (dhyāna-samādhi). Thus, we have all come together to visit this brahmin."

At that time, the brahmin, by means of his supernormal powers, manifested great ascetic practices and preached the Dharma for us, enabling us to extinguish all views, eliminate all pride, abide in great loving-kindness, practice great compassion, give rise to a vast mind, and awaken the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
We constantly beheld all Buddhas and perpetually heard the wondrous Dharma; in all places, our minds were without attachment.
Obstruction. Furthermore, ten thousand māras were in the void, scattering celestial maṇi jewels upon the brahmin and addressing the youth Sudhana:
"Good son, when this brahmin scorched his body with the five fires, the radiance of those flames eclipsed all my palaces and ornaments, making them appear like a mass of ink. It caused me—
Without giving rise to attachment therein, I and my retinue went to that place.
This brahmin preached the Dharma for me, causing myself and immeasurable sons and daughters of the gods to attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, ten thousand kings of the *Īśvara* devas, in the void...

Each scattered celestial flowers and spoke these words: "O son of good family, when this brahmin scorched his body with the five fires, the radiance of that fire eclipsed all our palaces and ornaments, making them appear like a mass of ink.
This caused us to lose all attachment to them, and so we came here together with our retinues to where this brahmin was. This brahmin—
May the Gate preach the Dharma for me, so that I may attain mastery over my mind; attain mastery amidst the afflictions;
attain mastery over the process of rebirth; attain mastery over all karmic obstructions;
attain mastery over all samādhis; attain mastery over all ornaments; and attain mastery over the span of my life.

this is because such individuals, although they encountered the conditions of the Triple Gem and gave rise to the aspiration for the Path in past lives, were subsequently obstructed by evil conditions in the interim.

In this world, those who by nature are respectful and obedient, honoring the teachings of their teachers, addressed their teacher, saying:

He further resolved, "I shall now cause him to die," and addressed him, saying, "Kill one person and take one finger from each; once you have killed a thousand people, [you shall die]."

There is none who does not cherish their own life; take yourself as a metaphor for others.
