The discourse was exceedingly long, extending even to the Brahma King, the Four Heavenly Kings, Maheśvara, and the tree spirits, each of whom offered him robes, yet he accepted none of them.
They all engaged him in debate, but there was not one whose arguments did not fail and who was not humbled by his eloquence.
This included the Venerable Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Ānanda, Rāhula, Aniruddha, Nandasena, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and others. All of them—
Even when debating with the Great Venerable One, he was once again confounded;
yet when faced by the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī—who manifests in human form—he became speechless.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse to Aṅgulimāla:
"Come, Aṅgulimāla! Leave the household life and receive the Three Refuges.
Then Aṅgulimāla spoke in verse:
This vehicle is the Mahāyāna; it is called unimpeded wisdom. The One Vehicle is the one refuge;
the Buddha is the ultimate truth. The Dharma and the Buddha are of one meaning.
Regarding the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s wondrous Dharma-body, it is said that the Tathāgata is himself the Saṅgha—namely, the Dharma and the community of Bhikṣus.
The second is the reliance on skillful means; the Tathāgata is not a reliance on skillful means. This is the reliance on the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Therefore, today I take refuge in the Tathāgata. Among all objects of refuge, the Tathāgata is the true reliance.
Just as one who wishes to eat the utpala flower should take the real thing, so too should one rely on the reality.
Abandoning the true and consuming the false, Bringing no benefit to oneself or others— Such deluded people as these, even a thousand Buddhas cannot save.
Thus abandoning the one reliance And practicing the reliance on expedient means— These are the masses of the ignorant; Even a thousand Buddhas cannot save them.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Aṅgulimāla: "You should receive and uphold the pure precepts of a *kumārabhūta* (a novice monk is specifically termed a *kumārabhūta*).
Then Aṅgulimāla asked in verse:
"What is meant by 'the youthful' (kumāra)? What is the perfection of precepts? What is a true śramaṇa?
And what is the field of merit?
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent. Aṅgulimāla spoke again in verse:
If one does not know the single refuge, which is the ultimate refuge, one cannot know the two refuges established through skillful means.
One should know that such a person is a worldly youth who has not received full ordination; how can they be called a śramaṇa? They do not know the single refuge.
What is a pure refuge? If one does not know the Tathāgata as the ultimate refuge, that is an impure refuge.
How can one be a śramaṇa if one does not know the true refuge?
How can one be a field of merit? Regarding these two refuges—the ultimate and the expedient—[one must understand them both].
"Lacking knowledge of distinctions—this is the worldly *kumāra*.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Aṅgulimāla: "You should uphold the precept of non-killing.
Aṅgulimāla replied in verse:
I can certainly never uphold the precept against killing; I shall always uphold the severing of the lives of sentient beings.
As for what is called "sentient beings," they are the immeasurable afflictions;
if one can constantly harm them, this is called upholding the precept of killing.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed him, saying: "You should receive and uphold the precept against false speech.
Aṅgulimāla replied in verse:
"I am now certainly unable To receive and uphold the precept against false speech; I shall [abide] within all dharmas..."
To uphold the words of false speech, to uphold the discourse of delusion—this is what the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have taught as "false. All phenomena are empty;
furthermore, there are the dharmas of delusion belonging to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as the practices of the bodhisattvas, which accord with worldly affairs.
Furthermore, there are deceptive dharmas; I have appeared in the world.
By receiving and maintaining the complete precepts, one attains the state of an Arhat. Thus, there are twenty-one verses in total, ending with:
"Therefore, from this day forward, I shall practice deceitful deeds, even unto the furthest limits of sentient beings."
The limit of all falsity is non-acceptance; by being free from falsity, my precepts are pure.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Aṅgulimāla: "You should receive and uphold the precept against drinking alcohol.
Aṅgulimāla replied in verse:
I am now likewise unable to uphold the precept of not drinking alcohol;

constantly violating the precept against drinking, I have been perpetually indulgent throughout the long night. Because of this, I cry out in distress as I wander through all five realms of existence.
That which is exclusively and utterly pleasurable is what is called "alcohol," born from that Great Vehicle.
This unsurpassed wine of the Buddha-treasury—this wine I now drink. Sufficient for myself, I exhort all sentient beings to abide eternally without change;
with joy I praise it as "excellent! With human voices I proclaim it loudly, intoxicated without end.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Aṅgulimāla: "You should now receive the pure precept of celibacy.
Aṅgulimāla replied in verse:
"I am likewise unable now To uphold the precept of celibacy; I shall instead always uphold [The precept of] non-killing."
Clinging to what others love, one sports with them; Taking the bliss of samādhi as wife,
the Dharma of ultimate truth as son, The mind of compassion as daughter, and the emptiness of phenomena as the dwelling,
With the immeasurable pāramitās as a high and broad couch, And all afflictions as the attendants.
Concealment is taught as food; the dhāraṇī is the grove.
Adorned with the flowers of the seven factors of awakening, the discourse on the Dharma is the forest trees, and the wisdom of liberation is the fruit.
These are called the world’s supreme and most excellent enjoyments—the natural state of the wise, not the domain of the foolish.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Aṅgulimāla: "You should now receive the precept against taking what is not given.
Aṅgulimāla replied in verse:
Even now, I am unable to uphold the precept against stealing; I constantly take what is not given, plundering the wealth and property of others.
Since there is no one who gives and no one who bestows, I take for myself what is not given.
Therefore, while I practice taking what is not given, the Buddha sits beneath the Bodhi tree.
Neither gained nor lost—this is the nature of phenomena (dharmas). It is supreme and unsurpassed.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Aṅgulimāla: "You should now receive the precept against singing and dancing.
Aṅgulimāla replied in verse:
I shall practice dance and music, singing the verses of the gandharvas; I shall proclaim the Tathāgatagarbha and exclaim, "Excellent!
In the presence of the Buddhas of the ten directions, I shall hear that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, reciting it with a wondrous voice as if chanting the Mahāyāna sūtras like a kiṃnara.
With the music of gandharva maidens and immeasurable, wondrous sounds, they make offerings to these various sūtra scrolls.
If those sentient beings constantly perform such offerings, all Buddhas will bestow upon them the prediction that in the future they shall share the same name.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught Aṅgulimāla by means of counting from one.
Having completed the response by counting from one up to ten, he again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, you have said: 'I abide at the limit of non-arising.'"
Regarding the meaning of this teaching and so forth: the Buddha commanded them to accompany Mañjuśrī and together proceed to the north.

They passed beyond one *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [Ganges-sand] number of buddha-fields, up to ten *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* numbers of fields. To the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, they likewise passed beyond one *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* number of fields, up to ten.
In those ten buddha-fields, there was a Buddha in each and every field, all of whom were Śākyamuni Tathāgatas.
Under these alternative names, he addressed the two men, saying: "Sons of good family, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni is none other than my own body.
Return and speak to that Buddha, saying: 'The Buddhas such as Amitaprajña have sent us back, saying, "That Tathāgata shall explain it for you.
Śākyamuni Tathāgata then explained its meaning for them, as detailed in the sūtra text.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Aṅgulimāla! Come, bhikṣu!
He immediately became a śramaṇa, his deportment complete and perfect, just like a bhikṣu of long standing. Then Aṅgulimāla prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, having now come here, I have immediately attained the fruit of Arhatship upon hearing your voice.
The Buddha further told him, “Come to the Jeta Grove to extensively deliver sentient beings; go together with Mañjuśrī and all the great venerable ones.
Arriving at the Jeta Grove, he ascended the lion throne, and the earth of the trichiliocosm became as level as a palm.
From his palms grew soft grass, like that of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Great Bodhisattvas from all directions all desired to come and see him as Aṅgulimāla preached the sublime Dharma, as described in detail in the sūtra.
At that time, King Prasenajit mobilized the fourfold army, intending to go forth on a campaign of conquest.
Among his ministers and troops, there was none who did not tremble with fear; not a single one responded to his command. Leading his host, the king went to the place where the Buddha was staying.

He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, his face bearing an expression of terror and sweat pouring from him. The Tathāgata, knowing this, asked intentionally: "Great King, for what reason are you sweating today?"
The king said to the Buddha, "There is currently a rākṣasa named Aṅgulimāla who has killed nine hundred and ninety-nine people.
He wears their fingers as a garland and smears their blood upon his body. He has arrayed these four divisions of the army and intends to go and attack him.
The Buddha asked the great king, "If Aṅgulimāla were to come here, what would you do? The king said to the Buddha, "If he..."
"Coming here in this manner constitutes one [instance]. At that time, the World-Honored One pointed him out to the king, saying, "This is Aṅgulimāla.
The Great King exclaimed, "How marvelous, World-Honored One! You are truly the foremost yoke of those who tame; you are truly the unsurpassed teacher of gods and humans.
That such a violent person with evil karma could be skillfully established in the True Dharma—how extraordinary!"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses in praise:
"One who was formerly heedless, But later ceases and commits no further transgressions, Shines upon the world Like the moon when the clouds have vanished.
If a great bodhisattva first manifests heedlessness and later manifests merit, they shine upon the world like the moon when the clouds have vanished.
He delivers immeasurable sentient beings and manifests the merits of the Tathāgata. Great King, you should know that he is not an evil person;
rather, this is simply the skillful means (*upāya*) of a Bodhisattva. For example, the trampling of a dragon-elephant is not something a donkey can endure.
Sixty-two *gaṅgā*-sands of world-systems to the south of here, there is a land named Sarvaratnavyūha. The Buddha there is named Sarvalokadhātūpapanna.
"Aṅgulimāla is none other than that Tathāgata, the Greatly Valiant One (Mahāvīra), whom you have just seen.
The realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable. His mother, his teacher, and his teacher’s wife—all were transformed by me for the sake of benefiting them, so as to perform the work of a Buddha.
At that time, the king, the great assembly, the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings—"
The entire assembly bowed their heads at the feet of Aṅgulimāla. With one mind and in unison, they spoke these verses in praise:
Homage to the Tathāgata of Boundless Body! Homage to the skillful Aṅgulimāla!
I now prostrate at the base of your holy feet; I repent before the soft and supple feet of the World-Honored One.
I now repent before the Honored One, the Tathāgata, Aṅgulimāla, who has come here for our sake in his second birth.
Manifesting the form of a Buddha with supreme radiance that illumines all sentient beings, you are capable of preaching;
I repeatedly repent for my immeasurable transgressions.
Without support, you are the support; O Perfectly Awakened One, you act as a kinsman for those without kin or refuge.
How marvelous that two Buddhas have appeared in the world!
Such an unprecedented phenomenon proceeds in the world, like a lotus blooming within fire; it is rare for two Buddhas to be seen together in the world.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this sutra, the devas, nāgas, spirits, śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and King Prasenajit, along with the entire assembly, all admired the conduct of Aṅgulimāla and Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva;
they vowed to be born in that land and all gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. They leaped for joy and rejoiced.
The commentary states: Aṅgulimāla is a manifestation of the Tathāgata Sarvalokapriyadarśana-mahā-vīrya.
Furthermore, his mother, his teacher, and his teacher’s wife were all emanations of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
As for the nine hundred and ninety-nine people he killed, since no teaching of skillful means (upāya) was heard [at that time], these must have been actual killings.

If one then finds that [a person] is corrupting the state and harming the people in this world, obstructing the Way and causing alarm among the masses, such that killing them would certainly be beneficial, only then does one kill them.

Although it is called "killing," in reality, it is a "measuring" (of the situation). Why? Because there has never been anyone who possesses the power of the roots of goodness of universal benevolence.

To regard even ants as one’s own infants, yet recklessly kill them—by this we know that those who meet the blade and sever their fingers are none other than those who slay the thieves of affliction and discard the finger that points to the moon.

For instance, when Xianyu executed five hundred Brahmins, he consequently fell into hell; however, upon realizing his remorse and gaining reverent faith in the Mahāyāna, he attained rebirth in the Heaven of Joyful Transformation.
In the land of King Drumābharaṇa Buddha, they further obtain an extension of their kalpa-longevity;

it is not that he intends to grant them long life, but rather that he must firmly take away their short lifespan. It is not that he intends to reverse their right views, but rather that he must firmly punish their false views.
As for the Buddha’s demonstration of the precepts of perpetual youth (*kumārabhūta*), these all invert the names while expanding upon their meanings. Regarding their nature...
Regarding the gateway of unwholesome dharmas, he then expounds upon them with firm clarity, ensuring that all who hear them will contemplate their meaning upon encountering the names.
Furthermore, he secretly reveals the realms manifested by Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, and Great Beings, which are truly beyond the reach of thought or speculation.
Regarding the second [case], the circumstances of King Ajātaśatru’s commission of grave evil, his subsequent remorse, and the extinction of his offenses, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"At that time, in the great city of Rājagṛha, King Ajātaśatru was by nature depraved and cruel, delighting in slaughter.

He possessed the four evils of speech—slander, harsh words, lying, and frivolous talk—and was gripped by greed, hatred, and delusion. His mind burned with passion; he perceived only the present and did not see [the future]."

In the future, he will have only evil people as his retinue. Because of his greedy attachment to the pleasures of the five desires of the present life, he will perversely commit the crime of regicide against his father, the King, though he was innocent.
Having killed his father, remorse and fever will arise in his heart. He will cease to wear his various necklaces and ornaments, nor will he enjoy music or entertainment.
Because of this mental remorse and fever, sores will break out over his entire body; these sores will be foul-smelling and filthy, making him impossible to approach. Thereupon, he himself...
He thought to himself, "This body of mine has already received its flower-retribution; the fruit-retribution of hell is now close at hand.
At that time, his mother, named Vaidehī, applied various medicinal ointments to it, but the ulcer only increased and did not subside.
The king then said to his mother, "Such an ulcer as this arises from the mind; it does not originate from the four great elements. If one were to say...
"It is impossible for there to be anyone among sentient beings capable of curing this.
At that time, a great physician named Jīvaka went to the king's presence and asked, "Great King, have you been able to sleep peacefully? The king then replied with a verse:
If one can forever sever all afflictions, And is not stained by attachment to the three realms, one attains peaceful sleep.
If one attains Great Nirvana, Expounding the most profound meaning, such a one is called a true Brahmin;
Only then does one attain peaceful sleep, With no evil karma remaining in the body.
With speech free from the four faults, And with a mind devoid of the net of doubt, One attains peaceful sleep;
body and mind are free from feverish distress. Abiding in a place of tranquility, One reaches unsurpassed bliss and attains peaceful sleep.
With a mind free from grasping and attachment, One remains far removed from all enemies.
"Always harmonious and free from contention, one may then attain peaceful sleep.
Thus, he spoke in total sixteen and a half verses in response to Jīvaka. He further said: "Jīvaka, my illness is now grave."
He rose up against the King of the True Dharma with evil and rebellious intent to do him harm. No physician, no excellent medicine, no incantation, and no skillful treatment could cure him.
Why was this? My father, the former king, governed the country according to the Dharma and was truly without fault;
yet he was treacherously harmed. Like a fish cast upon dry land, what joy could there be? Like a deer caught in a snare, he had not the slightest heart of happiness. Thus...
When it was asked, "How may one obtain peaceful sleep? Jīvaka replied to the king: "Excellent, excellent!
Although Your Majesty has committed a transgression, you have given rise to profound regret and harbor a sense of shame. Great King, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, always speak these words:"

There are two wholesome qualities (*śukladharma*) that can rescue sentient beings: first, a sense of shame (*hrī*); second, a sense of dread of blame (*apatrāpya*). One who possesses a sense of shame does not commit offenses themselves; one who possesses a sense of dread of blame does not instruct others to do so.
One with a sense of shame feels inward remorse; one with a sense of dread of blame discloses their faults to others. One with a sense of shame is ashamed before people.
To feel shame before the heavens is called *hrī* (moral dread) and *apatrāpya* (shame). Those who lack *hrī* and *apatrāpya* are not called humans; they are called animals.
Those who possess *hrī* and *apatrāpya* are able to revere their parents, teachers, and elders.

Because of the existence of *hrī* and *apatrāpya*, it is said that there are parents, brothers, sisters, and the elder statesman Jīvaka, who expounded various teachings for the King. If one is capable of feeling *hrī* and *apatrāpya*, then one can...

It extinguishes transgressions. Furthermore, it proclaims the various merits of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, which can give rise to all the goodness of sentient beings and extinguish all the evils of sentient beings.
If Your Majesty goes there to seek the Buddha’s repentance for your transgressions, they will be immediately eliminated.

At that time, the Great King replied: "Jīvaka, because the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is by nature already disciplined and gentle, he has attained a retinue that is likewise disciplined and gentle.
He is like a sandalwood forest, surrounded exclusively by sandalwood trees; the Tathāgata is pure."

All his retinue was likewise purified. He continued, saying: "Since I am now an utterly evil person, shrouded by evil karma, my body is foul and stinking, and I am bound for hell; how could I possibly go to where the Tathāgata is?
Even if I were to go there, I fear he would not deign to look upon me or engage me in conversation. Although you have exhorted me to go to the Buddha's presence, nevertheless—"
Today I deeply reproach myself and lament; I have no intention at all of departing.

At that time, although his father, King Bimbisāra, had encountered his son’s assassination, he had already attained the fruits of the Path by hearing the Buddha-dharma. He was also exhorted from the air to go to the Buddha’s dwelling and seek refuge through repentance.
Upon hearing the voice from the sky, the king’s heart was filled with terror, and his entire body trembled; his five limbs [were overcome].
Trembling like a plantain leaf, he looked up and replied, "Who are you? You do not manifest a physical form, yet there is only sound.
The voice from the void answered, "I am your father. You must now follow what Jīvaka has said. Upon hearing this, the king fainted and fell to the ground;
his bodily sores worsened, and their foul stench became twice as intense as before, such that even though he was treated with cooling medicinal ointments, they were of no avail.

The festering sores were filled with toxic heat; they only increased and did not diminish. At that time, the World-Honored One, the Greatly Compassionate Guide, for the sake of King Ajātaśatru, entered the Moon-Love Samādhi (*candrakānta-samādhi*).
Having entered this samādhi, he emitted a great radiance. This light was cool and refreshing, proceeding to illuminate the king’s body.
The sores on his body were immediately healed, and the burning heat was extinguished. When the king realized his sores had healed and his body was cool and refreshed, he spoke to the Elder...
Jīvaka said, "I have heard it said that when the kalpa is about to end, three moons will appear simultaneously.
At that time, the sufferings and afflictions of all sentient beings will be entirely removed. Since that time has not yet arrived, from where does this light come?
Jīvaka replied, "Great King, you should know that this is the light emitted by the God among Gods. The King asked, "By what causes and conditions did that God among Gods emit it?"
He emitted this radiance and replied, "Great King, this is an auspicious sign. It is intended to reach you;

because the King previously stated that there is no skilled physician in the world to treat both body and mind, he has emitted this light first to heal the King's body, and will subsequently attend to his mind."
The King said, "Jīvaka, does the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, also think of them? Jīvaka replied, "Suppose a man has seven sons.
Among these seven sons, if one son falls ill, the hearts of his parents do not fail to regard them with equal affection."
"However, his heart is especially inclined toward his sick son. Great King, the Tathāgata is likewise. Toward all sentient beings, he is not unequal;
yet his heart is particularly weighted toward those who have committed offenses.

His heart is filled with compassionate mindfulness for those who are heedless, while toward those who are not heedless, his heart is relaxed and equanimous (and so forth). The king asked again: 'What is called the Moon-Love Samādhi?'"
Jīvaka replied, “It is like the light of the moon, which causes all the *utpala* flowers to bloom and become radiant.
The Moon-Loving Samādhi (*candrakānta-samādhi*) is likewise; it causes the virtuous minds of sentient beings to bloom.
For this reason, it is called the Moon-Loving Samādhi. Thus, five similes were spoken to illustrate five meanings. The King said, “I have heard that the Tathāgata...”
He does not dwell, sit, or rise together with evil people, nor does he converse or laugh with them;

he is like the great ocean that does not harbor a corpse, like the ruddy sheldrake that does not dwell in a latrine, or like Śakra-devānām-indra who does not reside with ghosts, or like the *kūṭa-rāja* bird that does not roost in a withered tree.
The Tathāgata is likewise. How may I go to see him? Even if I were to see him...
"I see that I am about to sink into the earth," [the King] said.

Jīvaka replied, "Great King, it is like a thirsty person hastening toward a clear spring, a hungry man seeking food, one in fear seeking rescue, a sick person seeking a skilled physician, one in heat seeking cool shade, or a cold person seeking fire.
Your Majesty’s current seeking of the Buddha should be just like this. Great King, the Tathāgata still acts for the sake of even those such as the icchantikas."
He expounded the essential points of the Dharma. How much more so, Great King, as you are certainly not an icchantika. Thus he exhorted him with these words on many occasions.
The King said to Jīvaka, "If it is indeed as the Tathāgata has stated, then tomorrow I shall select an auspicious day and a favorable moment."
Only then did he set out. Jīva addressed the King: "Great King, within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, there is no selection of auspicious days or favorable moments.
Great King, even a person with a grave illness does not examine the day; they seek only a skilled physician. Your Majesty’s illness is now grave."
One seeks the Buddha, the Physician of Men; one should not select auspicious or inauspicious days. If one reaches the presence of the Buddha, all sins shall be extinguished.
I only pray that Your Majesty will go there with haste this very day. Thereupon, the Great King immediately commanded his ministers to quickly prepare offerings.
Accompanied by his consort, he prepared twelve thousand carriages and proceeded along the road with his retinue of ministers and subjects, whose number was immeasurable.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"For all sentient beings, no cause or condition for the unsurpassed bodhi is more proximate than a virtuous friend. Why is this? If King Ajātaśatru had not followed the Elder..."
Regarding the words of Pāṭaliputra: "On the seventh day of the coming month, you will certainly meet your end and fall into the Avīci Hell.

Therefore, as for proximate causes, none is equal to a virtuous friend. Furthermore, King Ajātaśatru heard on the road ahead that King Vairūḍaka of Śrāvastī had encountered fire while traveling by ship at sea and died;
and that the bhikṣu Kokālika had entered the earth alive and reached the Avīci Hell.
Sunaḥkṣatra immediately encountered various evils, but upon reaching the presence of the Buddha, his manifold sins were extinguished.
Having heard these words, he said to Jīvaka: "Although I have now heard these two accounts, I am still not yet certain. Come here, Jīvaka!"
"I wish to ride upon the same elephant as you. Should I fall into the Avīci Hell, I hope that you will hold me fast so that I do not fall.
Why is this? For I have heard in the past that those who have attained the Way do not enter hell."
Then the Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying: "King Ajātaśatru still harbors doubts; I shall now act to bring him a mind of certainty.
At that time, the Great King went to the space between the twin śāla trees and approached the place where the Buddha was.
He gazed up at the Tathāgata, whose thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics were like a mountain of exquisite, pure gold. At that moment—

The World-Honored One emitted eight kinds of sounds and addressed him, saying, "Great King. At that time, Ajātaśatru looked around at his left and right and thought, "In this great assembly, who is the Great King?
Since I am both a transgressor and devoid of merit, the Tathāgata should not address me as 'Great King.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata again called out, "Great King Ajātaśatru! When the king heard this, his mind...
Filled with great joy, he immediately spoke these words: "The Tathāgata today has looked upon me and addressed me;
I now truly know that the Tathāgata’s great compassion and pity for all sentient beings is equal and without distinction. He said to the World-Honored One, "I now have no lingering doubts whatsoever;
I know for certain that the Tathāgata is truly the unsurpassed Great Teacher of all sentient beings. At that time, Ajātaśatru...
The king immediately took up banners, parasols, flowers, incense, and music to make offerings.

He approached and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed his salutations, withdrew to sit to one side. At that time, the Buddha addressed King Ajātaśatru, saying: "Great King!"
I shall now explain for you the essential points of the True Dharma. You should listen with single-minded attention.
An ordinary person should always bind the mind and contemplate that this body possesses twenty matters. Namely: (1) within this body of mine, it is empty and devoid of outflows;
(2) it lacks all roots of goodness; (3) I have not yet attained mastery over this cycle of birth and death; (4) I fall into a deep pit without doubt or fear.
(4) By what skillful means can one perceive the Buddha-nature? (5) How does one cultivate meditative concentration to perceive the Buddha-nature?

(6) Birth-and-death is constantly characterized by suffering, impermanence, non-self, and impurity. (7) Among the eight difficulties, it is difficult to escape these hardships. (8) One is perpetually pursued by enemies.
(9) There is not a single dharma capable of obstructing the various realms of existence. (10) Within the three evil destinies, [one has not yet...]
(11) Attaining liberation. (12) Being fully possessed of various evil and heterodox views. (13) Furthermore, never having created the means to cross over the five evil torrents.
(14) Birth and death being without limit, one has not yet reached their end. (15) Not performing various karmas, yet not retreating from their retribution.
(16) There is no such thing as "I" performing an action while another receives the fruit. (17) Not creating the causes of happiness, there will ultimately be no fruit of happiness. If there is...
The fruits of the karma one creates are never lost. (18) One is born because of ignorance, and likewise dies because of it.
(19) In the future and the present, one constantly practices heedlessness. (20) Great King, an ordinary person should constantly perform these twenty kinds of contemplations regarding this body.
Having performed these contemplations, one will take no pleasure in birth and death. By taking no pleasure in birth and death, one attains śamatha and vipaśyanā. Thus it is said.
Ajātaśatru said: "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, from the past until now, I have never before contemplated these twenty matters;
therefore, I committed various evils. Because I committed various evils, there arose the fear of death and the fear of the three evil realms.
World-Honored One, I have brought calamity upon myself by committing this grave evil: my father king was innocent, yet I have perversely harmed him."
"Regarding these twenty matters, whether one contemplates them or not, one will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell. The Buddha told the Great King:
"The nature and characteristics of all dharmas are impermanent; there is no fixed certainty. Why, O King, do you say that one will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell?
King Ajātaśatru addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if all dharmas have no fixed characteristics,"
"The sin of my killing should likewise be indeterminate. If killing were determinate, then all dharmas would not be indeterminate.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach that all dharmas are entirely without determinate characteristics.
Since you, O King, can further understand that killing is also indeterminate, you should know that killing has no determinate characteristic. Thus he spoke in various ways for his sake.
"Form-dharmas are fundamentally empty; there is no place where one can be killed. ... [The text] continues:
"Great King, all the sinful karma of sentient beings is of two kinds: first, light; second, heavy. If it is committed by mind and speech, it is called light.
If it is committed by body, speech, and mind, it is called heavy. Great King, as for the retribution obtained when one thinks in the mind and speaks with the mouth, but does not act with the body..."
"It was light. Great King, in the past you did not issue an oral command to kill; you merely said to 'trim the feet.
Great King, in former times King Bimbisāra harbored an evil intent while wandering for the hunt on Mount Vipula; he traversed the entire wilderness but obtained nothing at all."
He saw only a single seer, fully endowed with the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*). Upon seeing him, he immediately gave rise to a mind of anger and malice, thinking:
"It is precisely because of this seer that my hunting today has been unsuccessful. Drive him away! He then commanded his attendants to kill him.
As that man was approaching death, he gave rise to a mind of anger and malice. He lost his supernormal powers and made this vow:
"I am truly innocent, yet you have wantonly subjected me to slaughter through your mind and speech. In a future life, I shall likewise harm you with my mind and speech.
When the king heard this, he immediately felt remorse and made offerings to the corpse. Such was the conduct of former kings.
"Even such a person would receive only a light retribution and not fall into hell; how much less so for Your Majesty? How could You possibly have to undergo the fruit of retribution in hell?
What the former king himself committed, he alone must return to experience. How, then, can you, O King, be made to incur the sin of murder? (And so forth.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, following the Buddha's instructions, contemplated form and so on, up to and including consciousness. Having performed this contemplation, he immediately addressed the Buddha:
The Buddha said, “World-Honored One, it is only now that I have come to know that form is impermanent, and so on, up to consciousness being impermanent.

World-Honored One, had I been able to know this from the beginning, I would not have committed these offenses. World-Honored One, I have seen in the world that from the seed of an *eranda* tree grows an *eranda* tree;
I have never seen an *eranda* tree grow from a sandalwood tree. Now, for the first time, I see [that] from the seed of an *eranda* tree [grows a sandalwood tree].”
The sandalwood tree and the eranda tree were my own body. The sandalwood tree was my rootless faith in the mind.
This "rootless faith" means that at first I did not know how to revere the Tathāgata, nor did I have faith in the Dharma or the Saṅgha;
this is what is called "rootless. World-Honored One, had I not encountered the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas...

Kalpas ago, I underwent immeasurable suffering in the great hells. Now that I have seen the Buddha, by means of the merit obtained from this sight of the Buddha, may I destroy all afflictions and evil minds of sentient beings. The Buddha said, "Great King, excellent, excellent!
I now know your mind; you are able to destroy the evils of sentient beings. "World-Honored One, if I am truly able to destroy [the evils] of sentient beings..."

"May those who give rise to evil thoughts cause me to remain constantly in hell for immeasurable kalpas, undergoing great suffering and affliction for the sake of all sentient beings, yet not regarding it as suffering.
At that time, immeasurable people of the kingdom of Magadha all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because these immeasurable people had thus resolved their great minds, [the Buddha’s lifespan was extended].
The grave sins of King Ajātaśatru were immediately rendered slight. At that time, King Ajātaśatru said to Jīvaka:
"Though I am not yet dead, I have already attained a celestial body; I have cast off a short life and obtained a long life, and I have cast off an impermanent body and obtained an eternal body.
May all sentient beings likewise resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
The mind is itself the celestial body, the long-lived and eternal body; it is the disciple of all Buddhas.
Having spoken these words, he immediately made offerings to the Buddha with various jeweled banners, flags, canopies, incense, flowers, necklaces, and exquisite music.
He further praised him with verses, as described at length in the sutra.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised King Ajātaśatru, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
If there is anyone who can resolve to attain bodhicitta, you should know that such a person adorns the great assembly of all Buddhas.
Great King, in the past, you already first resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi before Vipaśyin Buddha; from that time until now—"
Since my appearance in the world, I have never fallen into hell to undergo suffering during that interval.
Great King, you should know that the bodhicitta yields such immeasurable rewards. Great King, from this day forward, you should diligently cultivate the bodhicitta.
Why is this? Because through these causes and conditions, one shall eliminate immeasurable evils. At that time...
King Ajātaśatru and the people of the kingdom of Magadha rose from their seats, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and took their leave to return to the palace.
The commentary states:
King Ajātaśatru followed the evil counsel of his friend Devadatta; he murdered his father to establish himself, and furthermore desired to...
To harm one’s mother is the ultimate extreme of cultivated evil, and such cultivated evil inevitably leads to rebirth in hell.

That you have now been spared from the suffering of falling into hell is due to four causes and conditions: first, having deep remorse; second, encountering virtuous friends; third, meeting the Buddha;
and fourth, hearing the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra. By means of this, you have realized that cultivated evil is identical to inherent evil.
The inherent evil of nature is interfused and harmonious; there is no dharma that does not tend toward it.

Spontaneously encompassing and attaining the inherent goodness of the Buddha-realm, one thus gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and acquires rootless faith. What is meant by "rootless faith"?
It is like the seed of the *eranda* tree producing sandalwood. The *eranda* is an object of extreme stench, yet its seed is fit to produce sandalwood from within that extreme stench.
From the tree of stench, there now emerges upon the *eranda* seed the sandalwood tree of supreme fragrance.
Is this not the realization that evil is precisely the nature of evil? Its nature is interfused; does it not spontaneously encompass the Buddha-realm and the virtuous nature of sandalwood?
The Dharma may be sought through analogies; from this it can be understood.
The guest said: "At first, I was indeed so inclined. Habituated to what I had constantly heard, I mistakenly took the cultivation of evil in the human realm to be the nature of evil."
Furthermore, it was not known that "inherently evil nature" (*xing-è*) is but another name for Buddha-nature (*foxing*).

Consequently, upon first hearing the term "inherently evil nature" from the Tiantai teachings, one’s ears were startled and the heart was alarmed, giving rise to all manner of doubts and difficulties.

Now, having received instruction through many methods of exposition, I finally understand that the expression "cultivated evil" (*xiu-è*) encompasses a vast range, extending downward to the hells and upward to Bodhisattvas; whereas the expression "cultivated good" (*xiu-shan*) is what it subsumes.
It expands gradually from the human and celestial realms to culminate in Buddhahood. As for the ultimate limit of inherent goodness, it resides solely in the Buddha;

as for the inherent evil possessed by nature, it pervades all nine realms. Although one speaks of good and evil, they are in fact non-differentiated yet differentiated, and differentiated yet non-differentiated.
Thus, the principles of inherent goodness and inherent evil are mutually integrated. This means that the inherent evil of the nine realms is omnipresent.
This is because the nature of the Buddha-realm is inherently and universally pervasive. Thus, the ninefold dharma-realm arises from inherent evil to produce cultivated evil.
Whether they be bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, devas, humans, asuras, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals.

All bodies as the fruit of retribution, and all lands as the environment of support—from the heavens above to the earth below, including rivers, nations, grasses, shrubs, humans, and animals—all are products of cultivated evil (*xiū-è*).
There is nothing that does not arise from the omnipresence of inherent evil (*xìng-è*).
Thus, where cultivated evil pervades, inherent evil pervades; there is nothing that is not entirely water, which constitutes water, and yet returns to ice.
It is precisely water. Taking the entirety of waves as water, one sees that water inherently possesses waves. Taking the entirety of space to pour into a vessel, every vessel is entirely empty.
Extending this to the entirety of springtime, all things are brought forth, yet every single thing is spring itself.

Thus, within the midst of daily life and at the moment of seeing and hearing, in every head and every object, in every matter and every mind, there is nothing that is not the cultivation of evil. It is precisely this.

This is the inherent evil of nature. When this inherent evil is harmonized and integrated, it spontaneously encompasses the inherent goodness of the Buddha-realm without the need for any shifting or turning.
By clarifying this mind, one perceives this nature: when it is in humans, it is simply human—this may be called being a "straightforward person.

When it is in devas, it is simply a deva—this may be called being a "righteous deva. When it is in śrāvakas, it is simply a śrāvaka; by means of the sound of the Buddha-way, it causes all beings [to awaken].
If one hears [the Dharma], it may be called a true Śrāvaka. If one abides as an Arhat, then one is an Arhat;
one should universally receive offerings therein, and it may be called a true Arhat. If one abides as a Bodhisattva, then one is a Bodhisattva;
filling the mind with the six perfections and myriad practices, striving to bring awakening and conduct to fulfillment—it may be called a true Bodhisattva. As for... [descending]...

Taking on the forms of the evil realms is the skillful work of a Bodhisattva’s great transformative power (*mahopāya*). When the future fruit is realized, these are established in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*);
none of them fall outside that nature. For now, one must strive to take this very cultivation of evil as the very nature of evil, making it one's own personal practice.

If heaven were to fully manifest its nature of evil and give rise to wondrous function, using supernatural powers to startle and move others, and employing wisdom and eloquence to proclaim [the truth]—[this would be the case].
I proclaim what is called the Dharma-gate of the inherent evil of nature (*prakṛti-pāpa*). Although my disciples possess this intention, they have not yet reached its core.

For now, let them first give rise to empty vows, taking this treatise as their guide to expound it for others and carve it for circulation, so that every person may awaken to their own nature and each know their place of return.
It is my hope that they will dedicate this profound mind to serve all lands as numerous as motes of dust.
This is what is called repaying the kindness of one's teacher. [The disciples] joined their palms in *añjali*, gazed up with reverence, and withdrew.
Volume Six of the *Treatise on the Nature of Good and Evil*, carved for circulation by the assembly of disciples who received the precepts at Yutang Temple in Yongjia County, is hereby completed.
